Lunar Elevation & Fission

7. The Poles

Why the Poles Are Crowded
Parts A–E
Zohar Duran
Independent researcher, Ramla, Israel
ORCID https://orcid.org/0009-0005-3194-9387

The Moon's poles carry more craters than its equator. The count is made in the Robbins catalogue with the maria and South Pole–Aitken removed on both sides. On that clean count, the density of craters of 20 km and more within 30° caps about each pole is 1.20 ± 0.05 times that of the equatorial belt.

HTMLPDFCode and data
Abstract

Crater density analysis: polar caps versus the equatorial belt

According to the Robbins catalogue data, a significant difference is recorded in the density of craters 20 km in diameter and larger between the polar regions and the equatorial belt of the Moon. In the raw count, the polar caps (within 30° of each pole) show a density of 219 craters per million km², while the equatorial belt shows a density of 166 craters per million km², giving a density ratio of 1.32. For craters 40 km in diameter and larger, this ratio rises to 1.51.

The raw count is affected by a structural bias, since most of the maria and basalt plains – characterised by young, crater-poor floors – are concentrated in the equatorial region. To make a neutral comparison between ancient surfaces only, a "clean count" procedure is applied, in which the areas of the maria and of the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin are removed from the calculation on both sides.

In the clean count, a density ratio of 1.20±0.05 in favour of the poles is established for all craters larger than 20 km in diameter. This ratio shows a rising trend as a function of crater diameter, as detailed in the following table:

Crater diameter range (km)Density ratio (poles vs. equator)

Dynamic mechanism: the model of flattening, corotation and rounding of the young Moon

The geophysical hypothesis presented here rejects the assumption that the craters were formed by a uniform fall of asteroids or of returning terrestrial material (as proposed in Paper 6), since a uniform fall cannot produce a bipolar density concentration along a single symmetric axis. The present pattern is explained through the morphological evolution of the young Moon during the stages of its separation from the Earth:

1. Stage of gathering and initial flattening: A low-density sialic mass of about 1,300 kg/m³ consolidated at the tip of a pear-like structure, began to move outward and flattened on an initial base 6,000 km wide.

2. Expansion toward the corotation line: As the mass moved outward, its base narrowed to a width of 3,000 km. The body remained rotationally locked with the Earth at a period of about 5.5 hours. Near the corotation line – the dynamic distance at which the rotational velocity equalled the free orbital velocity – the body was subject to two opposing stress vectors: the Earth's gravity pulled inward (on the near side), and the centrifugal force pulled outward.

3. Triaxial geometry and stretched volume: Under these stresses the body took on a flattened and stretched triaxial shape (axis ratio of roughly 1.8 : 1.4 : 1), defined as long toward the Earth, intermediate along the rotational path, and short along the polar axis. In this inflated stage the density of the body stood at about 1,700 kg/m³. Most of the large craters formed near the peak of this stage, as a result of material that was ejected and returned.

4. Release at peak flattening, and rounding after the release: The Moon was released from the Earth about 210 km beyond the corotation line at the peak of its flattening, reached at that moment: inflated (about 1,700 kg/m³) and flattened (about 1.8 : 1.4 : 1), held by its rigid outer shell. After the release, as the Moon receded beyond the corotation line, the stretching that had held the flattening – between the Earth's gravity and the point of attachment on the near side, and the centrifugal pull outward – disappeared, and the Moon's rotation slowed, lowering the outward centrifugal push; with no force left to hold it, the flattening decayed, the body rounded with a self-driven decrease in volume, and its density rose toward 2,600 kg/m³ and beyond. The crowding of the polar surface took place in this decay of flattening, and stopped when the imperfectly round shape of today froze.

This geometric transition from a highly flattened body to a spherical body caused the surface to contract, which led to a mechanical crowding of the existing craters. The degree of crowding was maximal at the poles and minimal at the equator. Ancient craters that formed close to peak flattening underwent the maximum contraction and crowding (1.53), whereas later craters, formed when the body was already close to its spherical shape, were hardly crowded at all (1.09).

Empirical tests and statistical findings (Part D)

The following is a summary of the four main tests carried out in Part D to examine the validity of the contraction and rounding model:

Test numberDefinition of the scientific testEmpirical findings and numerical valuesOverall status
1Pole/equator density ratio in the clean countA ratio of 1.20±0.05 for all craters (≥20 km). Rising from 1.09 to 1.53 with diameter.Passed (consistent with the formation-order prediction).
2Change in crater diameterThe craters kept their original morphology and size on a rigid crust. The polar median is 1.06 times the equatorial median (confidence interval: 1.01–1.12).Passed (confirms a richness of large craters at the poles).
3Distribution of young (post-rounding) cratersRatio values of 0.92 and 1.12 were measured in two independent samples.Consistent (awaiting an enlarged dating sample; no significant evidence of an excess).
4Symmetry between the two polesAfter removing the SPA basin, 300 craters per million km² were counted at one pole versus 305 craters per million km² at the opposite pole.Passed (difference within the counting error).

In addition, five complementary morphometric tests were carried out (examining the largest craters per equal area, the shape of the size distribution, a comparison of ancient versus fresh craters, the degree of ellipticity, and the structural transition from simple to complex craters), designed to check whether the craters themselves physically shrank together with the surface. Four tests established unequivocally that crater diameter was preserved, and not a single test showed signs of shrinkage of the craters themselves, a finding that confirms the craters were carried as rigid, intact elements on the contracting crust.

External rotational differentiation. We propose that the high crater density at the lunar poles is the record of a single process during the attachment to the Earth. As the pear grew, the body flattened, the outer shell at the poles was stretched and thinned, and material landed on the lunar surface in a uniform distribution. When the body rounded, the polar surface contracted toward the pole centres and the craters were crowded together. The same process left a thin, compacted crust beneath the poles, which is measured today (C.8, D.6).

What this paper proposes

Summary of the scientific proposal: the model of structural deformation and rounding of the young Moon

The paper proposes a geophysical and dynamic mechanism that explains the excess of craters at the Moon's poles compared with its equator. According to the model, the varying crater density is not the result of non-uniform impact, but of a mechanical contraction of the lunar crust during the transition from a highly flattened triaxial body to a rigid spherical body.

1. The central claim: the morphological evolution of the Moon

  • Stage of maximum flattening: The young Moon moved outward on the tip of a pear-like structure, while remaining rotationally locked with the Earth (a period of about 5.5 hours). Near the corotation line (a base width of about 3,000 km), a balance of opposing stresses acted on it: the Earth's gravity pulled the near side inward, and the centrifugal pull drew it outward. Under these stresses the body was stretched into a highly flattened triaxial shape (axis ratio of roughly 1.8:1.4:1) and was in an inflated state with a low density of about 1,700 kg/m³. The craters formed uniformly on this flattened shape.
  • Release and the decay of flattening: The Moon was released about 210 km beyond the corotation line at the peak of its flattening, reached at that moment, held by its rigid outer shell. After the release the stretching that held the flattening disappeared, and the Moon's rotation slowed as it receded (about 14 hours at 30,000 km); the flattening decayed, the body rounded, became smaller and denser, and the polar surface crowded. The crowding stopped when the shape froze, leaving today's small fossil flattening.
  • The crater-crowding mechanism: The geometric transition from a flattened body to a sphere caused the surface to contract in a highly non-uniform way – the mechanical crowding and contraction of the surface were maximal in the polar regions and minimal in the equatorial belt, which raised the density of the existing craters at the poles.
  • External rotational differentiation (the key statement): We propose that the high crater density at the lunar poles is the outcome of a single process in two stages. While the young Moon was attached to the Earth and rotating with it at the rate dictated by the Earth, the body flattened as the pear grew and the material at its tip consolidated: the light material of the outer shell flowed gradually from the poles to the equator, and heavier material from beneath rose at the poles and made room for it. The polar shell remained thin through the long build-up of flattening, tens of millions of years, and during this time material landed on the lunar surface in a uniform distribution. The flattening reached its peak at the moment of release. After the release, as the stretching that held it disappeared and its rotation slowed with recession, the flattening decayed: the heavier material sank back to the depths it had come from, the polar surface contracted toward the pole centres, and the craters were compressed into a smaller area. The build-up of flattening draws material out of the poles, the decay of flattening returns what was drawn out, and the crater record above responds with a corresponding density. The crater density at the poles, and the thin, compacted crust beneath them, are the record that the process left behind (C.8, D.6).

2. The numerical measures and the scientific predictions

  • Reading the shape from the crater record: Counting the craters (in the diameter range ≥20 km) around the six ends of the body's three axes reconstructs a structural shape of 1.37:1.15:1. A theoretical rounding of this shape predicts a clean density ratio of 1.21 between the poles and the equator, a value that matches closely the measured empirical ratio (1.19), without any parameter tuning.
  • Range of predictions by formation order: The model does not predict a single fixed value, but a range of values that depends on the timing of crater formation relative to peak flattening:
    • Craters formed at peak flattening (large craters): underwent the maximum contraction (rounding from a shape of 1.8:1.4:1), and therefore a density ratio of about 1.5 in favour of the poles is predicted for them.
    • Craters formed early in the build-up of flattening: formed on a body that was still only slightly flattened (a shape of about 1.20); they were stretched apart with the surface as the flattening grew and compressed back in the decay, and keep only the net contraction, and therefore a density ratio of about 1.17–1.2 is predicted for them.
    • Young craters (later impacts from space): formed long after the shape froze, on a body whose shape no longer changed, and therefore their density ratio is 1.0 (no polar excess).
  • Agreement with the empirical data (the clean count): Removing the maria and the SPA basin (30° caps versus the equatorial belt ∣ϕ∣<15∘) gives an overall ratio of 1.20±0.05 for craters of diameter ≥20 km, showing a consistent and clear rise as crater diameter increases (a finding confirming that the large craters are the most ancient, formed close to the peak):

  • Independent density checks: The shape of the Moon at peak flattening (b/c≈1.4) matches precisely the Maclaurin spheroid, which represents the equilibrium of a uniform fluid rotating with a period of 5.5 hours for a body with a density of 1,600–1,750 kg/m³. To allow the ends of the Earth-facing axis to contract during rounding, the physics dictates that the peak density must be lower than 1,800 kg/m³.

Chronology of events and the crater-formation window

The geodynamic model defines an overall timeline of about 600 million years from the start of the formation of the original bulge to the release (dated to 3.873 billion years before present), followed by a short post-release decay of flattening. Together they form the morphogenetic window of the craters in this paper:

  • Initial pear stage (about 400 million years): the uplift of the sialic mass on the extension of the Earth's material and the growth of the bulge.
  • Dynamic flattening stage (about 200 million years): the build-up of flattening, which reached its peak at the release; the polar shell is thin and craters form on the flattened body in a uniform distribution.
  • Decay of flattening after the release (short, set by the rate of recession): the stretching that held the flattening disappears and the rotation of the released Moon slows; the body rounds and compacts, and the polar surface crowds; the stage ends when the shape froze, near 16 Earth radii.

Basic definitions and mechanical measures for reading the table

  • Tidal axis a: the spatial axis running along the symmetric line that directly connects the forming Moon with the centre of the Earth.
  • Motion axis b: the axis perpendicular to the tidal axis, directed along the body's orbital velocity vector.
  • Polar axis c: the geographic axis perpendicular to the plane of the system, connecting the poles (the shortest axis during flattening).
  • "Holds itself together": the mechanical ability of the body to maintain integrity and a closed geometric shape within the equations of a fluid body, under the influence of self-gravity and structural strength (it does not mean neutralising the external tidal forces).
  • "Detachment": physical separation and full mechanical opening of the contact layer and interface between the Moon and the pear material of the Earth.
  • Physical confirmation of the peak density (≈1,700 kg/m3): this value is supported by two independent dynamic checks:
    1. The rotational flattening of the body (b/c≈1.4) matches mathematically the exact equilibrium shape of a Maclaurin spheroid for a homogeneous fluid rotating with a period of 5.5 hours at a density of 1,600–1,750 kg/m3.
    2. The upper mechanical limit for the contraction of the tidal-axis ends during rounding physically requires a peak density lower than 1,800 kg/m3.
  • The rigid Roche limit (10,314 and 12,994 km): computed from the structural equation 1.26R⊕​(ρ⊕​/ρ)1/3. A lighter body (1,300 kg/m3) has a weaker self-gravitational hold, and therefore its Roche limit lies farther from the source (12,994 km) – where it first succeeds in stabilising an independent shape while still attached.

The free-fluid stability criterion (the k measure)

The mechanical stretching is assessed using the system measure:

k=ρr3ME​​
  • Fluid stability threshold: set at k<0.09. When the value of the measure is below this threshold, a free fluid body can maintain a closed, stable shape without breaking apart under the Earth's tidal forces (ME​).
  • Parametric sensitivity: Since the orbital distance (r) appears to the third power, the value of the measure k falls rapidly as the body recedes. Conversely, since the density (ρ) is in the denominator, a body of higher density will bring the value of k below the critical threshold earlier and closer to the source. A free fluid body at the release density (about 1,700) would require a distance of about 23,200 km to reach stability – a distance not reached at release, and hence the structure held together thanks to its rigid shell alone until it receded and compacted.

Introduction — the question and how it is tested

1. Research methodology: definition of the counting regions and the empirical measures

To carry out the morphometric comparison and to prevent biases arising from incomplete identification of small craters, a firm minimum threshold is set for the diameter of the counted craters. The data are based on the Robbins catalogue (2019) and are analysed by the following geometric units:

  • Normalised density measure: defined as the total number of craters in a given region divided by its static area. The measure is expressed in craters per million km², and thus allows a neutral comparison between area cells of different geometric dimensions.
  • The polar caps: two geometric caps of equal area, defined by an angular radius of 30∘ from the Moon's centre around the rotation poles (perpendicular to the equatorial plane).
    • The northern cap: extends from latitude 60∘ N to 90∘ N.
    • The southern cap: extends from latitude 60∘ S to 90∘ S.
  • The equatorial belt: a global band defined by the latitude range between 15∘ S and 15∘ N.
  • Spatial assignment: each crater is catalogued and assigned to the relevant counting region according to the coordinates of its geometric centre point.

2. Findings of the raw count versus the clean-count procedure

The initial empirical count shows a significant density excess in the polar regions, which becomes more pronounced as the diameter of the examined craters increases. However, geological analysis shows that the raw count suffers from severe structural biases that require mathematical correction:

  • The equatorial-belt bias (maria and basalt plains): The basalt and maria areas (the LROC feeding system) are young floors on which the ancient craters were melted or covered by thermal activity and by crust melted by the Earth's heat. These areas make up 22% of the equatorial belt but only 1% of the polar caps. Including them in the raw count artificially lowers the equatorial density and inflates the pole/equator ratio.
  • The polar-cap bias (the South Pole–Aitken basin): The SPA basin physically erased the craters at its centre. Since 24% of the area of the polar caps (mainly in the south) lies inside the basin, including it makes the poles look emptier than they really are and lowers the ratio.
  • The clean-count procedure: removing the areas of the maria and the SPA basin from both sides of the equation uniformly. This is the only procedure that allows ancient surfaces (Highlands) to be compared with ancient surfaces, and from it is derived the firm system ratio on which the study rests: 1.20±0.05.

3. The dynamic starting assumption and the mechanical contraction mechanism

  • The assumption of uniform material distribution: Within the LEF model (Paper 6), the ancient crater population was created by the landing of returning terrestrial material on the crust while it was still spread as a bulge above the parent body (the Earth). For the purpose of the analysis, a working assumption is set of a completely uniform distribution of material per unit area. This assumption neutralises the question of source asymmetry: any non-uniformity in density seen on the surface today must stem from later mechanical processes that acted on the crust that carried the craters.
  • Rejection of alternative hypotheses: In the course of the study, six different physical mechanisms were examined as possible explanations for the density difference; all six explanations were rejected and set aside.
  • The seventh explanation (rounding and volume decrease): The young Moon behaved physically as a flattened, squashed body (like a balloon pressed between hands that gradually loses volume). At peak flattening, owing to the symmetric rotational stresses around the rotation axis, the body was wide and flat at its ends and narrow at its equator. The craters were imprinted uniformly on this morphology.
  • Crowding of the poles: After the release, as the stretching that held it disappeared and the rotation slowed with recession, the flattening decayed and the body tended toward a spherical shape with a decrease in volume. In this geometric process, the flat, wide parts converged inward toward two small polar caps. Since the rotation axis passes through the poles and the flattening was symmetric around it, every meridian retreated toward the two end points, which the rotation never moved dynamically (C.3).
  • Morphometric preservation of the craters: The Moon's outer shell was rigid enough (C.7) to carry the craters as intact, isolated elements. The craters themselves kept their original diameter and size; it was the elastic surface between them that shrank and contracted (the surface closed by a quarter of the average area and by about half of the polar area), which brought a direct rise in the density measure in the polar regions compared with the equatorial region (where the surface converged the least).

1. Predictions of the geometric model and the differential crowding mechanism

The degree of mechanical crowding of the craters is not a direct function of chronological age alone, but a geometric record of the body's shape and dynamic flattening at the moment of crater formation. Since material was ejected and returned throughout all the stages of the transition, the level of structural deformation was preserved within the crustal morphology according to the following principles:

  • Formation at peak flattening: Craters that formed when the body was at the peak of triaxial deformation (1.8:1.4:1) were carried through the entire rounding sequence. As a result, they underwent the mechanical maximum of surface contraction, and today show a predicted density ratio of 1.49 in favour of the polar caps.
  • Formation early in the build-up of flattening: Craters that formed when the Moon was still only slightly flattened (a shape of about 1.20) were stretched apart with the surface as the flattening grew and compressed back in the decay; they keep only the net contraction, and therefore their predicted density ratio drops to 1.17.
  • Young craters (later impacts from space): Craters that formed long after the shape had frozen experience no surface contraction at all, and therefore their predicted ratio is 1.00 (a completely uniform distribution).
  • Correlation between crater diameter and timing of formation: Most of the largest craters formed near the peak of the stage of ejection and return of the terrestrial material. Therefore, the model consistently predicts that the density ratio will rise as crater diameter increases.

2. Empirical correlation: the model prediction versus the clean-count measures

The whole group (≥20 km) shows an almost complete match between the mechanical prediction of the six axes (1.21) and the finding on the surface (1.20±0.05). The largest crater class (100–300 km) carries a wide statistical uncertainty (±0.38) owing to a small sample.
  • Productivity of the method: The row-by-row pairing serves as a physical guide to reading the morphological trend, and is not a claim that each crater was assigned chronologically and exclusively to the specific stage.

3. Preservation of crater diameter on a contracting crust

One of the central questions in developing the geophysical model is: if the polar surface contracted mechanically during rounding, why did the craters themselves not contract with it (which would have taken them below the 20 km counting threshold and made the effect disappear)?

  • The isolated rigid-crust mechanism (C.7): Within the physical model, the craters kept their morphological integrity and their original diameter. They were carried as rigid elements on a solid upper crust, while the contraction of the surface was accomplished by the closing and narrowing of the elastic spaces between the craters. Therefore, the crater diameter measured today reflects precisely the original diameter at the moment of impact.
  • Mathematical evidence from the size distribution (D.2): Had the craters contracted physically together with the surface, the crowding effect would have become statistically invisible at any fixed counting threshold. The rise in the number of craters per unit area would have been entirely neutralised by the drop in diameter of the borderline craters below the 20 km threshold (the two opposite effects in the size distribution of lunar craters cancel each other under homogeneous contraction). The very existence of the significant measured excess (1.20) is direct empirical proof that the craters kept their original size.

4. Structure and order of the parts of the paper

The remainder of the scientific analysis in the paper is organised in the following firm structure:

  • Part A (the empirical observation): presentation of the full count data by latitude, by longitude, within the polar caps and around the six geometric axes of the body (in both the raw and the clean versions).
  • Part B (rejection of alternative hypotheses): a detailed analysis of the six alternative scientific explanations that were examined and the mechanical reasons for their rejection.
  • Part C (the physical mechanism): the mathematical calculation of the differential area changes that accompany the transition from a flattened triaxial body to a perfect sphere.
  • Part D (the four structural tests): presentation of the results of the four statistical tests of the model's validity (density ratios, median diameters, young populations and polar symmetry).
  • Part E (summary and remainders): definition of the topics and open questions left for future research.
PART A

Part A — The empirical observation

Part A presents the raw empirical findings as they are counted on the surface, before applying any physical interpretation or formation models. The observation is based on a normalised count: the number of craters in each area cell is divided by the geometric area of that cell.

In this part, four independent counts are made on the same database and with the same methodology:

  • A.1 (latitudinal section): division of the Moon into latitude bands parallel to the equator, to examine the density difference between the poles and the equator.
  • A.2 (longitudinal section): division of the Moon into longitudinal segments from pole to pole, to examine the density difference between the different sides of the Moon (a separate and distinct pattern).
  • A.3 and A.4 (clean procedure): an exact repetition of sections A.1 and A.2 after removing young floors (maria, basalt plains) and large basins (SPA) and recalculating the remaining areas.
  • A.5 (summary of observations): a compilation of the four spatial tests and their conclusions.

A.1 Crater density by latitude (raw data)

The spatial analysis in this section is designed to determine whether there is a non-uniformity in crater density along the geographic latitude axes.

Methodological criteria and calibration of the count:

1. Completeness of the database (Robbins catalogue): The count is limited to craters with a fitted diameter of 20 km and larger. This limit is firm and guarantees full counting completeness at all latitudes: it neutralises optical biases (low illumination and long shadows at the poles that hide small craters) and filters out secondary craters (clusters and chains of debris smaller than 20 km in diameter, which would produce misleading local densities).

2. Control group and confirmation of the trend: A second series is made for craters 40 km in diameter and larger, to verify that the spatial pattern does not rest on the population of the smallest borderline craters.

3. No initial masks: The first count presents the surface as it is, without artificially omitting the maria, on the view that they form part of the structural prediction (the effect of removing them is analysed separately in Part A.3).

4. Calculation of differential geometric areas: The Moon is divided into 12 latitude bands of fixed width 15∘. The area of each band is computed by the spatial equation:

Area=2πR2(sinϕ2​−sinϕ1​)

where the adopted mean radius is R=1,737.4 km (IAU standard), and ϕ1​,ϕ2​ are the boundaries of the band.

According to this equation, the area of a band on a sphere is determined not by its angular width but by how far it extends along the polar axis (like the height of a label on a cylinder). Near the equator the band is tall along the axis, while near the poles the surface curves sharply and the circumference of the ring is small. As a result, the band areas vary considerably: the equatorial band (0−15∘) extends over 4.909 million km², while the polar band (75−90∘) extends over only 0.646 million km² (a ratio of about 7:1). This geometric difference requires the use of the density measure (craters per 10⁶ km²) rather than absolute numbers.

Analysis and conclusions from the spatial profile

Reading the density columns and the graphic profile yields the following main findings:

  • A firm bipolar upturn: Both ends of the table show the maximum density values in the system. The band adjacent to the north pole (75−90∘ N) reaches a peak density of about 300 craters per million km², a value 1.80 times that of the equator. The band adjacent to the south pole (75−90∘ S) stands at a density of 215, 1.29 times that of the equator.
  • The equatorial minimum zones: The most crater-poor rows lie north of the geographic equatorial belt, in the ranges 0−15∘ N and 15−30∘ N, with minimum density values of 155 and 151 respectively.
  • Sharpening of the trend at larger sizes: In the control group of craters of diameter ≥40 km, the bipolar density difference sharpens and shows extreme ratio values of 1.89 in the north and 1.54 in the south relative to the equatorial reference.
  • Mid-hemisphere asymmetry: The profile does not rise in a perfectly linear and smooth way from the equator to the poles. The southern hemisphere is richer in crater density than the northern hemisphere at mid-latitudes (a value of 230 in the 45−60∘ S sector versus 174 in the 45−60∘ N sector). The gradient rises and falls in different places, but the structural conclusion is firm: the end bands adjacent to both poles carry an exceptional density excess that no intermediate band reaches. Part of the low value at the centre stems from the concentration of maria at the equator, a factor treated and neutralised in section A.3.

A.2 Crater density by longitude (raw data)

Whereas section A.1 found a significant density excess in the polar regions, this section examines the uniformity of the spatial distribution in the perpendicular direction – along the Moon's global circumference. The aim of the analysis is to isolate and prevent a statistical mixing between the latitude effect (the central topic of the study) and potential asymmetries between different hemispheres along the longitude axes.

Methodological criteria and segment geometry:

1. Structure of the counting cells: The lunar surface was divided into 12 longitude bands (segments) of fixed width 30∘. Each band extends continuously from pole to pole and includes all latitudes (like a segment of an orange).

2. Built-in equality of areas: Unlike the latitude bands, all longitude segments on a sphere have exactly equal areas. This geometric form removes the need for correction factors or normalisation by cell size, and allows a direct comparison between the absolute crater numbers (the raw counts) and the density ratios.

3. Surface dimensions: The area of each band is computed exactly by:

A=124πR2​

For a radius of R=1,737.4 km, the area of each longitude segment is fixed at 3.161 million km² (1/12 of the total lunar surface).

4. The dynamic coordinate system: The band covering the sector 345∘−15∘ east contains the sub-Earth point (0∘ N,0∘ E) – the centre of the face permanently turned toward the Earth owing to tidal locking.

5. Definition of the orbital elements ("leading" vs. "trailing"): The terms are applied according to the accepted mechanical definitions:

    • The leading point: the apex of the Moon's orbital motion vector, located at (0∘,90∘ W). It faces forward in the direction of the orbit (the front of the body).
    • The trailing point: the point facing backward along the direction of orbital flight, located at (0∘,90∘ E).

6. Fixed normalisation base: The reference point (1.00) remains exactly the same as that set in section A.1 – the density of the full raw equatorial band (15∘ S−15∘ N). Its value is 166.436 craters per million km² for the ≥20 km group, and 53.170 for the ≥40 km group. Keeping this fixed base allows a direct and fair comparison between the four analysis tables of Part A (from A.1 to A.4).

Analysis and conclusions from the global longitudinal profile

Examining the measures and the graphic profile yields the following main findings:

  • Severe non-uniformity around the body's circumference: The lunar surface shows an extreme asymmetry along the meridians. The far side and the sectors surrounding the trailing meridian (90∘ E) show consistently high densities, ranging from 1.22 to 1.51 times the equatorial reference value in the ≥20 km group.
  • The global peak and minimum zones:
    • Maximum density: recorded in the eastern sector of the far side, in the range 105∘−135∘ east, with 793 craters and a density of 251 per million km² (a ratio of 1.51).
    • Minimum density: recorded on the western near side, in the range 315∘−345∘ east, with only 267 craters and a density of 84 per million km² (a ratio of 0.51).
  • Magnitude of the longitudinal pattern: The extreme variance ratio between the peak segment and the minimum segment stands at almost a factor of three (251/84=2.97 for the ≥20 km group, and 90/31=2.88 for the ≥40 km group). This difference is considerably higher than the raw density differences measured between the poles and the equator in section A.1. This finding confirms that this is an independent and entirely separate geographic pattern, which requires methodological isolation.
  • Geophysical and morphological context (the LEF model): The extreme minimum sector (315∘−345∘) hosts the Mare Imbrium basin. Within the LEF model, this structure acted as the main feeding and heat-conducting vent from the Earth into the lunar interior, and not as a site of ejection and throwing out of material. This sector, together with the extensive western maria concentrated in it, is characterised by crust that was melted and thermally reset, and therefore carries few craters today. Conversely, the prominent crater excess on the trailing side is read in the model through the distribution of returning ejecta that lagged behind the rotational velocity and landed behind (Paper 6).

A.3 Crater density by latitude after removing the basins and maria

Whereas sections A.1 and A.2 counted the global surface in full, this section applies a firm geological mask to remove area units whose crater record was affected by endogenic factors (thermal and volcanic activity and mechanical erasure) unrelated to geographic latitude.

Rationale for removing the geological units:

1. The system of maria and basalt plains (LROC mask): The mare floors represent young feeding vents above magmatic domes (Paper 5), in which the ancient craters were melted. The basalt plains (such as Procellarum, Tranquillitatis, Fecunditatis, Insularum, Frigoris) represent crust that was melted by the global heat radiated by the Earth, without a local feeding dome. In both cases, the lack of craters stems from a thermal reset of the record. Since these units are concentrated on the near side and at low latitudes, they artificially lower the equatorial density.

2. The large basins (≥500 km): these impact structures extend over large portions of the latitude bands (mainly in the polar regions). Their floors and rims have a distinct morphological history that independently affects the statistics of the band.

3. Aim of the procedure: to isolate the historically most stable crustal parts (Highlands), in which the record was preserved uniformly, in order to obtain a reliable measure of the original crater distribution.

Methodology for applying the geological mask

  • Definition of the mask: a combination of the LROC global mare polygons (LROC_GLOBAL_MARE_180) and the 20 largest basins with outer rim diameter ≥500 km from the Neumann et al. (2015) catalogue (Table 1).
  • Basin geometry: each basin is represented as a spherical cap centred on the source coordinates, with an angular radius of D/(2RMoon​).
  • Filtering rule and residual area: a crater is removed from the count if its geometric centre point falls within a basin or a mare polygon. Spatial overlaps are removed only once. The residual area is computed on a high-resolution global grid of 0.05∘×0.05∘ using exact spherical cell areas based on great-circle distance.
  • Keeping the reference point for comparison: to allow the eye to follow the movement of the bands, the static reference base of section A.1 is kept (value 1.00 = density of the full raw equatorial belt without a mask). Its value is 166.436 (for ≥20 km) and 53.170 (for ≥40 km).
  • Definition of the density-change measure (Δρ): a measure that compares each band with itself before and after the mask:
Δρ=(ρbefore​ρafter​​−1)×100%

A positive value indicates that the removed area was crater-poor relative to the rest of the band (and therefore its removal raised the residual density).

Analysis of the spatial effects and the built-in bias of the static base

Comparing the masked profile with the raw profile yields the following scientific insights:

1. Behaviour of the edge cases in the change column:

    • Zero polar change in the north (75−90∘ N): this band does not physically touch the mask (it contains no maria or large basins). Its area (0.646×106 km2) and its crater count (194) remained constant, and therefore Δρ=0.0%.
    • Maximum equatorial change in the north (15−30∘ N): this band loses more than half of its geometric area (a drop from 4.574 to 2.153 million km²) owing to the concentration of near-side maria. The residual density on what remains jumps by +48.4% for the 20 km group, and by +55.9% for the 40 km group (the sharpest rise in the system).

2. Robustness of the endogenous polar excess: Applying the mask significantly raises the low and middle latitudes (especially in the north), and thus flattens part of the spatial difference. However, the two bands adjacent to the poles remain the densest regions on the lunar body. In the ≥20 km group, the south pole reaches 305 and the north 300 per million km², while the 10 intermediate bands are lower (values of 202 to 246). In the ≥40 km group, the south pole leads the entire system with a peak value of 124 (a ratio of 2.32). This finding proves that the polar excess is not an artefact of the presence of maria at the equator; it is embedded in the solid ground itself.

3. Methodological clarification on a like-for-like comparison: The ratio column in this table divides a masked band (a numerator that has lost its maria) by a raw equator (a denominator that has kept them), and thus produces a mathematical exaggeration of the predicted excess (ratio values of 1.40–1.48). If the two masked polar caps (882 craters on 3.706 million km², giving a density of 238.0) are compared with the equatorial belt masked with exactly the same mask (1,216 craters on 5.856 million km², giving a density of 207.7), the true ratio value is 1.15. Therefore, for the final scientific test of the paper, the clean count of sections A.11 and D.1 is applied (simultaneous removal of the maria and the SPA basin from both sides), yielding the firm normalised ratio value: 1.20±0.05.

A.4 Crater density by longitude after removing the basins and maria

This section applies the firm geological mask (the 20 large Neumann basins and the LROC mare polygons) to the 12 longitude bands of section A.2. Its main aim is to determine which part of the extreme east–west asymmetry stems directly from the presence of the young maria and the basins, and which part is embedded in the ancient highland crust itself.

Area-calculation methodology and calibration of the system:

1. Loss of equal areas in the longitude bands: Unlike the raw count, in which all longitude segments are equal in size, applying the mask changes the band areas differentially. A band that held a large portion of maria or basins loses more area. The actual residual areas now range widely, between 1.073 and 2.729 million km², which requires relying exclusively on the density measure and not on absolute counts.

2. Consistency and mathematical closure of the mask: Summing all 12 bands gives full agreement with the data of section A.3: both geometric sectioning methods (latitudinal and longitudinal) divide exactly the same residual crustal area, which makes up slightly more than half of the Moon (21.570 million km²) and contains exactly the same number of craters (4,848 in the ≥20 km group, and 1,599 in the ≥40 km group).

3. Keeping the fixed reference base: The reference point (value 1.00) remains completely fixed – the density of the full raw equatorial belt without a mask (166.436 for ≥20 km, and 53.170 for ≥40 km).

Dynamic analysis of the effect of the mask on the longitudinal asymmetry

Examining the residual measures and the geological change column yields the following insights:

1. Filling of the extreme western trough: The longitude band 345∘−315∘ east – which hosts the Mare Imbrium basin and most of the western near-side maria – shows the sharpest rise in the system: a density jump of +108.5% (the density more than doubles, from 84 to 176 per million km²). This finding proves that the extreme minimum measured in section A.2 stemmed directly from the resetting of the record by the young basalt floors.

2. Anomalous behaviour in the trailing region: The sector around the trailing meridian (105∘−75∘ east) is the only band in the system in which the residual density decreases after applying the mask (a drop of -7.8% in the 20 km group, and -9.0% in the 40 km group). This means that the parts removed in this sector (local basins) were richer and denser in craters than the crust that remained around them.

3. Reduction of the magnitude of the longitudinal pattern: The filtering mask dramatically reduces the east–west asymmetry and draws the profile into a narrower range. The extreme ratio between the peak segment and the minimum segment drops from 2.97 to 1.68 for craters ≥20 km (a peak of 266 in the 135∘−105∘ sector versus a minimum of 158 in the 315∘−285∘ sector), and from 2.88 to 1.79 for craters ≥40 km (92 versus 51).

4. Robustness of the residual circumferential pattern: Despite the mathematical reduction, the basic spatial pattern does not disappear. The far side beyond the trailing meridian firmly keeps its status as the densest region in both control groups, while the near side beyond the leading meridian remains the poorest. This residual pattern is analysed later in the paper using the six-axis model (A.9). For solving the polar puzzle, the isolated measurement itself and the separation of the longitudinal effects provide the required methodological foundation.

Colour scale: left, “low density” (soft yellow); right, “high density” (soft red).

A.5 Summary and conclusions of the four band tests

This section compiles and analyses the combined findings of the four spatial band tests carried out in sections A.1–A.4. The analysis is designed to answer a firm, structural question: is the excess crater density in the polar regions a real geophysical property of the lunar crust, or is it an artificial statistical bias arising from the way the area is divided or from the presence of large local geological formations?

The methodology is based on cross-checking four complementary tests:

1. Distribution by latitude without a mask (A.1): examining the equator-versus-poles trend on the raw surface.

2. Distribution by longitude without a mask (A.2): examining the global circumferential trend (east versus west) on the raw surface.

3. Masked distribution by latitude (A.3): cleaning out endogenic effects (maria, basins ≥500 km) along the latitude axes.

4. Masked distribution by longitude (A.4): cleaning out endogenic effects along the longitude axes.

The combination of the four tests makes it possible to separate two perpendicular sectioning directions (latitude versus longitude) and at the same time to control how far the record depends on the young basalt surfaces and the giant basins.

A.5.1 Separating the patterns: two independent spatial arrays

The first scientific insight arising from the summary is that there is no single spatial profile able to explain the global crater distribution. The latitude axes and the longitude axes reveal two entirely separate and distinct geographic patterns:

1. Characteristics of the latitude profile (bipolar trend):

  • The extreme density difference: In the raw count (without a mask), in the diameter group ≥20 km, the band adjacent to the north pole (75−90∘ N ◐) shows a peak density of about 300 craters per million km², while the minimum band (15−30∘ N ◐) stands at about 151 per million km² – a difference of almost a factor of two (ratio 1.80) [A.1]. In the control group ≥40 km a similar ratio is recorded: about 101 per million km² at the north pole versus about 51 per million km² in the low-latitude zones (15−30∘ N) [A.1].
  • Non-monotonic behaviour: The spatial profile does not rise in a smooth, continuous and consistent gradient from band to band along the way from the equator to the poles; it includes local fluctuations, rises and falls [A.1].
  • The restricted structural conclusion: The scientific argument is not about a smooth linear gradient, but about a firm edge property: the end bands adjacent to both poles reach exceptional density values that no intermediate band along the way can attain [A.1]. An observer moving from the equator toward the pole will see a fluctuating count, but the final band, where the polar section takes place, will show a density roughly twice that of the poorest band measured along the way [A.1].

2. Characteristics of the longitude profile (circumferential asymmetry):

  • The extreme density difference: In the raw count, in the ≥20 km group, the density ranges from an absolute minimum of about 84 per million km² in the western near-side sector (315−345∘ E ◐) to a global peak of about 251 per million km² in the eastern far-side sector (105−135∘ E ◐) [A.2]. In the ≥40 km group the range is between about 31 and about 90 craters per million km² [A.2].
  • The non-uniformity measure (peak/minimum ratio): The variance factor (the density of the richest segment divided by the density of the poorest segment) stands at 2.97 for the 20 km group, and at 2.88 for the 40 km group [A.2].
  • Comparing the magnitudes of the effects: The degree of non-uniformity along the circumference (a difference of almost a factor of three between east and west) is sharper and wider than that measured along the latitude axes (a factor of two between the poles and the equator) [A.1, A.2]. This means that circumferential movement around the equator produces more extreme density changes than vertical movement from the equator to the poles [A.2].

Methodological analysis: ruling out a mixing of the patterns

The fact that the asymmetry along the meridians reaches a range of a factor of three could lead to the claim that the polar excess (which is smaller, a factor of two) is merely a by-product or a statistical distortion caused by the larger longitudinal pattern. The study rules out this claim through the following geometric explanation:

  • Complete structural perpendicularity: The two profiles are computed and measured in directions fully perpendicular to each other.
  • The geometric offsetting mechanism: Each latitude band is a complete ring encircling the Moon over 360∘. This means that each latitude band takes in exactly all the global meridians – the richest meridians (the far and trailing sides) and the poorest meridians (the western near side) enter the statistical denominator of every latitude band in the same fixed geometric proportion.
  • Isolation of the effect: The simultaneous existence of two different profiles proves that the presence of a crater-rich or crater-poor region along the circumferential axis is not, in itself, an explanation or a source of the density excess embedded in the polar latitudes. The longitudinal asymmetry is an independent and separate pattern treated within the six-axis model (A.9) [A.2]. The present analysis successfully isolates the polar pattern in order to examine precisely what remains of it under uniform control conditions.

A.5.2 The mask as a control test

Sections A.3 and A.4 are not a recount of a new crater population, but an exact methodological repetition of the two band tests (latitudinal and longitudinal) under the filtering conditions of a uniform geological mask. This mask removes from the calculation the 20 basins of diameter ≥500 km and the LROC mare polygons [A.3, A.4]. A crater whose geometric centre falls within the mask boundaries is omitted from the count, and the area of the sector is reduced accordingly in the density denominator [A.3, A.4].

The scientific rationale for the choice of the filtered surfaces:

  • Maria and basalt plains (thermal reset): These units are geologically young floors. A mare acts as a vent above a magmatic feeding dome that melted the early craters, while a basalt plain represents crust melted under the general heat load radiated by the Earth. Their paucity of craters stems from resurfacing and not from a low impact rate. Since they are statistically concentrated in the equatorial region, including them distorts the latitude measure [A.3].
  • The giant basins (mechanical erasure): The formation of these impact structures physically erased the crater population that existed within them before them [A.5.2].
  • The like-for-like comparison rule: To determine whether the density difference stems from a latitude-dependent geodynamic effect, physics requires comparing crustal units with a uniform history (ancient ground versus ancient ground). Including partially resurfaced areas would measure the rate and distribution of the thermal resurfacing activity and not the effect of the body's geometry [A.5.2].

The mathematical dynamics of the density measure:

A decrease in the absolute number of craters (N) following the application of the mask does not necessarily imply a decrease in the residual density [A.3]. The density equation is governed by the changing ratio between numerator and denominator on the same ground [A.3]:

ρafter​=Arearemaining​Nafter​​

If the mask removes a relative share of area larger than the share of craters it omits (a situation typical of crater-empty mare areas), the overall density of the residual surface will show a rising trend [A.3]. The mechanism works like computing a trees-per-dunam measure in a forest containing a lake: removing the lake area (empty of trees) from the denominator of the total area will mathematically raise the density value of the remaining land, even though not a single physical tree has been added to the system [A.5.2].

Applying the same analytical operation to both perpendicular sectioning axes produces a powerful control tool: had the two spatial effects (latitudinal and longitudinal) been the exclusive product of the presence of the maria and basins, applying the mask should have changed both profiles in a coherent and similar way. The empirical findings rule this out and show a clearly differential behaviour [A.5.2].

A.5.3 Response of the longitude profile to the filtering mask

Unlike the latitude profile, the effect of the mask on the longitude profile is dramatic and fundamentally changes the raw amplitude (Mesa) of the system [A.5.3]:

1. Convergence of the extreme values and reduction of the amplitude along the circumference:

  • The western minimum segment (315∘−345∘ east): in the raw count (without a mask), this segment showed a minimal density of about 84 craters per million km² [A.2]. With the mask applied and the areas of Mare Imbrium and the western maria cleaned out, the density computed on the remaining highland surface jumped to about 176 per million km² (a rise of +108.5% relative to its raw state) [A.4].
  • The global non-uniformity measure (peak/minimum ratio): Following the rise in the minimum values, the overall variance factor along the longitude axes was considerably reduced: for the ≥20 km group, the ratio dropped from 2.97 in the raw count to 1.68 in the masked count [A.2, A.4]. In the control group ≥40 km a parallel behaviour was recorded, with the ratio falling from 2.88 to 1.79 [A.2, A.4]. This consistency in both size groups confirms that the original wide amplitude in longitude stemmed mainly from a geological bias in the distribution of the maria [A.5.3].

2. Collapse of the asymmetry between the trailing and leading meridians:

The statistical analysis of the full longitude bands (stretching from pole to pole) reveals the collapse of the significance of the orbital asymmetry at band level [A.5.3]:

  • In the raw count: the trailing band (75∘−105∘ east) numbered 750 craters (ρ=237) versus 487 craters (ρ=154) in the leading band (255∘−285∘ east) [A.2]. This difference gave a significant ratio of 1.54, a value representing 7 counting standard deviations (7σ), which entirely rules out the probability of a random fluctuation (the natural variance of a crater count scales as the square root of the count N​, and in a sample of hundreds of craters the uncertainty is a few per cent) [A.5.3].
  • After applying the mask: the leading band kept a larger residual area (2.044×106 km2, 417 craters) than the trailing band (1.692×106 km2, 370 craters) owing to a more extensive concentration of maria on the trailing side [A.4]. As a result, the masked density values converged to 219 versus 204 craters per million km², giving a residual ratio of only 1.07 [A.4]. Since the inherent counting uncertainty of this ratio is about 7%, the remaining difference equals only one standard deviation (1σ) and does not hold statistical significance at band level (for the ≥40 km group a residual value of 77 versus 74 was recorded) [A.4, A.5.3].

3. The geometric effect: averaging over bands versus concentration in caps:

Despite the collapse of significance at the level of the long band, the longitudinal pattern does not vanish entirely from the solid crust [A.4]. The reason lies in the geometric limitation of full longitude bands: a band stretching from pole to pole tends to dilute and obscure local excesses by averaging them with ordinary ground along the whole meridian [A.5.3].

When the geometric method is changed and focused caps with a radius of 30∘ are examined around the two orbital end points (section A.9), the masked population keeps density values of 252 per million km² on the trailing side versus 174 on the leading side [A.5.3]. This difference yields a ratio of 1.45, representing 5 standard deviations (5σ), and holds strong significance. This finding proves that the crater excess that survives the mask is concentrated locally around the core coordinates of meridian 90∘ east, and is not spread homogeneously along the whole band [A.5.3].

Methodological summary:

Applying the control mask has a twofold result: it changes and reduces a considerable part of the raw longitudinal amplitude (confirming the role of the young maria), but it does not entirely cancel the residual non-uniformity along the circumference [A.5.3]. However, for solving the polar puzzle and confirming the paper's model of rounding and mechanical contraction, it is enough that the longitudinal pattern has been measured, defined and statistically separated, and therefore the physical explanation of the east–west asymmetry remains outside the central argument of the present study [A.5.3].

A.5.4 Response of the latitude profile to the filtering mask: stability of the polar excess

Unlike the longitude profile, in which the mask erased a considerable part of the asymmetric amplitude [A.5.3], the latitude profile responds to the filtering procedure in a way that confirms the robustness of the polar effect in the ancient rocky crust [A.5.4]. The behaviour of the end bands reflects the mechanics of the residual density equation [A.3, A.5.4]:

  • The band adjacent to the south pole (75°-90° S ◐): in the raw count (without a mask), 139 craters were counted in this band (ρ ≈ 215 per million km²) [A.1]. Applying the mask removed a huge portion of area from the sector, leaving only 84 craters [A.3]. However, since the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin – the giant structure covering a considerable part of this band – is characterised by a crater-poor floor owing to mechanical erasure (the "dry pool" effect), the mask removed a relative share of area much larger than the number of craters omitted [A.5.4]. As a result, the available area shrank to about 0.275 × 10⁶ km², and the density computed on it jumped to about 305 craters per million km² [A.3].
  • The band adjacent to the north pole (75°-90° N ◐): in the raw count, 194 craters were counted in this sector, giving a density of about 300 per million km² [A.1]. Since this northern band is almost unaffected geographically by the mask polygons (no large basins or extensive maria near the north pole), the area and numerator data remained unchanged, and the residual density settles at about 300 craters per million km² [A.3].
  • Convergence of the bipolar end values: Cleaning the geological records leads to a fundamental mathematical correction. In the raw count, the southern hemisphere gave a misleading appearance of paucity relative to the northern one (215 versus 300) [A.1]. After applying the mask, this artificial asymmetry collapses, and the two bands adjacent to the poles converge almost to the same firm, high value: 305 in the south and 300 in the north [A.3].

A.5.5 Scientific insights from the comparison of the poles and the equal-surface test

The convergence of the values between north and south is one of the central methodological findings of the control test, and provides a firm lesson in processing planetary data [A.5.5]:

  • Collapse of the raw north–south asymmetry: The original raw comparison was flawed in that it set a northern polar band made of pristine, ancient, almost undamaged crust against a southern polar band most of which is made of the floor of a giant impact basin that erased the early record [A.5.5]. This comparison represented not a real property of the latitudes but a property of the type of ground [A.5.5].
  • Establishing a like-for-like comparison: Once a uniform control mask is applied that omits the same geological units from both sides, the two bands are measured on the same type of surface (pristine Highlands), and the internal asymmetry between them drops to zero in the ≥ 20 km group [A.5.5].
  • The morphological conclusion: Neutralising the raw difference does not produce one dense pole and one sparse opposite pole, but reveals two polar caps of similar, stable density, considerably higher than the rest of the surface [A.5.5].

A.5.6 Summary of stage one of the spatial observations and the geometric limitations of the bands

The four band tests (A.1–A.4) fully settle the question of the validity of the morphological finding and allow the scientific problem to be narrowed down to four firm conclusions and one structural limitation [A.5.6]:

Established conclusions:

1. The effect is global and bipolar: The high polar density is not a local feature of the northern hemisphere alone; it is shared by both polar end bands after the biases are cleaned out [A.5.6].

2. The excess does not depend on the mask: The effect does not disappear or fade after the removal of the large basins and the maria. On the contrary, at the south pole cleaning the area brought out and raised the true density of the remaining crust [A.5.6].

3. Complete isolation from the longitudinal asymmetry: The polar density is not an indirect expression of the east–west asymmetry. The longitude profile shows a different amplitude, a separate geometric behaviour and an entirely opposite response to the mask (collapse of most of the longitudinal amplitude at band level versus preservation and enhancement of the density at the polar ends) [A.5.3, A.5.6].

4. No requirement for a smooth monotonic profile: The empirical data on the surface do not support the claim of a smooth gradient climbing continuously from the equator to the poles. The precise scientific finding – and the physically stronger one – establishes that the bands adjacent to the poles settle significantly at the absolute upper end of the global latitude distribution [A.5.6].

The built-in geometric limitation of bands (The Ring Averaging Limitation):

Despite settling the initial question and confirming the robustness of the finding, the use of full latitude bands (75°-90°) runs into a clear analytical barrier:

  • A latitude band encircles the Moon over 360° around the rotation axis, and thus it compresses and averages into a single statistical number all the global meridians contained within it [A.5.6].
  • The geometry of the band cannot indicate how the density is organised and arranged within the polar area cell itself [A.5.6]. An average value of 300 per million km² can arise physically from several different morphological scenarios: a very dense point accumulation right next to the polar apex, a circumferential ring structure at a certain angular distance, an asymmetric concentration on one flank of the cap, or a uniform, homogeneous distribution [A.5.6].
  • The analytical method is like determining the average number of people per m² in a round hall: the global figure gives the overall degree of crowding, but it cannot tell whether the crowd stands concentrated at the centre of the room, spread along the walls or distributed evenly [A.5.6]. Resolving this limitation and decoding the internal structure of the caps requires moving to the next methodology of the study: the analysis of focused caps and the count around the six axes of the body (A.6–A.9) [A.5.3].

A.5.7 — End of the band stage and the move to caps

At this point, the analytical work that latitude and longitude bands can perform in the system has come to its full conclusion [A.5.7].

Summary of the findings in one line:

The existence has been established of an exceptionally high crater density at both polar ends of the latitude profile, fully isolated from the east–west spatial pattern, and standing stable and firm even after the effects of the basins and maria have been cleaned out [A.5.7].

In broader methodological detail, the band analysis fulfilled four main control aims [A.5.7]:

1. Spatial location: defining the exact location of the density anomaly relative to the latitude axes.

2. Separation of patterns: complete isolation of the polar effect from the orbital asymmetry along the meridians.

3. Geological response: quantitative examination of how the two patterns change under the constraint of a fixed, uniform geological mask.

4. Bipolar balance: revealing the fact that after cleaning out the geological biases, two polar bands (northern and southern) are obtained with similar, high and balanced density values in the system.

Change of analytical method: the move to the geometric question

Despite the robustness of the findings, the mechanics of bands runs into a structural barrier and cannot answer the next scientific question [A.5.7]. Up to this stage, the questions examined were: are the polar latitudes characterised by a higher crater density, and does this finding survive spatial control procedures [A.5.7]?

From here on, the scientific argument changes its character and becomes a firm geometric and morphological problem [A.5.7]:

How is the crater density arranged and organised within the polar space itself?

To decode the internal structure of the anomaly, the study fundamentally changes the form of measurement and the geometric sectioning of the crust [A.5.7]:

  • Eliminating circumferential averaging: abandoning the division into closed global bands that encircle the body over 360° and average the meridians [A.5.6, A.5.7].
  • The focused-cap method: defining each geographic pole as the exclusive structural centre of a spherical area cell (a polar cap) [A.5.7].
  • Distance-vector analysis: examining and mapping the distribution of crater density as a direct function of the angular and radial distance from the polar apex [A.5.7].

Therefore, the next section – section A.6 (the polar caps) – is not a statistical repetition or a further count of the same population [A.5.7]. It represents the next stage in the development of the argument, following directly from the mechanical limit of the band test: a sharp move from proving the very existence of a high polar density to decoding the spatial geometry and internal arrangement of the craters within the polar cap [A.5.7].

A.6 The polar caps, without a mask

In this section, the study formally changes the geometry of the measurement and moves from circumferential bands to the analysis of six concentric (nested) spherical caps around each pole, with angular radii of: 10∘,15∘,20∘,30∘,45∘, and 60∘ [A.6]. The aim of the test is to decode the internal structure of the anomaly and to examine how the cumulative density changes as the analytical space converges inward, toward the end point of the rotation pole [A.6].

Principles of the geometric structure of the caps:

1. Definition of angular radius (θ): a cap of radius θ takes in all craters whose arc distance from the polar apex satisfies ≤θ (for example: a cap of 30∘ extends from latitude 60∘ to 90∘ at the pole) [A.6].

2. The differential area equation: the area of each spherical area cell is computed exactly by:

A(θ)=2πR2(1−cosθ)

For a radius of R=1,737.4 km, the area factor grows non-linearly: the narrow core cap (10∘) extends over 0.288 million km², while the wide cap (60∘) extends over 9.483 million km² (an area more than 30 times larger) [A.6].

3. Cumulative (nested) structure: The rows in this table do not represent isolated, independent annular regions, but a cumulative summation profile [A.6]. The mechanism is like the rings on a dartboard: the cap of 30∘ is not only the outer ring, but the whole board from the bullseye (0∘) out to 30∘ [A.6].

    • If the craters are physically concentrated near the pole: the small caps will show high density values, and the density will fall consistently as the cap widens and takes in ordinary ground [A.6].
    • If the distribution is homogeneous: all the nested caps will show similar density values, independent of radius [A.6].

4. Keeping the static reference base: The reference point (value 1.00) remains completely fixed – the density of the full raw equatorial belt without a mask (15∘ S−15∘ N). Its value is 166.436 (for ≥20 km) and 53.170 (for ≥40 km), which allows a direct comparison with the data of sections A.1–A.4 [A.6].

5. Sample sensitivity and the size factor: The inner caps (10∘) cover small area cells and contain a limited number of craters, and therefore their confidence intervals are wide and carry the highest statistical uncertainty (the full analysis is given in D.4) [A.6]. The control group (≥40 km) represents an older crater population; a higher ratio compared with the 20 km group indicates a sharpening of the effect in the ancient craters (discussed in A.8.5) [A.6].

Morphological analysis of the raw radial profile

Reading the measures and the graphic behaviour of the two hemispheres yields the following findings:

1. Dominance of the overall polar excess: No polar cap, at any diameter and in either hemisphere, shows paucity relative to the equatorial belt [A.6]. The minimum ratio value in the system is 1.14 (the widest northern cap of 60∘), which proves that the interiors of all the caps are in a built-in density excess relative to the raw equator [A.6].

2. The differential behaviour of the north pole: The northern profile (the dark-blue line) shows a classic inward mechanical convergence and concentration [A.6]. As the measurement radius narrows, the density climbs continuously: from 189 in the wide cap (60∘), through 227 in the average test cap (30∘), up to a peak of 300 craters per million km² in the 15∘ cap [A.6]. In the extreme core cap (10∘) the profile settles at an almost identical value (298), giving a ratio of 1.79 [A.6]. In the control group of large craters (≥40 km), the northern concentration trend sharpens and reaches a peak ratio of 2.02 in the 10∘ cap [A.6].

3. The flat behaviour of the raw south pole: The southern profile (the red line) shows an entirely different trend at first sight [A.6]. Over most of the measurement range (15∘ to 60∘), the density curve remains flat, horizontal and almost independent of distance from the pole, with constant values in the narrow range of 207–221 per million km² [A.6]. Only in the innermost core cap (10∘) is a sharp rise recorded, toward a value of 250 (a ratio of 1.50) [A.6].

The limit of geophysical interpretation at this stage:

The raw empirical findings seem to show a deep structural difference between the two poles: the north is characterised by a sharp inward concentration, while the south shows a flat, homogeneous distribution [A.6]. However, the physics of the model recognises that the southern profile is cut and averaged over the floor of the giant South Pole–Aitken basin, which erased a large part of the record [A.6, A.11]. To determine which part of the variance stems from the deformation of the body's shape and which part is the distortion of a single impact basin, the geological filtering mask must be applied [A.6].

Colour key: a continuous transition from soft yellow (“low density”) to soft red (“high density”).

A.7 The polar caps after removing the basins and maria

This section examines whether the differential behaviour between the two hemispheres observed in section A.6 (a concentrated northern profile versus a flat southern profile) is a property of the original crater population, or a distortion caused by the type of ground and by the resurfaced geological floors [A.7]. To this end, the firm filtering mask (the 20 Neumann basins of diameter ≥500 km and the LROC mare polygons) is applied to the six concentric caps [A.7]. This procedure ensures a precise, like-for-like comparison on an ancient, uniform surface outside the sites of thermal and mechanical erasure [A.7].

Measures and methodological calibration:

1. Computing the residual area and numerator: Craters whose centre point falls within the mask are omitted, and the area of the mask is subtracted exactly from the denominator [A.7]. The measurement grid is based on exact spherical cells at a resolution of 0.05∘×0.05∘, with overlaps cleaned out only once [A.7]. Where the sectioning geometries overlap (the caps of 30∘ versus the latitude bands 60∘−90∘ in A.3), full consistency and mathematical closure of the area data and counts are obtained [A.7].

2. Setting the fixed reference scale: The reference point (value 1.00) remains unchanged – the density of the full raw equatorial belt without a mask (166.436 for 20 km, and 53.170 for 40 km) [A.7]. This choice is deliberate and serves as a fixed static scale for quantitatively tracking the degree of geological change of each cap, and not as a measure of the final polar excess [A.7].

3. The density-change measure (Δρ): compares each concentric cap with itself in its raw state in A.6:

Δρ=(ρbefore​ρafter​​−1)×100%

A positive value indicates a rise in the density of the remaining area following the removal of crater-poor units [A.7].
