Geodynamic analysis of the masked radial profile

Examining the residual measures and the shared graphic behaviour (Figure 6) yields the following insights:

Figure 6. The same six caps around the two poles after removing the basins and maria (A.7), craters of 20 km and larger. The northern line does not change within 20°; the southern line rises in its inner caps, and the two draw closer. (In the plot: horizontal axis — "cap radius around the pole", 10°, 15°, 20°, 30°, 45°, 60°; vertical axis — "craters ≥ 20 km per 106 km²", 150–350; the dark-blue line — "north pole"; the red line — "south pole".)

1. Zero geological effect in the northern core: The three inner caps in the north (10∘,15∘,20∘) show constant change values of 0.0% [A.7]. This proves mathematically that there are no Neumann basins or basalt maria within 20∘ of the north polar apex; therefore, the high core profile measured there (300 per million km²) reflects precisely the pristine state of the crust [A.7].

2. The extreme effect in the southern core and the erasure by the SPA basin: The smallest caps in the south show the effect of the extreme mechanical erasure by the SPA basin [A.7]. In the southern 10∘ cap, the measurement area shrinks by more than half (a drop from 0.288 to 0.104 million km²), indicating that most of the inner southern core was covered by the basin floor [A.7]. Cleaning out this floor raises the true density of the residual highland crust by +39.1% in the 20 km group (a value of 348, a ratio of 2.09) and by +49.8% in the 40 km group (a value of 135, a ratio of 2.54) [A.7].

3. Morphological convergence to a uniform concentration curve: Comparing Figure 6 with Figure 5 reveals a morphological reversal [A.7]. Whereas in the raw state the southern line was completely flat, applying the control mask equalised the type of crust and raised the inner caps of the south [A.7]. Now the southern (red) curve changes its shape entirely and climbs steeply inward toward the pole, like the northern (dark-blue) curve [A.7]. Once both poles are counted on the same type of surface, both show a single firm correlation: craters becoming denser as the polar apex is approached, a finding that confirms the geodynamic surface-contraction model [A.7].

Methodological clarification on the clean excess values:

The ratio column in this table compares a masked numerator with a raw denominator (which keeps the empty equatorial maria), and therefore serves only as a tracking scale [A.7]. To derive the true clean polar excess, the paper applies a like-for-like comparison (simultaneous removal of the maria and the SPA basin from both sides) on the standard caps of 30∘ versus the equatorial belt (∣ϕ∣<15∘) [A.7]:

  • Full raw catalogue (including maria): a ratio of 1.32 [A.7].
  • Removal of maria only, from both sides: a ratio of 1.11±0.04 [A.7].
  • Removal of maria and the SPA basin from both sides (the clean count): a ratio of 1.20±0.05 [A.7].

The standard deviation (±0.05) reflects the random fluctuation of the count; the confidence interval of 95% is twice as wide, and establishes with full statistical confidence that the true ratio lies in the range between 1.10 and 1.30 – a value clearly above the uniform-distribution baseline (1.00), and on which the scientific conclusion of the study rests [A.7].

A.8 Summary and conclusions of the cap test

Sections A.6 and A.7 examined the polar regions in a concentric (nested) geometry fundamentally different from the spatial averaging of the band tests [A.8]. Instead of measuring the average density in global latitude rings that encircle the body over 360°, each rotation pole was defined as the structural centre of six concentric spherical caps with angular radii 10∘,15∘,20∘,30∘,45∘ and 60∘ [A.5.6, A.8]. The test was carried out first on the raw Robbins catalogue without masks, and then under the firm constraint of a geological mask (removal of the 20 large Neumann basins and the LROC mare polygons) [A.8].

Cross-checking the two procedures methodologically separates two core questions [A.8]:

1. What is the observed spatial geometry of crater density as the distance vector converges inward toward the end point of the rotation pole [A.8]?

2. Which part of this radial geometry is embedded in the ancient pristine crust, and which part is a residual distortion caused by later endogenic activity (basins and maria) [A.8]?

The central finding establishes that applying the control mask fundamentally changes the statistical morphology and the way in which the structural difference between the two poles should be defined physically [A.8].

A.8.1 The raw state (without a mask): an internal morphological asymmetry

In the initial empirical count without a mask (A.6), the two hemispheres show two clearly different and distinct radial profiles [A.8.1]:

  • The inward concentration at the north pole: for the ≥20 km crater group, the crater density climbs consistently as the measurement radius narrows: from 189 craters per million km² in the wide cap (60∘), through 198 (45∘), 227 (30∘), 270 (20∘), up to a peak plateau of about 300 and 298 in the inner core caps (15∘ and 10∘ respectively) [A.8.1]. The profile does not require a smooth monotonic definition all the way to the apex itself (since the 10° and 15° values are statistically identical), but the spatial trend is firm: the inner core is considerably denser than its wider surroundings [A.8.1].
  • Confirmation by the control group in the north: the group of large craters (≥40 km) shows coherent behaviour: the density climbs from 63 in the wide cap (60∘), through 71 (45∘) and 87 (30∘), up to a peak range of 100–108 per million km² in the core caps (20∘−10∘) [A.8.1]. This finding proves that the convergence of craters in the north is not a statistical distortion tied to the 20 km threshold alone [A.8.1].
  • The flat profile of the south pole: In its raw state, the southern hemisphere shows the opposite behaviour [A.8.1]. In the ≥20 km group, the density curve remains flat, broad and almost independent of distance from the pole, keeping constant values of 207–221 per million km² over the whole range between 15∘ and 60∘ [A.8.1]. Only within the narrowest core cap (10∘) is an isolated jump to 250 per million km² recorded [A.8.1]. The ≥40 km group reflects a similar broad profile (72–82 per million km² in the range 15∘−60∘ versus 90 in the 10∘ cap) [A.8.1].

Had the scientific analysis stopped at this stage (A.6), the only physical conclusion would have been that the two poles differ fundamentally both in the strength of their absolute density and in their internal structural geometry (a concentrated north versus a homogeneous, flat south) [A.8.1]. The data of section A.7 prove that this description is incomplete and stems from a severe geological bias [A.8.1].

A.8.2 Behaviour of the northern profile under the mask constraint

One of the clearest and most important results of applying the geological control mask (A.7) is the complete robustness of the structural heart of the north pole [A.8.2]:

  • Zero change in the pristine northern core: In the three inner core caps of the northern hemisphere (10∘,15∘, and 20∘), the filtering mask changes neither the number of craters (N) nor the geometric area at the level of the calculation [A.8.2]. The density values remain completely fixed at 298 (at 10°), 300 (at 15°), and 270 (at 20°) per million km² for the 20 km group [A.8.2]. In the 40 km group exactly the same raw source values are kept: 108, 101, and 104 per million km² respectively [A.8.2].
  • Geophysical meaning: This finding proves that the inward convergence of density in the north is not an artefact of the presence of basins or maria [A.8.2]. Within 20∘ of the north polar apex, the mask removes nothing, since no mare polygon or Neumann basin comes that close to these coordinates [A.8.2]. The northern core is ancient pristine crust (Highlands) whose record was clean and normalised from the outset [A.8.2].
  • Effect of the mask on the northern circumferential background: The effect of the filtering begins to be measurable only as the cap radius widens beyond the core [A.8.2]. In the northern 30∘ cap, the 20 km density rises slightly from 227 to 233 (a change of Δρ=+2.8%) [A.8.2]. In the 45∘ cap it climbs from 198 to 232 (+16.7%), and in the wide 60∘ cap from 189 to 235 (+24.2%) [A.8.2]. This trend is reproduced exactly in the ≥40 km group [A.8.2].

The mask thus changes the spatial background surrounding the northern polar region, but leaves the core as it is [A.8.2]. Before the mask, the structural contrast between the core (15∘) and the surroundings (60∘) was extreme (300 versus 189) [A.8.2]. After the mask, while the core is stable at 300, the 60∘ surroundings rose mathematically to 235 owing to the cleaning out of the maria lying within them [A.8.2]. Therefore, the inward concentration firmly survives, but its amplitude (Contrast) is reduced [A.8.2]. The mask proves that part of the original raw contrast stemmed from the biased distribution of young surfaces outside the core, and not from an impact asymmetry [A.8.2].

A.8.3 The geodynamic reversal of the southern profile

Unlike the north, where the inner core was immune to the mask, in the southern hemisphere the filtering mask fundamentally changes the morphological picture, already within the narrowest caps [A.8.3]:

  • The southern 10∘ core: applying the mask removes a huge portion of the cap area and of the raw crater population [A.8.3]. The number of 20 km craters drops by exactly half (from 72 to 36) [A.8.3]. However, since the available geometric area shrinks relatively much more (a sharp drop from 0.288 to 0.104 million km²), the residual density on what remains jumps by +39% and reaches a peak value of 348 craters per million km² [A.7, A.8.3].
  • The southern 15∘ cap: in the raw count, 139 craters (ρ≈215) were counted in this sector [A.6]. After cleaning by the mask, 84 craters remain on a reduced residual area of 0.275 million km², and the true density of the crust jumps by +42% and settles at a value of 305 craters per million km² [A.7, A.8.3].
  • Sharpening of the trend in the ancient craters (≥40 km): in the 15∘ cap, the group of large craters shows the sharpest change in the system, with the residual density jumping from 82 to 124 per million km² – a structural jump of Δρ=+51% [A.7, A.8.3].
  • Decay of the filtering effect as the radius widens: In the southern 20∘ cap a significant rise is recorded (the 20 km group rises from 207 to 280, and the 40 km group from 73 to 98) [A.7, A.8.3]. As the radius widens and takes in ordinary highland ground, the effect of the mask decays: a rise of about 17% in the 30∘ cap, settling at a moderate rise of about 11%−12% in the wide caps of 45∘ and 60∘ [A.7, A.8.3].

The geophysical mechanism:

Within 20∘ of the south polar apex, the only structural component of the mask is the giant South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin [A.8.3]. The floor of this basin is characterised by an extreme paucity of craters owing to complete mechanical erasure of the early record [A.8.3]. Removing the basin areas mathematically subtracts a huge portion of area (the denominator) and very few craters (the numerator), and therefore reveals the true high density of the residual pristine highland crust around it [A.8.3]. This firm finding entirely rules out reading the original flat southern profile as the record of a pristine crater population; it is a local distortion caused by a single impact basin, successfully neutralised [A.8.3].

A.8.4 Bipolar convergence and statistical equality after the mask

Once both poles are measured and computed on the same type of crustal surface (pristine Highlands outside the sites of thermal and mechanical resetting), the morphological ordering changes and presents a uniform, coherent picture [A.8.4]:

The 15∘ cap≈300≈3051.020.78 – 1.32Complete mechanical equality (the interval contains the symmetry value 1.00) [A.8.4].
The 20∘ cap≈270≈280——Close structural proximity of the crustal density values [A.8.4].
The 10∘ cap≈298≈348—0.77 – 1.74The south is higher than the north, but based on a small sample of only 36 craters (wide uncertainty) [A.8.4].
  • Comparison with the raw unmasked state: The geological cleaning removes the apparent asymmetry in which the southern caps showed low values (215 versus 300 at 15∘, and 207 versus 270 at 20∘) [A.8.4].
  • Coherent closure with the band test: These findings detail and geometrically confirm the results of section A.3 (in which the end bands 75∘−90∘ became fully equal after the mask) [A.8.4]. The concentric caps prove that the bipolar convergence is not a product of averaging over a complete circumferential band; it penetrates inward and establishes a close equality of density even within the inner core caps of 15∘ and 20∘ [A.8.4].
  • Non-overlap of details in the control group (≥40 km): despite the general convergence, the poles do not become completely identical in every local measure [A.8.4]. In the ≥40 km group, in the 15∘ cap, 101 were measured in the north versus 124 in the south; at 10°, 108 in the north versus 135 in the south; and at 20°, 104 in the north versus 98 in the south [A.8.4]. The values firmly keep the same physical order of magnitude, but their local geometric structure shows a moderate internal variance [A.8.4].

Final methodological conclusion:

The full statistical analysis of the confidence intervals (95%) detailed in section D.4 establishes that, since the perfect symmetry value (1.00) is contained within the uncertainty intervals of the samples in all caps and at both diameter thresholds, the two poles are defined as fully equal and balanced within the limits of random counting error [A.8.4]. Therefore, the precise scientific formulation does not state that "the mask makes the poles completely identical", but rather: the geological filtering mask neutralises and removes most of the apparent raw contrast that existed between the inner profiles of the north and the south, and brings them to converge on ranges of similar, high and fully balanced crustal density [A.8.4].

A.8.5 Comparison of the linear diameter thresholds and the crater-size factor (a coarse chronological clock)

The differential use of two firm diameter thresholds (≥20 km and ≥40 km) is an essential methodological control tool, ensuring that the observed geodynamic trends are not the product of a statistical anomaly embedded in a specific size population [A.8.5]:

  • Morphological synchronisation in the north: At both diameter thresholds an identical raw profile of inward concentration is recorded (higher density in the core relative to the wide caps) [A.8.1, A.8.5]. Under the mask constraint, the central core (10∘−20∘) remains immune and numerically unchanged in both samples, while the circumferential background undergoes a rise in both [A.8.2, A.8.5].
  • Morphological synchronisation in the south: Both thresholds respond to the collapse of the SPA basin with a sharp density jump in the inner caps [A.8.3, A.8.5]. In the southern 15∘ cap, a residual rise of +42.0% is recorded in the 20 km group, and a sharp rise of +50.7% in the 40 km group [A.7, A.8.5]. In the 20∘ cap the rise settles closely at +35.2% and +34.7% respectively [A.7, A.8.5].

This consistency in both hemispheres proves that the general morphological ordering does not depend on the choice of diameter threshold [A.8.5]. However, a constant difference of deep physical significance is recorded: the ratio values relative to the equatorial belt are consistently higher in the ≥40 km group than in the ≥20 km group [A.8.5]. In the raw northern cap of 30∘, the ratio stands at 1.64 (at 40 km) versus 1.36 (at 20 km); in the masked southern cap of 15∘, it sharpens to 2.32 versus 1.83 [A.6, A.7, A.8.5].

The chronological-clock mechanism of crater diameter:

Within the physical model, the diameter of a crater acts as a coarse chronological clock – the giant craters (≥40 km) are statistically assigned to the earliest stages of the impact record, while smaller craters accumulated through the later sequence [A.8.5].

  • Had the density excess been caused by a static, time-independent factor, the density ratios would have been identical across all size classes [A.8.5].
  • The fact that the polar excess rises as a direct function of diameter (as further confirmed in the clean count of D.2, in which the ratio of the 30∘ caps to the belt climbs from 1.09 in the 20–30 km class to 1.53 in the 60–100 km class) proves that the mechanical crowding process took place simultaneously with, and in parallel to, the continued landing of the crater population [A.7, A.8.5].

The earlier a crater formed (close to the peak geometric flattening of the young Moon), the larger the share of the subsequent rounding and volume decrease it experienced, and therefore it underwent the maximum of the mechanical surface contraction that converged on the poles [A.8.5].

A.8.6 Structural integration: cross-checking the band and cap data

Combining the two geometric sectioning levels of Part A makes it possible to form a coherent and isolated physical picture of the body's crust [A.8.6]:

  • The band test (A.1–A.4): answered the question of the very existence of the phenomenon, and firmly established that the polar latitudes are characterised by a real density excess that remains stable and balanced between the two hemispheres (north and south) after the young basalt floors and the basins are cleaned out [A.8.6].
  • The cap test (A.6–A.7): answered the precise morphological question and decoded how the density is organised inward, toward the end points of the poles [A.8.6]. Whereas in the raw state an illusion of asymmetry was obtained (a concentrated north versus a flat south), applying the mask removed the bias of the SPA basin and raised the values of the southern core, and thus brought the inner caps of both poles to a similar morphological convergence (especially in the ≥20 km group) [A.8.1, A.8.3, A.8.6].

The cross-check reveals a critical distinction between two types of information: the polar excess at high latitudes is a stable physical property that survives the mask, whereas the initial geometric variance between north and south is a transient local distortion that does not survive the control [A.8.6]. This distinction prevents a serious methodological error, and makes it possible to separate the present state of the crust as preserved today from the primary properties of the geodynamic phenomenon [A.8.6].

A.8.7 Summary of the empirical conclusions of stage one

After working through sections A.1–A.7, five firm observational conclusions are established, which delimit the phenomenon that the physical mechanism is required to explain [A.8.7]:

1. Significant latitudinal non-uniformity: The global crater population is not distributed homogeneously by latitude; the polar bands settle decisively at the upper end of the density profile [A.8.7].

2. Robust endogenous resistance: The polar density excess is not a function of the presence of the 20 large basins or of the mare surfaces, and it fully survives the application of the geological mask [A.8.7].

3. Residual bipolar symmetry: Cleaning out the geological biases reveals similar and balanced density values between the two poles, both at the level of the global average of the bands and within the internal structure of the inner caps (≥20 km) [A.8.7].

4. Instability of the north–south asymmetry: The morphological difference between the concentrated northern curve and the flat southern curve collapses under the control, and is shown to be the product of a local basin impact in the south and not a primary property [A.8.3, A.8.7].

5. Multi-threshold consistency: The general trend is reproduced and appears simultaneously at both the ≥20 km threshold and the ≥40 km threshold, and does not rest on the choice of a single diameter [A.8.7].

A.8.8 Limits of the control test and the bounds of knowledge at the present stage

To maintain scientific precision, the study defines three firm analytical limits on the interpretation of the data at this stage [A.8.8]:

  • The static-correction limitation of the mask: Applying the geological mask is a spatial control and filtering tool only, and does not purport to carry out a full palaeogeographic reconstruction of the ancient lunar surface [A.8.8]. It does not mechanically correct gradual processes of crustal resurfacing, does not restore craters that were completely erased, and is not absolute proof that the remaining residual highland crust preserved the full integrity of the original population [A.8.8].
  • The cumulative-measurement limitation of caps: Since the geometric caps are nested one inside the other (the 30∘ cap mathematically contains the narrow caps of 20∘,15∘, and 10∘), a change in the cumulative density value between two rows does not directly reflect the local density within the isolated ring between them [A.8.8]. Determining the exact location of the radial change will in future require an analysis of independent rings, but this is not needed to establish the cumulative findings presented [A.8.8].
  • The resolution limit of small samples (random uncertainty): As the cap radius converges inward, the area cell becomes small and the number of craters falls, especially at the ≥40 km threshold [A.8.8]. In the 10∘ core only 86 craters were counted in the north and 36 in the south [A.8.8]. Owing to the small sample, the uncertainty intervals (as detailed in the 95% matrix of section D.4) widen considerably [A.8.4, A.8.8]. Therefore, it is scientifically inadmissible to use small numerical fluctuations between 10° and 15° as evidence of a fine internal structure, without the support of appropriate statistical significance tests [A.8.8].
  • Isolating the mask components in the southern core: Within the narrow range of 20∘ from the south polar apex, the SPA basin is the only mask component, and there the data of the overall mask and of the single basin overlap completely [A.8.3, A.8.8]. The distinct internal structure of the crater population within the basin itself is separated and analysed separately in section A.10 [A.8.8].

A.8.9 End of the cap test and definition of the scientific phenomenon

This section formally summarises and closes the morphological question that led from the band analysis to the stage of nested caps, and consolidates the pristine database of the residual crust [A.8.9].

Summary of the analytical dynamics:

  • The limitation of stage one: The band tests (A.1–A.4) proved that the polar latitudes are denser and that the effect survives the filtering mask, but owing to the circumferential averaging over 360∘ they could not indicate how the density is organised within the polar space itself [A.5.6, A.8.9].
  • Decoding in stage two (without a mask): Section A.6 filled this gap and revealed a sharp geometric asymmetry [A.8.9]. The north showed a classic inward concentration (a drop from 300 in the 15∘ core to 189 in the 60∘ cap for the 20 km group) [A.8.1, A.8.9]. The south, by contrast, showed a flat, horizontal and homogeneous profile (constant values of 207–221 per million km² over most of the range) [A.8.1, A.8.9]. Stopping at this stage would have led to the mistaken conclusion that the two poles differ fundamentally in geometry [A.8.1, A.8.9].
  • The reversal in stage three (applying the mask): Section A.7 revealed that the morphological asymmetry was the result of geological biases [A.8.9]. In the northern core (10∘−20∘), the mask removed nothing, proving that the crust there was pristine and clean from the outset (preservation of the values of 300 and 270 per million km²) [A.8.2, A.8.9]. In the south, the mask cut inward into the smallest caps; removing the crater-poor floor of the SPA basin erased a relative share of area (the denominator) larger than the number of craters omitted (the numerator) [A.8.3, A.8.9]. As a result, the residual density in the south jumped: from 215 to 305 in the 15∘ cap, and from 207 to 280 in the 20∘ cap [A.7, A.8.9].

Collapse of the asymmetry and convergence of the residual data

Cleaning the geological records led to a dramatic reduction of the bipolar differences and to a structural convergence of the density values within the inner cores [A.8.9]:

The 20∘ cap270 vs. 207 per million km²≈270≈280Full convergence [A.8.9]

The narrow and precise finding establishes that the bulk of the geometric asymmetry initially observed between the inner caps is not stable, and dissipates under uniform control conditions [A.8.9]. This result complements and confirms the findings of the bands: at band level, the mask equalised the 75∘−90∘ sectors to values of 300 and 305; at cap level, the same firm convergence is reproduced and does not disappear even as the analytical space narrows gradually toward the polar apex [A.3, A.7, A.8.9]. The two different sectioning geometries point exactly to the same physical vector: the high density excess is not a local feature of a single pole [A.8.9].

Defining the bounds of the mechanical control of the SPA basin

The study maintains a firm scientific separation between the empirical description and the mechanical mechanism [A.8.9]:

1. Identifying the mask components: The filtering mask is defined as the union of the mare polygons and the 20 large Neumann basins [A.7, A.8.9].

2. The geodynamic role of the SPA basin: The South Pole–Aitken basin is the main giant component that penetrates deep into the southern polar space, and its morphological geometry provides the physical rationale for why the mask acts on and lifts the values in the south so exceptionally relative to the pristine north [A.8.3, A.8.9].

3. Isolating components step by step: The overall masked calculation is not a test of the SPA basin alone [A.8.9]. Therefore, it is methodologically inadmissible to attribute the entire morphological reversal in the south to SPA alone, without isolating its residual contribution from the other components of the mask [A.8.9]. This separation is carried out and confirmed on two firm levels:

    • Within the 20∘ range of the southern core: SPA is the only masked component in the system, and therefore there is complete numerical overlap there between it and the overall mask [A.8.8, A.8.9].
    • At the stage of the final physical test (A.11 and D.1): the explicit "clean count" procedure is applied, which actively and in a balanced way omits the mare areas and the SPA basin from both sides of the equation simultaneously (both from the caps and from the equatorial belt) [A.7, A.8.9].

The consolidated database: definition of the crustal anomaly

With the completion of the cap test, the pristine physical phenomenon is defined which the rest of the paper is required to explain through the equations of geodynamics and the mechanical contraction model [A.8.9]:

  • Δρpolar​>1.00 — a significant bipolar density excess, present at both poles simultaneously
  • ρ∝θ1​ — a continuous radial crowding that sharpens toward the apex of each rotation pole
  • ρNorth​≡ρSouth​ — a balanced mechanical equality between the two poles within the limits of random counting error
  • Δρ≥40​>Δρ≥20​ — multi-threshold consistency, with the structural excess sharpening in the large diameter classes

On the basis of these four core measures, the study now moves to the stage of geometric integration and physical testing of the body's axes [A.8.9].

A.9 The six axes and the definition of the triaxial geometry of the young Moon

This section widens the bounds of the analysis and sets a combined geometric test. Whereas sections A.1–A.8 examined the surface through a single counting direction at a time (latitude or longitude in isolation), this section combines the data on the basis of the three natural axes of a tidally locked body [A.9]:

1. The rotation (polar) axis: passes through the two poles. This axis governs all phenomena affected by centrifugal stresses, by rotational flattening and by the decay of that flattening after the release (the central mechanism proposed for the reduction and crowding of the surface at the poles) [A.9].

2. The Earth line (radial): runs from the sub-Earth point (the near side, permanently facing the Earth) to the anti-Earth point (the centre of the far side). This axis governs the external tidal stresses and the mechanical two-body interaction (such as the ancient contact zone with the pear of the parent body) [A.9].

3. The orbital direction (tangential): runs from the leading point (the apex of motion in space, 90∘ W) to the trailing point (the orbital rear, 90∘ E). This axis reflects dynamic asymmetries arising from the motion of the body through the flight of ejecta or thrown-out material [A.9].

The methodology is based on comparing the density within six equal-area caps with an angular radius of 30∘ (a radius of about 910 km on the surface) around the six ends of these axes, after applying the firm geological filtering mask (removal of the 20 giant Neumann basins and the LROC mare polygons) [A.9]. The built-in equality of areas allows a direct quantitative comparison free of size biases [A.9].

Dynamic analysis of the effect of the mask and confirmation of the sub-Earth minimum

Reading the density-change column (Δρ) and the statistical ordering gives a sharp answer to an expected methodological objection [A.9]:

  • The initial scientific objection: Since the near side hosts the vast majority of the young, crater-empty mare surfaces, one could argue that the extreme minimum value of the sub-Earth point is nothing but an indirect reflection of the presence of the maria [A.9].
  • Refuting the geological bias: Applying the mask rules out this hypothesis [A.9]. The sub-Earth cap does indeed gain the sharpest rise in the system following the cleaning out of the basalt floors (Δρ=+57.8%), but despite the theoretical jump it remains clearly at the bottom of the order as the sparsest cap on the Moon (148) [A.9]. It is not the maria that produce the sub-Earth minimum; it is physically embedded in the crust itself [A.9].
  • Behaviour of further edge cases: The trailing cap is almost unaffected by the geological filtering (−0.3%), indicating that its record was clean from the outset [A.9]. By contrast, the leading point shows a significant rise of +34.7% (from 129 to 174) [A.9]. A check at the level of the mask components shows that a decisive part of the leading cap's paucity in its raw state stemmed from the thermal erasure by the single Orientale basin, whose cleaning raises the residual value to 162 [A.9].

Reading the empirical order as the record of a flattened triaxial body

The numerical order preserved both before and after the mask (sub-Earth → leading → anti-Earth / poles → trailing) proves that the crater distribution is not governed by a single axis, but reflects the triaxial geometry of a deformed body [A.9]. The geophysical model interprets the spatial pattern as follows [A.9]:

1. Balance of the rotation axis (poles versus equator): The poles are fixed at a sharp density excess above the equatorial points (the sub-Earth and leading points), as dictated by the model of rounding and contraction of rotational flattening [A.9]. After the mask, the average of the two poles stands 1.12 times above the average of the two equatorial sides (the leading and trailing) [A.9].

2. Asymmetry of the Earth-line axis (free head versus contact disc): The two ends of the Earth-line axis show entirely different behaviour [A.9]. The anti-Earth end (the far side) stands at a high density excess (221) and merges completely with the level of the poles [A.9]. By contrast, the sub-Earth end (the near side) is the sparsest region in the system (148) [A.9].

    • The physical mechanism: This difference matches precisely the morphological structure of the young Moon while it was still attached to the Earth [A.9]. The anti-Earth end acted as a "free head" (the free summit of the dome) and underwent no contraction or mechanical erasure during rounding, and therefore it stands consistently at the level of the poles [A.9]. By contrast, the sub-Earth end coincided with the centre of the disc and the physical contact array of the pear structure with the Earth, through which a high source pressure flowed that depleted the original record for mechanical reasons unrelated to the global shape of the body (analysed in A.9.2) [A.9].

The combination of these stresses describes a body that was under symmetric rotational flattening around the polar axis (c), and at the same time extremely stretched along the radial axis (a) between the Earth's gravity inward and the centrifugal pull outward [A.9]. This structure defines a precise triaxial shape that satisfies the physical order: a long axis toward the Earth (a), an intermediate axis along the orbital vector (b), and a short, held axis through the poles (c) [A.9]. The theoretical shape of a free tidal body (C.2) reproduces precisely an identical order of ratios (ratio values of 1.66, 1.56, and 1.06 for poles versus sub-Earth, sides versus sub-Earth, and poles versus sides, respectively) [A.9].

Determining the geometric shape measures from the crater record

Instead of assuming a hypothetical shape, the equations of rounding and volume decrease (C.3) make it possible to read the original dimensions of the body directly from the empirical record of crater excess [A.9]:

  • Reconstructing the shape of the general population (≥20 km): fitting the density-excess values at both ends of the Earth line (combining the free-head effect and normalised arrays, and showing excess ratios of 1.12 and 1.30 versus the sides and the sub-Earth point) yields an original triaxial shape of 1.37:1.15:1 in the late stages of rounding [A.9].
  • The independent integration test: A theoretical rounding of the 1.37:1.15:1 shape toward a perfect sphere predicts, completely independently, a clean density ratio of 1.21 between the 30∘ polar caps and the equatorial belt [A.9]. This predicted value matches fully, and without tuning, the empirical density ratios measured on the surface in the clean count of section D.1 (1.19−1.20) [A.9]. Two entirely different geographic regions of the lunar crust are read and reconciled successfully through a single geometric equation [A.9].
  • Reconstructing the chronological peak shape from the large craters: Since crater diameter is a coarse chronological clock, the largest craters reflect the earliest and most extreme stages of deformation [A.8.5, A.9]. Processing the six-axis data for the size classes of 60–100 km and 60–300 km yields shapes of about 2.1:1.2:1 and about 2.0:1.3:1 [A.9]. Despite local uncertainty arising from the small sample in each cap (only 13–68 craters), the joint analytical combination of the six axes and the clean belt in the statistical scatter matrix (the tables detailed in C.3) converges precisely around the shape value of the system's peak flattening: 1.8:1.4:1 (the shape of a Maclaurin spheroid rotating at 5.5 hours) [A.9].

A.9.1 The orbital asymmetry: the trailing side versus the leading side

The two ends of the orbital-direction axis show a consistent and sharp statistical difference in all the spatial analysis measures applied in Part A, with the direction of the anomaly remaining firm without a change of sign, while the quantitative amplitude varies with the sectioning geometry [A.9.1]:

  • The control group (≥ 40 km): in the 30° caps, values of 84 versus 47 per million km² were measured in the raw state, and 92 versus 61 in the masked state, confirming the stability of the pattern in the ancient craters [A.9.1].
  • Ruling out the frontal-sweep mechanism (The Shielding/Sweep Effect): The empirical data reverse the simple physical expectation: a planetary body moving through space through a stream of particles or dust should receive an enhanced impact density on the front of its flight (the leading face), like the windscreen of a fast-moving car that collects insects relative to the rear window [A.9.1]. The Moon shows an entirely opposite anomaly, since the leading face is the sparsest and emptiest in the system, a finding that rules out direct collection from space and requires an internal, dynamic geophysical mechanism [A.9.1].
  • Explaining the difference between caps and bands (the spatial dilution effect): The collapse of the masked ratio in the bands (from 1.54 to 1.07) versus its survival in the caps (1.45) stems from the fact that a 30° longitude band extends continuously from pole to pole, and thus averages and dilutes the local anomaly with ordinary crustal areas at high latitudes [A.9.1]. By contrast, the cap precisely delimits the relevant area cell within a radius of about 910 km around the core point [A.9.1]. It is therefore established that the excess is not a global property of the whole meridian, but a focused geographic concentration held around the coordinates of 90° east [A.9.1].

A.9.2 The geological correlation: the distribution of mare and basalt surfaces

Isolating the local anomaly around 90° east raises the question of morphological variance: what exists in this area cell that does not exist on the opposite side [A.9.2]? A precise intersection of the LROC mare polygons with the geometry of the 30° caps yields the following quantitative measures [A.9.2]:

Of which: areas of the Oceanus Procellarum basin—192,134—

  • Inventory of geological structures on each flank:
    • On the trailing flank (90° E): the structures Mare Marginis, Mare Smythii, Mare Undarum and Mare Spumans are concentrated here, together with small vents in the craters Artamonov, Joliot, Hubble and Lomonosov [A.9.2].
    • On the leading flank (90° W): the structures of the Orientale basin system (Mare Orientale, Lacus Veris) and the extreme western margins of Oceanus Procellarum are concentrated here [A.9.2].
  • Neutralising the bias of the contact basin (Oceanus Procellarum): The Procellarum structure is a giant basalt plain (crust melted by the heat radiated by the Earth, without an independent magmatic feeding dome) that belongs geographically to the contact zone of the young Moon with the parent body, and not to the orbital leading face [A.9.2]. The centre of this contact zone (with a base width of 3,000 km) lies at 24.1° N, 335.2° E, and contains within it the Mare Imbrium basin – the main feeding vent from the Earth [A.9.2]. Since the Procellarum area enters the leading cap only through geometric stretching, omitting it reveals the true ratio of the side vents: the trailing side carries an excess of 2.36 times in the area of independent maria and 2.10 times in the number of vents relative to the leading side [A.9.2].
  • Identity of the pristine measures: If the margins of the near-side maria that spilled into the trailing cap (Mare Crisium and the Fecunditatis plain) are cleaned out of it, the residual area stands at 170,839 km² versus 87,336 km² on the leading side [A.9.2]. This gives a vent-area ratio of 1.96 – a value fully identical to the original raw crater-density ratio in the same caps (1.96) [A.9.1, A.9.2]. This numerical proximity is a firm observation that dictates a direct physical link: the face that hosts the crater excess is precisely the face that hosts the excess of independent maria [A.9.2].

A.9.3 The morphological balance equation: maria as ejection and feeding vents

The following scientific paradox requires a solution: why is the most crater-rich sector the one that hosts the excess of maria, while the maria themselves are young, crater-empty floors [A.9.3]? The answer is based on the mechanics of the LEF model [A.9.3]:

1. The ejection-and-return mechanism (Paper 6): Within the model, every mare is a crustal vent above an active magmatic feeding dome [A.9.3]. These vents ejected and threw up enormous quantities of material [A.9.3]. The ejected material kept its kinetic energy and angular momentum, and performed ballistic flights that returned and landed on the crust at velocities of 2 to 5 km/s (exactly the velocity at which it left the vent) [A.9.3]. These landings took place within a radius of 50 to 1,000 km around the source vent in the early stages, and narrowed later as the body rounded and became more compact [A.9.3].

2. The two-way effect of an ejection vent: The mare acts on the crustal record through two opposite and simultaneous vectors: it creates impact craters around it through the returning material, while its own floor remains hot, melting and resetting the craters imprinted on it (the floor froze and became fixed only after detachment) [A.9.3]. The geometric record on the surface is expressed precisely by the morphological balance equation:

Nobserved​(x)=Background(x)+Returned_Material(x)−Thermal_Melting(x)

Outside the mare boundaries, the thermal-erasure term drops to zero while the returned-material term is maximal; within them, the erasure term dominates and resets the numerator to zero [A.9.3].

Asymmetry in the action of the mask:

The equation explains why applying the mask (A.3) changes the values asymmetrically [A.9.3]:

  • On the trailing flank (90° E): the residual density remains completely constant (a minor movement from 253 to 252) [A.9.3]. This finding proves that the surface outside the maria in this sector was already saturated and dense with craters exactly like the cap as a whole, since it is the main landing zone of the returned material [A.9.3]. The mask does not restore what was erased in the maria; it only isolates the solid landing area [A.9.3].
  • On the leading flank (90° W): the residual density jumps from 129 to 174 [A.9.3]. This rise stems from the fact that the mask cleaned out of it the empty areas of Procellarum and the floor of Orientale, and thus removed a large area denominator relative to the small crater numerator of the sector [A.9.3].

A.9.4 Integration of the crowding mechanisms of the trailing side

The crater excess preserved on the trailing side is explained by a combination of two independent physical mechanisms acting in the same dynamic direction [A.9.4]:

1. The mechanism of local distribution of returned material:

The scale of the ballistic flights of the material (up to about 1,000 km) matches precisely the geometric dimensions of the 30° caps (≈ 910 km), and explains why the effect is preserved in the cap and collapses in the long bands (which average the area with pristine ground that the ejecta did not reach) [A.9.1, A.9.4]. The mechanical link is defined by the firm logical chain [A.9.4]:

Increased concentration of vents (maria) in the structure → increased volume of ejected and returned material → exceptional crater density in the crust around them

The full quantitative calculation of the ejection history, the crater yield and the flight geometries is developed and detailed in Part E.3 of the paper and in Part K of Paper 6 [A.9.4].

2. The dynamic rotational-lag mechanism (Lag Effect):

During the attached stage, the Moon remained rotationally locked and rotated simultaneously with the Earth [A.9.4]. Material thrown up forcefully from ejection vents located in other regions of the body experienced a physical lag relative to the fast rotation rate of the system (a period of 5.5 hours) [A.9.4]. The dynamics work like throwing a ball straight up from the floor of a spinning carousel: the body moves forward, and the falling material lands behind its point of origin [A.9.4]. Therefore, the orbital rear (the trailing side) acted as a dynamic momentum trap, which received and drew in residual quantities of material ejected from all parts of the body that landed behind, in addition to the returned material from its own original vents [A.9.4].

A.10 The South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin as an independent spatial object

In the course of processing the bipolar data, it was established that the South Pole–Aitken basin is not merely a passive filtering component; it holds a distinct internal structure and a significant non-uniformity in the distribution of the population within it [A.10]. The basin extends over a width of about 2,400 km on the far side and penetrates deep into the southern polar cap (covering 24% of the area of all the polar caps) [A.10].

The study rejects the use of a single global average for the basin, since applying a single monolithic number would produce a serious methodological distortion: a combined average of a completely empty centre and ordinary highland margins would present a crustal illusion of a moderately and homogeneously depleted basin at every point [A.10]. Therefore, to maintain strict academic precision, section A.10 isolates the structure of the basin and carries out a series of continuous radial measurements laid out in steps from its geometric centre outward toward the margins, in order to close the open questions of the crater record of Paper 7 [A.10].

A.10.1 Methodology of the radial analysis of the South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin

To decode the internal structural non-uniformity of the South Pole–Aitken basin, the geometric centre coordinates of the basin were set according to the same parameters used to build the filtering mask: 53∘ south, 191∘ east, with a firm outer rim diameter of 2,400 km [A.10.1].

  • Approximate angular radius: a diameter of 2,400 km gives a physical radius of 1,200 km, which divided by the lunar radius (1,737.4 km) yields an arc angle of 39.57∘ from the centre of the basin to its margins [A.10.1].
  • Structure of the counting cells (division into rings): instead of averaging the basin into a single value that would distort reality, the space was divided into four inner spherical rings and two outer control rings: 0−10∘,10−20∘,20−30∘, and 30∘−39.57∘ (up to the rim); and beyond the rim: 39.57∘−50∘ and 50∘−60∘ [A.10.1].
  • Isolated regions and spherical area calculation: unlike the series of nested caps, the rings here are not nested and each row represents an isolated, independent area cell [A.10.1]. The area is computed by the spatial equation:
A=2πR2(cosθ1​−cosθ2​)

The factor cosθ1​−cosθ2​ neutralises the curvature of the sphere, and dictates that a ring of width 10∘ far from the centre will be larger in area than a ring of the same width close to it [A.10.1].

  • The local reference scale: the reference value (1.00) of this section is defined as the density measured in the first control ring immediately outside the basin rim (39.57∘−50∘) [A.10.1]. This choice is local and deliberate: the residual ground outside the rim lies at the same latitudes and on the same far side of the body, and thus it neutralises and removes the effects of the polar excess and the longitudinal asymmetry of sections A.1–A.9, and isolates exclusively the geological anomaly of the basin itself [A.10.1].

Summary of crater-density data in rings around the SPA centre (A.10)

The following are the exact numerical measures obtained in the six independent rings, computed for the ≥20 km group and the ≥40 km group [A.10.1]:

A.10.2 The central region as the focus of the minimum (the step structure)

Analysing the density columns and the spatial profile (Figure 8) yields the following main scientific findings:
