  • The minimum disc of the core: The absolute minimum of the record lies within the geographic central core ring (0−10∘), which extends as a wide zone over an area of about 288,000 km² (and not as a singular point) [A.10.2]. Within this area cell only 38 craters of diameter ≥20 km were counted, giving a density of 132 craters per million km² [A.10.2].
  • The circumferential jump vector: Outside the core disc, the density does not climb in a moderate linear gradient (a slope), but shows the mechanical behaviour of a firm step [A.10.2]. Already in the transition to the second ring (10−20∘), the density jumps sharply to 193, and settles at almost equal, high values of 200 and 202 over the rest of the basin interior (20∘ up to the rim) [A.10.2]. On crossing the 2,400 km rim, the residual density rises to 222 per million km² [A.10.2].
  • The quantitative deficit factor: The density of the central core is a ratio of only 0.59 relative to the control ground outside the rim, a figure reflecting an extreme relative deficit of about 41% in the crater record of the basin centre [A.10.2].

A.10.3 Calibration of the control group (≥40 km) and the uncertainty intervals

The group of large craters (≥40 km) reproduces the morphological trend precisely and confirms the consistency of the direction of the result [A.10.3]:

  • The density in the core stands at 52, and climbs to a constant range of 68–71 in the outer parts of the basin, reaching a value of 75 outside the rim [A.10.3]. The ratio of the centre to the residual surroundings settles at 0.69 [A.10.3].
  • The resolution limit of the small sample: In the central core only 15 craters of diameter ≥40 km were counted [A.10.3]. Since the random scatter error and the natural fluctuation of a count grow as the square root of the count (N​), the relative statistical weight of the error grows as the sample shrinks [A.10.3]. A sample of 15 craters carries a much wider uncertainty than a sample of 38 craters [A.10.3]. Therefore, the 40 km group serves only as a qualitative control tool to confirm the direction of the curve, while the quantitative determination rests on the 20 km group [A.10.3].

A.10.4 Dynamic implications for the clean-count procedure (A.11)

The empirical findings prove that defining the SPA basin as a single block under the monolithic term "deficit" fails scientific precision, since the paucity of craters is physically limited to and concentrated within the core zone alone [A.10.4]. The three outer rings of the basin interior (10∘ up to the rim) show density values considerably higher than the centre (193–202), approaching the level of the ordinary highland background of the surroundings [A.10.2, A.10.4].

This structural insight is essential for understanding the clean-count procedure of sections A.11 and D.1 [A.10.4]:

  • Within the balanced clean count, the SPA basin is removed from the calculation in its entirety because its centre is depleted and distorts the data [A.10.4].
  • Applying this monolithic filter carries a statistical cost: it removes from the calculation the depleted centre (the required erasure term) and at the same time omits with it the three outer rings, which are not crater-poor and preserve a sound crustal record [A.10.4].
  • The proof that the deficit is limited to the heart of the basin delimits the observational conclusion: within the SPA basin there is a wide central zone in which the crater density is low and has clearly been reset, while the circumferential parts and the marginal ground survived without severe erasure [A.10.4]. The questions of the detailed non-circular geometry of the zone, the definition of its exact physical boundaries and the decoding of its geodynamic origin lie beyond the aim of Paper 7, and the full explanation of its formation is passed on to the sections of Paper 8 [A.10, A.10.4].

A.10.5 The research interface: the point of contact with Paper 8

The morphological finding of a crater-poor core zone within the South Pole–Aitken basin emerged independently from the control test of the polar craters in the present paper (Paper 7) [A.10.5]. Therefore, the identification of the anomaly and its numerical quantification are an integral part of the documentation of the empirical observation of this study [A.10.5].

However, establishing the existence of this central minimum poses a new physical and geodynamic question for the system: why does the inner geographic core of the SPA basin carry a crater density so exceptionally low relative to the circumferential rings and the outer marginal areas of the basin [A.10.5]?

The structural division of roles between the parts of the scientific series

To maintain a strict, restrained academic structure, a defined and firm division of roles has been set between the parts of the series, delimiting the scope of Paper 7 [A.10.5]:

  • The role of Paper 7 (the present paper): The analytical role of this paper rests on, and ends in full at, this point [A.10.5]. The paper identifies the morphological phenomenon, quantifies it precisely in separate rings, and makes a proven observational statement: the wide central region of the SPA basin is the absolute minimum point of the measured radial crater-density profile [A.10.5]. Paper 7 does not purport or attempt to propose a physical mechanism to resolve this puzzle [A.10.5].
  • The role of Paper 8 (the study of the SPA basin): The resolution of the mechanistic and dynamic question passes exclusively to Paper 8, in which the South Pole–Aitken structure becomes the central object of study and analysis [A.10.5]. Paper 8 will develop and examine the following complementary data:
    1. The detailed, non-circular geometry of the depleted region (the measures of ellipticity and structural asymmetry of the basin) [A.10.5].
    2. The exact location coordinates of the point of absolute minimum density [A.10.5].
    3. Potential antipodal relations (Antipodal Relations) and links across the lunar body [A.10.5].
    4. The geophysical and dynamic mechanisms able to explain the formation of the anomalous structure of the basin [A.10.5].

A firm methodological clarification

All the numerical values and data presented in this section were derived and processed consistently from the Robbins catalogue (2019), which serves as the fixed database throughout Part A [A.10.5]. It is firmly emphasised that the definition of the 10∘ boundary of the central core is an analytical division component only, for defining the inner ring, and is not presented or interpreted as a proven physical or geological boundary of the crater-deficit region [A.10.5].

A.11 The clean-count methodology and the bounds of the empirical measurement

This section brings together the mechanical rules and structural criteria behind all the counts of Part A, and defines the intervals of the equation of the paper's main and official ratio [A.11]. The analysis is designed to normalise the surface, to separate geological biases and to frame the methodological limits of the database [A.11].

1. Definition of the comparison regions (the spatial geometry):

  • The polar caps (the target cells): defined as a firm continuum from latitude 60∘ and above up to 90∘ (both in the north and in the south) [A.11].
  • The equatorial belt (the reference cell): a narrow global band defined by the latitude range of ∣ϕ∣<15∘ around the equator [A.11]. This belt is the narrowest sector holding a sufficiently large crater sample; it yields the sharpest and cleanest contrast (Contrast) in the system, since there the vector of rounding and volume decrease of the young Moon reaches its mechanical maximum (the poles are the critical meeting points of the meridians, while the equator is the region farthest from them) [A.11].
  • Calibration of the angular control: Widening the equatorial belt to a range of ∣ϕ∣<30∘ (light blue in Figure 9) yields an almost identical overall result (1.12 versus 1.11), but it dilutes and obscures the structural contrast because it takes in mid-latitudes where the contraction effect is moderate [A.11]. The numerical agreement between the two belts proves that the very existence of the anomaly is robust and does not depend on an arbitrary choice of sector width [A.11].

Figure 9. Where the counts are made: the polar caps (orange) versus the equatorial belt of ±15° (dark blue; the ±30° belt in light blue for comparison). The maria (grey) are removed from both sides; South Pole–Aitken (red outline) is removed from the clean count. Dots: craters of 60 km and larger.

The balanced clean-count procedure (removing biases)

To make a fair and neutral comparison, physics dictates comparing crustal units with a similar developmental history (ancient ground versus ancient ground) [A.11]. To this end, a simultaneous and balanced cleaning is applied to two geological surfaces that bias the records in opposite and contrary directions [A.11]:

1. The system of maria and basalt plains (grey): young floors on which the original record was thermally erased and reset [A.11]. These areas are concentrated at low latitudes and make up 22% of the equatorial belt but only 1% of the polar caps [A.11]. Including them in the raw count artificially lowers the density of the equatorial denominator and wrongly inflates the polar ratio (a raw ratio of 1.32) [A.7, A.11].

2. The South Pole–Aitken basin (red outline): a giant impact structure that mechanically erased the early crater population in the heart of its core (A.10) [A.11]. The basin lies on the far side and covers 24% of the area of all the polar caps (mainly in the south) [A.10, A.11]. Including it in the raw count artificially lowers the polar numerator and biases the ratio in favour of the equator [A.11].

3. The normalised balance: Subtracting these two elements from both sides of the equation at once neutralises the two opposite biases, and leaves pristine highland crust with a stable history (Highlands) both at the poles and at the equator [A.11]. The paper's conclusion (D.1–D.2) rests firmly on this clean, balanced count, which fixes the system ratio at 1.20±0.05 [A.7, A.11].

The five limits of knowledge and the analytical constraints of the count

To maintain a strict, restrained academic standard, the study explicitly defines five basic rules that limit and delimit what a crater count can prove [A.11]:

  • The historical accumulation rule (Accumulative Record): The crater record seen on the surface today is a cumulative function [A.11]. Every crater imprinted since the shell began to freeze and collect its record on the Earth has been preserved in it, unless a later surface (a mare or a basin) physically erased it [A.11]. The modern count reflects the sum of the populations from all periods together, and not a single chronological stage; the polar density excess is analysed as a mechanical pattern added on top of this overall background [A.11].
  • The diameter-threshold limit and the risk of saturation (Saturation Limit): The completeness of identification and the quality of the data change drastically as a function of crater size [A.11]. Below the 40 km threshold, catalogue completeness is affected by the type of ground and by the intrusion of secondary craters (post-impact debris clusters) [A.11]. Therefore, the ≥20 km class is used to derive the numerical values, while the ≥40 km class serves as a control tool to confirm the direction of the sign [A.11]. Below the firm 20 km threshold no comparison is made, since there secondary craters dominate and the surface is in a state of saturation (an equilibrium in which new craters erase old ones at the same rate, and the count stops growing) [A.11].
  • Neutralising optical biases and solar illumination: At the poles, sunlight strikes at a low angle to the horizon and casts long, giant shadows that bring out every furrow and small crater, producing a visual illusion of a far more cratered area than the equatorial belt (a sunset effect) [A.11]. To block this optical bias, the study rejects the use of images or photographs, and relies exclusively on topographic data and digital elevation maps that measure the actual ground and not its shadows [A.11].
  • The background presence of the contact basin: The anomaly of Paper 13 (the near-side minimum in the contact zone) is present as a basic background beneath the entire reported array [A.11]. The polar excess is measured relative to it and does not replace it; the six-axis model (A.9) presents and balances both patterns simultaneously [A.11].
  • The requirement of a uniform database: All the density data are taken from the global geometric catalogue of Robbins (2019), which is characterised by uniform resolution over the entire Moon [A.11]. The study rejects the use of classical geological maps, compiled from historical sources of unequal detail (several times denser on the near side than on the far side), in order to prevent a comparative distortion [A.11, D.3]. A valid scientific comparison exists only when both halves of the body are counted by the same method and with the same measuring tool [A.11].

Closing the descriptive stage and moving to the explanatory tests

With the completion of sections A.1–A.11, the descriptive part of the paper is fully closed [A.11]. The five spatial stations established the following database:

  • Identification of a sharp density excess at high latitudes [A.11].
  • Full separation and isolation of the polar pattern from the longitudinal (east/west) asymmetry [A.11].
  • Confirmation of the robustness of the bipolar effect even under the constraint of a firm geological filtering mask [A.11].
  • Decoding of the internal structure of the caps and proof that the cores converge to statistical equality [A.11].
  • Integration of the trends into a coherent geometric order that confirms the existence of an ancient triaxial body [A.11].
  • Isolation and quantification of the central minimum of the SPA basin and its transfer to the analysis of Paper 8 [A.11].

From here on, the scientific argument changes its face and moves from the question of empirical description (what is found on the surface and where) to the question of the physical mechanism (what can produce such a pattern) [A.11]. Every alternative model or hypothesis examined in the following sections of the paper will have to stand up to six firm boundary constraints set by the observation, with no room for exception [A.11]:

  • 1. An exceptionally high crater density in both polar regions simultaneously
  • 2. Coherent reproduction of the trend at both isolated diameter thresholds ( 20 km and 40 km)
  • 3. Survival and full robustness of the end excess after applying the mare and basin mask
  • 4. An explanation of the differential variance in the response of north versus south to the mask (the collapse of the SPA basin in the south)
  • 5. Morphological convergence to similar density values in the residual inner cores of the caps
  • 6. Preservation of the six-axis order, with the sub-Earth point fixed as the sparsest cap
PART B

Part B — What we tried before the answer

Part A defined the density anomaly quantitatively and spatially: lunar craters are significantly denser in the regions of both poles than in the equatorial belt, with the effect organised in a global pattern around a complete ring of the surface and not as a single singular point [B]. Part C will develop and present the geodynamic equations of the mechanism of rounding and mechanical contraction proposed as the scientific solution [B].

This section (Part B) is the stage of preliminary mechanistic testing, and presents the six alternative hypotheses and interpretations that were examined and rejected during the study [B]. Their mechanical rejection is what led the study to the rounding solution, since the combined analysis of the six failures proves that the physics of the system leaves room for only one kind of generating cause [B].

The matrix of four structural questions:

Each alternative hypothesis is examined consistently and strictly against four firm questions, whose values are derived directly from the observational data of Part A [B]:

1. The sign test (Sign Test): Does the proposed physical mechanism actually create a density excess at the poles relative to the equator, or does it act the other way and deplete them [B]? (A mechanism that depletes the poles is rejected immediately at the outset) [B].

2. The magnitude test (Magnitude Test): If the dynamic sign is correct, can the mechanism produce the measured empirical ratio values – 1.32 in the raw count, 1.20±0.05 in the clean count, together with the significant rising trend as crater diameter increases (D.1–D.2) [B]?

3. The shape test (Morphology Test): Does the mechanism place and organise the density excess in the exact geographic space where it is observed – held at both poles to a similar degree, and arranged according to the triaxial order of the six axes (A.9) [B]?

4. The mask test (Mask Test): Can the density excess produced by the mechanism survive the application of the geological mask (removal of the maria, the large basins and the SPA basin from both sides of the equation), as it actually survives in the residual counts of Part A [B]?

The tests are arranged in a methodological order from the coarsest test (sign) to the finest test (mask), so that most hypotheses are decided and rejected at early stages of the analysis [B].

B.1 Preservation on ancient highlands (Highlands Preservation Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

This hypothesis holds that the density excess at the poles is nothing but a reflection of the degree of surface preservation and of varying geological age [B.1]. The polar regions are ancient, pristine highland crust (Highlands) that did not experience the late volcanic flooding of the dark basalt plains and maria, which erased and covered the early record at the low latitudes of the near side [B.1]. Therefore, the poles are dense because they are older and were not affected by endogenic alterations, and not because some dynamic mechanism actively concentrated or collected craters there [B.1]. This is the initial explanation accepted in the planetary community, since crater density serves as the classical indicator for determining the relative age of surfaces [B.1].

The morphological prediction of the hypothesis (what it predicts):

The model dictates that the density curve must follow linearly the chronological age and the degree of preservation of the area cell [B.1]. The density is required to be completely uniform and homogeneous across all the unflooded highland crustal units, and to show low values (pits) only where a young mare or basin extends [B.1]. The hypothesis rules out the existence of an anomalous centre or apex, since an ancient highland of the same age is uniform in space [B.1]. Had thermal preservation been the only factor, the pole would show values identical to any other highland area of the same age on the body, and the global density map would consist of flat plateaus and local pits, without a concentrated peak curve [B.1].

Analysis of the empirical findings from the counts (what the surface shows):

The effect of geological preservation and the thermal impact of the maria is entirely real, and it does shape the lunar surface on the largest scale (as reflected in the exposure regions of Paper 13, in which the far side hosts a raw density of 219 craters per 10⁶ km², the marginal belt 164, and the sub-Earth contact disc only 99) [B.1]. However, three firm observations from Part A rule out the interpretation and lead to its rejection [B.1]:

1. Robustness of the excess under the decisive mask test: The filtering mask of section A.3 omits from the calculation precisely the elements on which the hypothesis rests – the mare polygons and the giant basins [B.3, B.1]. This procedure normalises the denominator and ensures a clean comparison of highland versus highland on both sides of the equation [B.1]. Had preservation differences been the sole cause of the phenomenon, the residual density ratio would have fallen exactly to the uniform-distribution value (1.00) once the replaced crust was removed [B.1]. In practice, the raw ratio falls from 1.32 to 1.11 (removal of maria), and climbs back to a firm value of 1.20±0.05 once the SPA basin is also neutralised [B.1]. The ratio does not drop to 1, and it continues to show a rising trend as a function of crater diameter up to a value of 1.53 in the large classes [B.1]. Any density difference that survives this like-for-like procedure cannot be attributed to the difference between flooded ground and pristine ground [B.1].

2. The bipolar peak stands above the oldest highland in the system: The far-side crown (around the coordinates of the anti-Earth point) represents in the dynamic model the oldest and safest crustal unit, which the mare surfaces hardly touched geographically [B.1]. After applying the mask, this sector carries a density of 221 craters per 10⁶ km² [B.1]. By contrast, the two residual polar caps show considerably higher values: 233 in the north and 246 in the south [B.9, B.1]. The poles stand morphologically above the oldest highland, not level with it [B.1]. Had the chronological age of the crust been the deciding factor, the far-side crown should have led the global order; the findings on the surface rule this out [B.1].

3. The existence of a radial concentration (a centre) in the pristine northern core: Within the space of the north pole, where no mare polygon or Neumann basin penetrates within 20∘ of the apex, the density is not homogeneous and flat but shows a sharp concentration curve [B.1]. The density measure climbs continuously from 189 in the wide cap (60∘) to a peak value of 300 craters per million km² in the inner 15∘ cap [B.6, B.1]. A uniform, static highland crust cannot produce a radial convergence of density toward a defined geographic point [B.1]. The northern core is the cleanest observation site for refuting the hypothesis, since it contains no foreign geological element requiring filtering by the mask [B.1].

Verdict:

The hypothesis of preservation on ancient highlands passes only the sign test, and fails completely in the mask test and the shape test [B.1]. The wide spatial variance on a global scale (such as the near-side versus far-side ordering) is explained through the geometry of the contact zones of the tip of the pear (Paper 3) and the distribution of the hardest ballistic landing vectors concentrated on the far side (Paper 6), and not as a function of static preservation [B.1].

The study keeps the preservation mechanism solely as the physical reason why the mare areas and young impact basins show low density values (resetting of the record), and not as a source or explanation of the polar density excess [B.1]. The presence of ancient highlands on the near side south of the crater Tycho, which show an exceptional density of 302 craters within 15∘, is a further mechanical reminder that the density of an ancient surface is not a function of chronological age alone [B.1]. What the preservation hypothesis leaves without a physical answer is precisely the core of the paper's study: a significant density excess preserved at the level of a highland-versus-highland comparison, and holding a geometric centre anchored on the body's rotation axis [B.1].

B.2 Rotational flattening during attachment (Rotational Flattening Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

This hypothesis is based on the mechanical principle that a viscous/soft body rotating rapidly about its axis undergoes a flattening deformation – it widens along the equatorial belt owing to centrifugal stresses, and shortens along the polar axis, like pizza dough that stretches and flattens when spun in the air [B.2]. Since the young Moon in the attached stage rotated in rapid synchronisation with the Earth (a period of about 5.5 hours), it underwent a severe global flattening (C.1) [B.2]. The initial idea holds that these compressive stresses physically pressed the polar regions inward, and thus mechanically brought the craters they carried closer together and raised their density [B.2].

The morphological prediction (what it predicts):

The physical geometry of a flattening deformation at constant volume (a state in which material is neither added to nor removed from the system, but only changes its configuration) shows a behaviour entirely opposite to the crowding prediction [B.2]:

  • In the polar space: the upper and lower surfaces are squashed and force the material to spread sideways, which causes a two-directional stretching of the surface within the plane of the pole [B.2].
  • In the equatorial space: the surface is stretched along the circumference of the equator, but shortens along the meridians [B.2].

As a consequence, the number of craters per unit area (ρcrater​) decreases and becomes depleted in the polar region, and the differential area-spreading equation is defined precisely by the axis ratio of the spheroid (a/c, where a is the equatorial radius and c is the polar radius) [B.2]:

ρpolar​=(a/c)2ρequatorial​​

This equation dictates that the more flattened a body is, the sparser and emptier of craters per unit area its poles become (the exact inverse of the rounding equation developed in C.3) [B.2]. For the axis-ratio values of the Maclaurin spheroid at a low density (a/c = 1.69, density 1,300 kg/m³, rotation of 5.5 hours) and for a dense body (a/c = 1.20, density 2,600 kg/m³, period of 5.77 hours), the flattening mechanism would leave the poles at a theoretical disadvantage of only 0.59 and 0.83 relative to the equator (a structural deficit of 41% and 17% respectively) [B.2].

What the empirical counts say:

The physical data on the surface show a sharp density excess at the poles (a ratio of 1.32 in the raw count and 1.20±0.05 in the clean count) [B.2]. Therefore, the mechanical sign of the hypothesis is fundamentally wrong; rotational flattening dilutes the craters at the apex, whereas the observations on the surface show them at maximum density [B.2].

Verdict:

The rotational-flattening hypothesis fails completely in the sign test [B.2]. If an elastic ball is pressed from above and below, the surface of the upper end does not contract – it spreads and widens, and points imprinted on it move apart [B.2].

However, the hypothesis understands the general geometry of the body correctly when it is read in the opposite direction: a crustal surface that was stretched during the build-up of flattening, and later, after the release, freed from the stress constraint as the flattening decayed, will contract sharply in the polar regions [B.2]. This reversed understanding is the mechanical heart of section C.3 [B.2]. This finding caused a fundamental methodological change during the study: instead of searching for a dynamic mechanism that produces flattening, the search began for the geodynamic process that undoes the flattening (the decay of flattening and the rounding back to a sphere) [B.2].

B.3 The polar axis shortened by the tide — the Roche effect (Roche Tidal Stretching Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

During the attached stage, the young Moon was subject to the Roche effect – extreme tidal stresses that stretched its volume along the Earth line (the radial axis a) owing to the dynamic difference between the Earth's gravity, which pulled the near side inward, and the centrifugal pull of corotation, which drew the mass outward, while the interior of the body was held on the tip of the pear structure [B.3]. Since the volume of the body remained almost constant, the elongation of the radial axis came at the expense of a reduction of the two perpendicular axes [B.3]. Within the rotating system, the centrifugal term acted to stabilise and preserve the axis of orbital motion (b), and therefore the main burden of shortening and mechanical collapse fell on the polar axis (c) [B.3]. The poles were pressed and shortened toward each other, and the alternative idea holds that the craters on them were drawn and crowded together with them [B.3].

The morphological prediction (what it predicts):

The geometry of a free fluid body with a density of 2,600 kg/m3 under these tidal stresses is computed precisely as a triaxial axis ratio of 1:0.637:0.601 (for axes a:b:c) [B.3]. This structure produces an ellipsoidal body very long toward the Earth and shortest at the poles (an egg lying along the tidal axis) [B.3]. When this tidal stretching deformation is applied to a crust carrying uniformly distributed craters, the density measure in each area cell changes in inverse proportion to the contraction factors (the exact inverse of the C.3 values) [B.3]:

Spatial sector examinedChange vector under Roche stretchingChange vector under rounding back (C.3)
The polar regions (the short axis c)0.83× (dilution and moving apart)1.21× (mechanical crowding)
The leading and trailing points (axis b)0.88× (moderate dilution)1.14× (moderate crowding)
The sub-Earth point (the long axis a)1.38× (concentration and crowding)0.73× (widening and dilution)

Reading the matrix across proves that a polar axis mechanically shortened under tidal stretching stresses spreads and widens the surface above it, exactly as in the rotational-flattening mechanism [B.3]. The pole is the physically most stretched sector of the shape, and therefore the craters there move apart and become diluted (0.83) [B.3]. By contrast, the ends of the Earth line (the sub-Earth point) are the regions where the surface converges and crowds to the system maximum (1.38) [B.3].

What the empirical counts say:

The actual observations on the surface present an entirely opposite picture: the poles are the densest regions in the system, while the sub-Earth point is the sparsest and emptiest of the six main caps (a raw value of 94, and a masked value of only 148) [A.9, B.3]. The tidal stretching mechanism predicts precisely the opposite in these two sectors [B.3].

Verdict:

The Roche-stretching hypothesis fails the sign test as a crowding-generating mechanism [B.3].

However, the physical effect itself is real and its magnitude is firmly preserved within the model equations: it defines the triaxial starting shape of section C.2, and the geodynamic rounding back from it toward a perfect sphere is the scientific answer of the study [B.3]. The Roche effect is responsible for setting the peak deformation and stretching of the attached body; the subsequent decay of flattening after the release (the return to a sphere) is what drives and physically brings the craters closer together [B.3]. Reading the right-hand column of the table (the rounding vector) reproduces in full agreement the order of the counts: maximal poles, intermediate sides, and the sub-Earth point at the bottom as the minimum [B.3].

B.4 Stronger gravity at the pole (Polar Gravity Excess Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

In a planetary body characterised by a flattened shape, the polar apex lies geometrically closer to the body's centre of mass than the equatorial belt does [B.4]. In addition, at the geographic pole (which sits directly on the rotation axis) the linear velocity is zero, and therefore the outward centrifugal component does not exist [B.4]. The combination of these two factors produces at the poles an effective gravity value (the self-attraction minus the centrifugal contribution) higher than that at the equator [B.4]. The alternative interpretation proposes that this enhanced gravity field at the poles acted as a mechanical pump that drew loose elastic surface material along the crust toward the polar regions, and thus crowded the record around them [B.4].

The morphological prediction (what it predicts):

Physical law dictates that the gravity vector acts downward (radially toward the centre) and not sideways (tangentially along the surface) [B.4]. For crustal material to undergo active lateral motion along the surface toward the pole, the pole would have to function physically as the lowest point in terms of the body's effective potential (the floor of a potential valley, into which material slides and flows like water down a slope) [B.4].

In the dynamic system of the attached body rotating rapidly with the Earth, the physical situation is entirely the opposite [B.4]. In the rotating frame, the effective potential at the equatorial belt is lower than that at the pole by a firm factor of 21​Ω2R2 (where Ω is the rotation rate and R is the radius), a value representing the excess kinetic energy of motion that the equatorial belt has and that the polar axis lacks entirely [B.4].

For a dense body (density 2,600 kg/m³, period of 5.77 hours, mean radius R ≈ 1,890 km), under a surface gravity value of g ≈ 1.37 m/s² (C.7), the theoretical height equation is defined by [B.4]:

ΔH=g21​Ω2R2​≈120 km

This equation proves that on a flattened body that has not yet completed its collapse to its hydrostatic equilibrium shape, the polar regions stand as giant topographic hills about 120 km high "above" the equatorial belt in the energetic sense [B.4]. They are the points of highest potential (a hilltop), and therefore any loose material or elastic crust will experience an opposite push vector and slide away from them outward toward the equatorial potential valley [B.4]. This is the mechanism that produces flattening (B.2), not polar crowding [B.4].

What the empirical counts say:

The excess is located at the poles [B.4]. While the body was rotating, the combination of gravity and centrifugal acceleration acted to remove and dilute material from the poles, not to concentrate it there [B.4].

Verdict:

The enhanced-polar-gravity hypothesis fails completely as a lateral-displacement mechanism as long as the body is in the attached, rotating stage [B.4].

The effect is placed in its correct physical position only after the release: it is the Moon's self-gravity that held it together as a whole body and prevented its disruption beyond the rigid Roche limit (≈ 13,000 km at a density of 1,300) [B.4]. As long as the Moon was attached and rotating with the Earth, the rotation held the flattening. After the release, the stretching that had held the flattening – between the Earth's gravity and the point of attachment on the near side, and the centrifugal pull outward – disappeared and the rotation of the receding Moon slowed, and the flattening became an anomalous load that the body could not bear [B.4]. Only then does the pole of the flattened body turn from an energetic hilltop into the floor of a deep potential valley [B.4]. Now self-gravity acts as the main engine driving the flow and contraction of the surface inward toward the poles – this is the mechanism of the decay of flattening (C.4) [B.4]. The geometric difference of 120 km represents the exact scale of the energy that the rotation held up, and its release during the decay is what crowds the craters [B.4].

B.5 A drain at the pole (Polar Drain/Vortex Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

This hypothesis is based on the intuitive mechanical analogy of "suction inward": the existence of a draining mechanism, crustal subsidence, or an internal dynamic vortex beneath each geographic pole [B.5]. According to this model, the magmatic or geodynamic system acts like water on the floor of a sink flowing and gathering toward the drain, and thus it actively draws, concentrates and collects the surface and the craters on it toward a single end point [B.5].

The morphological prediction (what it predicts):

The dynamics of a drain dictate a concentration directed exclusively toward a singular point (The Vertex Point) [B.5]. Therefore, the density map is required to show a steep and unbounded rising trend (a statistical singularity) as one approaches the pole point itself, with the geophysical topography obliged to show a depression or deep pit at the centre point [B.5]. The model requires the action of a lateral mechanical force vector directed straight at the coordinates of the pole [B.5].

What the empirical counts say:

The data measured on the surface rule out the structure of a point singularity [B.5]:

1. Arrest and stabilisation of the pristine northern core: Within the clean space of the north pole, the crater density (≥20 km) does indeed climb radially: from 189 in the 60∘ cap, to 227 (30∘), and to 270 (20∘) [A.6, B.5]. However, on entering the extreme core, the density curve stops completely and levels off: a value of 300 in the 15∘ cap versus a value of 298 in the 10∘ cap [A.6, B.5]. The data reveal a global concentration toward a wide polar region (Highlands Plateau) and not a point convergence into a drain [B.5].

2. Sensitivity of the residual southern sample: In the south, after applying the mask, the inner caps show values of 305 (at 15°) and 348 (at 10°) [A.7, B.5]. However, analysis of the system shows that within 20∘ of the south polar apex, the mask consists of an overlapping union with the SPA basin alone, and the 10∘ cap rests on a small sample of only 36 craters [B.5]. In such a small sample, a random fluctuation of a handful of craters shifts the numerical value by wide margins, and therefore the rise in the south carries the local geometry of the impact basin and the error intervals of the count, and is not evidence of a drain [B.5]. The scientific weight of the test rests on the clean northern sequence [B.5].

3. Absence of topographic evidence: The actual planetary topographic data show no pair of gravitational or structural depressions corresponding to the geographic poles [B.5].

Verdict:

The drain hypothesis passes the sign test (positive), but fails completely in the shape test [B.5].

Within a rotating planetary body, every physical force vector must preserve axial symmetry about the rotation axis, and such symmetry produces the geometric structure of a ring (Ring) and not of a single point; there is no physical force able to converge on the pole point itself [B.5]. The true density excess prevails along a complete ring – the ring standing at a distance of 90∘ from the sub-Earth point, passing continuously through both poles and both sides (A.9, C.3) – and the poles lead the top of the order only because the rotation axis sets their geometric centre of convergence [B.5]. The drain interpretation holds the correct sign (an excess) but a spatial pattern that distorts: it requires a point peak, whereas the observations show a constant plateau over a wide area cell and a global crowding band encircling the whole body [B.5].

B.6 Uniform change (Isotropic Volume/Scale Change Hypothesis)

Definition of the interpretation:

This hypothesis proposes to explain the density excess through global isotropic (uniform) processes, such as: a uniform volume expansion, a uniform thermal contraction of the whole body during its cooling stages, or the action of a strong self-gravity that draws all crustal material equally toward the centre of mass – that is, a mechanical change in the dimension and size of the body (R) without a change in its geometric shape (structure) [B.6]. Each of these events is a real, documented physical process in the early history of a young, hot planetary body, and each of them moves and changes the position of the entire surface [B.6].

The morphological prediction (what it predicts):

A uniform change in the dimension of the body changes every element and every crustal area unit by exactly the same factor and ratio [B.6]. The geographic spacing between the craters grows or shrinks homogeneously at every coordinate on the body, and therefore the density measure changes by a constant, uniform factor both at the poles and at the equatorial belt [B.6]:

ρpolar′​=ρequatorial′​

For a uniformly cratered surface, a global change in size multiplies the numerator (the number of craters) and the denominator (the surface area) by exactly the same mathematical factor, and therefore the statistical ratio between them cannot change [B.6]. The mechanism works like the uniform inflation of a balloon: the operation makes all the points imprinted on it sparser, but it preserves equality and cannot produce a region denser or sparser relative to another [B.6].

What the empirical counts say:

The observations on the surface establish a sharp morphological difference: a ratio of 1.32 in the raw count, 1.20±0.05 in the clean count, and a consistent climbing trend as a function of crater diameter up to a value of 1.53 in the large classes [B.1, B.6].

Verdict:

The uniform-change hypothesis fails absolutely in both the sign test and the magnitude test, since it cannot produce any density excess or spatial variance at all [B.6].

However, this is the methodological interpretation that charted the analytical path of the study [B.6]. Once a process of uniform change in size had been physically ruled out, physics dictated a firm conclusion: a change in size cannot produce a polar excess; only a change in the shape of the body (Anisotropic Distortion) can produce such an anomaly [B.6]. This change of shape must be non-uniform in space in a defined way: it must mechanically contract the surface in the polar regions at the maximum rate, and it must preserve full axial symmetry about the rotation axis [B.6].

Since hypotheses B.2 and B.3 represent real changes of shape but with the wrong mechanical sign (dilution of the poles), the scientific solution of the puzzle requires their exact geodynamic reversal [B.6]. This stage narrowed the scientific question: the search was directed exclusively at finding the specific change of shape that contracts the polar surface more than any other region, and only one geodynamic process in the history of the model satisfies this constraint [B.6].

B.7 The answer, and why it is the one that remains (The Flattening Release / Spherical Rebound)

A single geodynamic change of shape in the system gives a precise and complete answer to all the boundary constraints set by the observations, in which the previous interpretations failed: the decay of flattening of a highly flattened triaxial body after its release from the Earth, as the stretching that held it disappeared and its rotation slowed, and it rounded back toward a sphere with a self-driven decrease in volume [B.7].

Closing the constraints and matching the physical setting:

1. The mechanical sign (positive): The mechanism is the exact geometric and mechanical reversal of hypotheses B.2 and B.3 [B.7]. The release of the stretching and the subsequent contraction act with the correct sign and crowd the crust [B.7].

2. The physical engine: driven by the self-gravity forces of section B.4 in their exact physical place – after the release, when the stretching that had held the flattening – between the Earth's gravity and the point of attachment on the near side, and the centrifugal pull outward – disappeared and the rotation of the receding Moon slowed, so that nothing held the flattening any longer [B.4, B.7]. As long as the Moon was attached and rotating with the Earth, the flattening was held; once released, it became an excess load that self-gravity undid [B.7].

3. The spatial geometry: it produces precisely the structure of the symmetric ring around the rotation axis (B.5), with the polar regions leading the peak of mechanical crowding and contraction because the rotation axis passes through them and all the meridians retreat toward them (the poles are the only points that the rotation never moved) [B.5, B.7].

4. The magnitude test and chronological consistency: The physical dimensions are derived directly from the shape that the craters themselves record around the six axes (A.9) and from tests of agreement with the hydrostatic equilibrium shape of a Maclaurin spheroid (C.1) [B.7]. The rounding model does not predict a static value, but a dynamic chronological ordering that matches fully the empirical findings of the clean count [B.7]:

    • Ancient giant craters (60−100 km): formed at peak flattening on the most deformed body (1.8:1.4:1, density 1,700 kg/m3), underwent the full rounding sequence and therefore show the peak crowding: predicted ~1.5 versus 1.53±0.19 empirical [A.8.5, B.7].
    • Small craters (20–30 km): formed early in the build-up of flattening, on a body that was still only slightly flattened; they were stretched apart as the flattening grew and compressed back in the decay, and keep only a small net contraction: predicted ~1.2 versus 1.09 ± 0.07 empirical [A.8.5, B.7].
    • The whole population (≥20 km): the six-axis model reconstructs a combined shape of 1.37:1.15:1, which independently predicts a ratio of 1.21, matching precisely the result of the residual clean count: 1.20±0.05 [A.9, B.7].

5. The mask test: The effect is robust and fully survives the cleaning out of the maria, the basins and the SPA system, since it is embedded in the mechanics of the solid crust itself [B.7].

6. Defined timing and formation window: The craters that record the full excess formed at peak flattening, before the release; the crowding itself took place after the final mechanical detachment, in the decay of flattening, and stopped when the shape froze [B.7]. The interior of the body was soft and viscous enough to follow the decay, while the outer shell was rigid enough to carry the craters as intact, isolated elements (the contraction closed the elastic spaces between them and built up the pressure of C.4) [B.7].

7. The state of the shell beneath the poles: if the polar surface contracted more than the equatorial surface, the material in it was pushed together and the crust there should have thickened [C.7]. Yet the polar crust is today thinner than the equatorial crust [D.6]. The explanation is that the polar shell was thinner still before the rounding: during the flattening the light material of the outer shell flowed from the poles to the equator (external rotational differentiation, C.8). The same answer therefore explains both the crater density at the poles and the crust beneath them [B.7, C.8].

The meaning of the rise with crater diameter:

The climbing trend of the density ratio as crater diameter increases is the clearest and most direct empirical evidence for a change of shape along the timeline [B.7]. The great majority of the craters formed before the release, and all of them were crowded after it; a crater records the net change of shape from its own formation to the sphere [B.7]. The largest craters, formed at peak flattening, record the whole transformation; the small craters, formed early on a body that was still only slightly flattened, were first stretched apart with it and record only a small net contraction [B.7]. No alternative hypothesis (from B.1 to B.6) can produce a structural dependence between the density excess and crater diameter; the rounding model requires it physically [B.7].

We now have a single physical cause that successfully passes all four empirical tests, and six hypotheses that were rigorously rejected [B.7].

PART C

Part C — The geodynamic mechanism and its numbers

Part B of the study ruled out all six alternative explanations [B.7]. The analytical rejection left one possible mechanical cause: the geometric transition of a highly flattened triaxial body that, after its release from the Earth, rounds back toward the shape of a sphere as its flattening decays, with a self-driven decrease in volume and a rise in density [B.7, C]. This part turns that answer into a quantitative physical mechanism: it defines the shape dimensions of the young Moon, the stress vectors that changed it, the spatial effect on the crust, and the energy that drove the process [C].

The sequence of deforming forces and the morphological evolution:

The geometry of the young Moon was set under a dynamic equilibrium equation between three main force vectors [C]:

1. The pull of self-gravity: tended to press all parts of the body uniformly inward toward the centre, and on its own would have produced a perfect sphere [C].

2. The centrifugal acceleration of the fast rotation: in the stage of synchronous attachment to the Earth (a period of about 5.5 hours), the rotation pushed the equatorial belt outward and lowered the polar regions [C].

3. The tidal stretching stresses (the Roche effect): stretched the body extremely along the radial axis between the Earth and the Moon [B.3, C]. The Earth's gravity pulled the near side inward, while the centrifugal force of corotation drew the mass outward, with the base of the body physically held on the tip of the pear structure [C]. This stretching shortened the two perpendicular axes, and forced the polar axis to absorb the maximum mechanical shortening [C].

The chronology of the shape sequence unfolds along the mechanical stages of separation [C]:

  • The initial gathering stage: a light sialic mass with a density of 1,300 kg/m3 consolidated at the tip of the Earth's pear structure and began to move outward on a base 6,000 km wide, with initial flattening under the Earth's constraint [C].
  • The stage of body stabilisation and maximum flattening: as the mass moved away, the base of the pear narrowed to a width of 3,000 km [C]. When the pear reached corotation, the two sides of the body were pulled in opposite directions and the body reached its peak geometric deformation near the 3,000 km base [C]. This peak shape is analysed in sections C.1–C.2 [C].
  • The attached stage and the release: the moment the Moon's centre of mass crossed the corotation line, the net pull that pressed it onto the base of the pear dropped to zero, and about 210 km beyond the line the Moon detached [C, C.6]. Up to the release the flattening kept growing and reached its peak, held by the synchronous spin and the tidal stretching, and its rigid outer shell carried it inside the fluid stability limit [C].
  • The decay of flattening after the release: after the detachment the stretching that had held the flattening – between the Earth's gravity and the point of attachment on the near side, and the centrifugal pull outward – disappeared, and the rotation slowed as the Moon receded; with no force left to hold it, the flattening decayed, and the body rounded with a sharp self-driven decrease in volume, becoming smaller, thicker and denser [C, C.5]. The crowding of the polar surface took place in this decay, and stopped when the shape froze [C].

C.1 The initial shape at peak flattening: rotation and density

The question of this section quantifies mathematically how flattened and deformed the Moon was at the peak of the flattening stage, and how its shape changed through the stages of inward collapse [C.1]. To compute the rotational component only two physical parameters are needed: the angular velocity of rotation (Ω) and the mean density of the material (ρ) [C.1].

For a self-gravitating homogeneous fluid (a body of uniform density held together by its gravity alone, with no initial mechanical strength), the exact hydrostatic equilibrium shape is defined as a Maclaurin spheroid (Maclaurin Spheroid) [C.1]. The degree to which the spheroid deviates from a perfect sphere is measured by its eccentricity, e=1−c2/a2​ (where a is the equatorial radius and c is the polar radius; e=0 gives a perfect sphere, and e→1 gives a flattened disc) [C.1]. The body remains stable at rest when the angular velocity Ω (expressed as 2π/T, where T is the rotation period) satisfies the structural equation [C.1]:

πGρΩ2​=e321−e2​(3−2e2)​arcsin(e)−e26(1−e2)​
  • The mechanics of the equation: The left-hand side compares the outward centrifugal force (Ω2) with the inward self-gravity of a uniform body (Gρ, where G is the universal gravitational constant) [C.1]. The right-hand side is a transcendental function of the geometric shape alone [C.1]. The right-hand side climbs from zero (for a sphere) to an absolute maximum of 0.4493, reached at an eccentricity of e=0.930 (giving a sharp axis ratio of a/c=2.72) [C.1]. Beyond this mechanical limit, no stable Maclaurin shape physically exists [C.1].
  • Parametric sensitivity: The faster the rotation rate relative to the density, the more flattened the equilibrium shape [C.1]. A body of low density (light) is more susceptible to flattening than a dense body at the same rotation rate, because its weak gravity field offers less resistance to the centrifugal stress [C.1].

Solution matrix of the dynamic axis ratio (a/c):

Solving the Maclaurin equation for the parameter values of the detachment stages yields the following matrix of ratios of equatorial radius to polar radius [C.1]:

  • Horizontal reading (the density vector): The geometric shape undergoes continuous rounding (the value of a/c falling toward 1.00) as the density of the material rises, since a fixed rotation rate cannot hold a flattened deformation against a self-gravity field that strengthens and pulls inward [C.1].
  • Vertical reading (the rotation vector): The shape rounds slightly as the rotation slows from 5.5 to 5.77 hours [C.1].
  • Calibrating the rotational flattening (the highlighted values): The matrix defines two reference values of the rotational flattening of the body: the stretched, inflated body at peak flattening (1.41 at a density of about 1,700 kg/m³, the shape at the release), and the dense body at the same spin (1.20 at a density of 2,600 kg/m³) [C.1]. After the release the spin slows, and the flattening decays below both values (C.5) [C.1].
  • The pear reference value (1.300 kg/m3): the value of 1.69 reflects the shape that the light mass gathered at the tip of the pear would have taken as a free fluid from rotation alone; this value serves as physical context only, and not as a measured peak value of the independent body [C.1].

The lower stability limit for the density of the material:

At a rotation period of 5.5 hours and a density of 1,000 kg/m3, the equation yields no equilibrium solution, because the centrifugal stress exceeds the maximum allowed point of the right-hand side [C.1]. In this hypothetical state, the body would break apart and shed mass from its equatorial margins [C.1]. This point defines a firm lower limit on the density of material required to keep the body intact at any rotation rate:

ρmin​=0.4493πGΩ2​

For a rotation period of 5.5 hours, the minimum density limit is set mathematically at 1,070 kg/m3; a planetary body lighter than this value cannot hold itself together as a fluid at such a rotation rate [C.1].

Location of the peak deformation and the triaxial geometry

  • Timing of maximum flattening: In the initial stages, the mass acted as an integral part of the tip of the pear (density 1,300, distance ≈ 8,991 km), and its shape was dictated directly by the Earth [C.1]. Independent morphological flattening developed once the mass became an independent body able to stabilise itself, a condition met on crossing the rigid Roche limit [C.1]. Beyond this limit, self-gravity and material strength overcome the disruptive tidal forces of the Earth [C.1]. For light material (1,300 kg/m³), the Roche limit lies farther out, at a distance of 12,994 km (the limit varies as ρ−1/3; for a density of 2,600 kg/m³ it is closer, at 10,314 km) [C.1]. The body moved outward beyond 13,000 km while its base narrowed from 6,000 to 3,000 km, and reached maximum geometric deformation and flattening as it approached the 3,000 km base, very close to crossing the corotation line (15,818 km at a period of 5.5 hours); its flattening kept growing up to the release, where it peaked [C.1].
  • The triaxial structure (an egg that is also flattened): The shape at peak deformation was not a symmetric biaxial spheroid [C.1]. While the rotation flattened the body about its axis, the two-body tidal stresses of the Earth actively stretched it along the Earth-line axis [C.1]. The combination of stresses imposed a triaxial shape with three distinct axes: a long axis directed toward the Earth (a), an intermediate axis directed along the orbital motion vector (b), and a short, held axis connecting the poles (c) [C.1].

The empirical crater-excess record reconstructs and confirms these dimensions precisely (sections A.9, C.3): the original peak shape stood at a ratio of roughly 1.8:1.4:1, within a morphometric scatter range of between 1.64:1.45:1 and 1.95:1.33:1 [C.1]. The whole population (≥20 km) converges to a combined average of 1.37:1.15:1 [C.1]. This is a moderate and physically clear deformation: the long axis is 1.6 to 1.95 times the polar axis, and the intermediate axis is 1.33 to 1.45 times it [C.1].

Confirmation of the peak density measures (≈1,700 kg/m3):

Determining the density of the body at peak flattening is based on cross-checking two independent dynamic tests, which yield full agreement [C.1]:

1. Confirmation of the rotational flattening by the Maclaurin relation: The rotational flattening of the shape (b/c≈1.4) is set exclusively by the rotational stresses [C.1]. To a first approximation, the difference between the intermediate and short axes of a tidally stretched body depends on the spin rate, and therefore it can be read directly from the Maclaurin equation [C.1]. At a rotation period of 5.5 hours, the Maclaurin relation gives an exact value of b/c=1.41 for a body with a density of 1,700 kg/m3 (the highlighted value in the table) [C.1]. The empirical scatter range (1.33−1.45) bounds the density within limits of 1,615 to 1,960 kg/m3, with the core concentrated at 1,600–1,750 [C.1].

2. The geometric surface-closure limit: The transition from a stretched body to a sphere after the release involves a decay of the stretching and a global decrease in volume [C.1]. The geometric equations (C.3) prove that had the density of the body at the peak been higher than 1,800 kg/m³, the available stretching volume would have been too small; in that case, the ends of the tidal axis would have been forced to expand and grow during rounding instead of contracting and closing [C.1].

The two tests fix the value of the body at the peak as a stretched, inflated body with a density of about 1,700 kg/m³, yielding an equivalent-sphere radius (the radius of a sphere of the same volume) of about 2,180 km [C.1]. The body is released with this density and radius; after the release it compacts to about 2,600 kg/m³ (radius about 1,890 km), and today its radius is 1,737 km [C.1]. The original sialic mass on the tip of the pear (1,300 kg/m³, equivalent radius about 2,380 km) is the early starting base, before the dynamic flattening stage came into play [C.1].

The stages of mechanical rounding

When the centre of mass crossed the corotation line, the body began the process of rounding back to a sphere, which took place in two separate mechanical stages [C.1]:

1. The egg part (the tidal axis a): on the corotation line the net pull that pressed the body onto the base of the pear fell to zero, and the base let go [C.1, C.6]. The stretching along the Earth line itself, held by the synchronous spin and the tide, persisted up to the release and decayed afterwards, as the Moon receded and the tide weakened [C.1].

2. The rotational flattening (b/c): held as long as the body rotated with the Earth (5.5 hours, lengthening to 5.77 at the line) [C.1]. After the release the rotation slowed with recession (6.6 hours at 18,000 km, 14 hours at 30,000 km), lowering the outward centrifugal push, while the density of the material rose from about 1,700 toward 2,600 kg/m³ [C.1]. Both effects reduce the flattening: the rotational component falls to 1.14–1.24 at 18,000 km, 1.03–1.04 at 30,000 km and about 1.005 at 60,000 km [C.1, C.5].

A fluid body completing a spin once every few hours must physically show a flattening deformation and cannot exist as a perfect sphere in a viscous state [C.1]. This is why the flattening was held as long as the Moon rotated with the Earth, and why it could decay only after the release, as the spin slowed [C.1]. The rounding is completed by the slowing of the spin itself: at 60,000 km (a spin of about 40 hours) the rotational flattening of a fluid body is only about 1.005 [C.1]. The small flattening that remained when the interior stiffened froze in place; today's fossil flattening (f ≈ 0.001) is its remnant (C.5, C.7) [C.1].

The Maclaurin equation is a basic physical law, and the solutions of the matrix depend on nothing other than the values of the angular velocity (Ω) and the density of the material (ρ) [C.1].

C.2 The tidal component: the free shape and the Roche effect

Whereas section C.1 computed the effect of the rotational stresses alone, this section brings in the second force vector that shaped the body morphologically: the Earth's tidal forces (the Roche effect) and the complex balance of potentials in the system [C.2]. The analysis serves as a geometric tool to illustrate the contribution of the radial stretching, and is not the basis for the statistical density test [C.2].

The two-body dynamics in the rotating system:

A planetary body in close proximity to the Earth and in synchronous rotational locking (the orbital period equal to the spin period Ω) is stretched extremely along the radial axis between it and the Earth [C.2]. In the attached stage, the mass is held at the tip of the pear structure, under a balance of opposing stresses: the Earth's gravity pulls the near flank inward, and the centrifugal force pulls it outward [C.2].

The classical physical model reproduces this structure by computing the shape of a free homogeneous fluid (with no contact constraint), which takes on the configuration of a Roche ellipsoid (Roche Ellipsoid) with three distinct axes (a:b:c): the tidal axis toward the Earth (a), the axis of orbital motion (b), and the short axis connecting the poles (c) [C.2]. Unlike the biaxial Maclaurin shape (which looks like a perfect circle when viewed from above the pole), the Roche ellipsoid is deformed and egg-like from every viewing angle [C.2].

The hydrostatic potential-balance equation:

The surface of a fluid body at rest must physically be an equipotential surface (Equipotential Surface), so that no material flows along it [C.2]. Within a uniform ellipsoid, the total potential is made up of the mathematical sum of three energy components [C.2]:

1. The self-gravity of the body: the energy rises as the square of the distance from the centre along the axes (x,y,z corresponding to the axes a,b,c), and the static coefficients A1​,A2​,A3​ (which satisfy the Chandrasekhar index equation: A1​+A2​+A3​=2) set the steepness of the rise [C.2]. The shortest axis (c) is assigned the maximum coefficient (A3​), since the mass is concentrated closer to it [C.2].

2. The tidal potential of the Earth: expressed as −μ(x2−21​y2−21​z2), where the stretching factor is μ=r3GM​ (M is the mass of the Earth and r the orbital distance) [C.2]. This component lowers the potential along the tidal axis (x) and raises it across it (y,z), an action that applies radial stretching and tangential compression [C.2].

3. The centrifugal potential of the orbit: expressed as −21​Ω2(x2+y2) (according to Kepler's third law in the system: Ω2=r3G(M+m)​) [C.2]. This component lowers the potential outward away from the rotation axis, and leaves the polar component (z) unchanged [C.2].

For the surface to balance in a closed shape, the net inward pull (gravity minus the rotation and tidal factors) multiplied by the square of the axis length must be exactly equal at all three ends [C.2]:

a2(A1​−πGρΩ2​−πGρ2μ​)=b2(A2​−πGρΩ2​+πGρμ​)=c2(A3​+πGρμ​)

This combined equation yields two sets of conditions for the two independent axis ratios: b/a and c/a [C.2].

  • Decoding the dimensions of the stretched shape (1:0.637:0.601): an extreme asymmetry is established, in which the tidal axis facing the Earth is two-thirds longer (≈66%) than the short polar axis [C.2].
  • Normalisation to an equivalent-sphere volume (Rs​): the mean radius of a sphere of the same volume is defined by Rs​=(abc)1/3 [C.2]. The last two columns quantify the degree of displacement of the surface during the geometric transition (the rounding) toward this equivalent sphere [C.2]:
    • The polar component: the value of Rs​/c=1.208 dictates that during rounding, the polar apex must rise and leap outward by about a fifth of its height (≈21%) [C.2].
    • The tidal-axis component: the value of Rs​/a=0.726 dictates that the sub-Earth point must collapse inward and sink by about a quarter of its length (≈27%) [C.2].

Geodynamic implications and the limits of the rigid Roche limit

The mathematical calculation establishes two basic physical rules that constrain the detachment stages [C.2]:

1. Ruling out a free fluid at release: at the source density of the pear (1,300 kg/m³), the fluid Roche limit lies very far out, at a distance of about 25,200 km, and at the release density of about 1,700 kg/m³ at about 23,200 km [C.2]. A body released at about 16,610 km therefore could not hold together as a free fluid; it was held by its rigid outer shell until it had receded and compacted (C.5) [C.2].

2. Pinning down the exact fluid Roche limit: at a density of 2,600, solving the equations shows that at 19,660 km the shape breaks apart, while at 20,595 it is stable; the exact fluid Roche limit is fixed between them – at 19,971 km according to the classical coefficient, and at 20,100 km (k=0.09) under the exact potential solution [C.2].

The rigid-crust limit in the dynamic sequence:

In the updated LEF model, the Moon is released and mechanically detaches much earlier and closer to the Earth – at a distance of about 16,400 km at the equator (16,399 km at a period of 5.77 hours) and 17,287 km at the latitudes of 22.5° [C.2]. At these close distances, physics dictates that no stable free fluid shape exists or can exist at the release density (the region lies deep within the fluid Roche limit: about 23,200 km at 1,700 kg/m³, and 20,100 km at 2,600) [C.2].

The physical meaning is firm: the young Moon held together and kept its structural integrity in this region thanks to its outer shell, which stiffened early, and not by virtue of a fluid hydrostatic equilibrium [C.2]. Therefore, the triaxial model of this section serves solely as an indicator and illustration tool showing how the external tidal stresses imposed a sharp radial stretching along the a axis in addition to the rotational flattening of the b/c axis (C.1) [C.2]. The density excess and the statistical anomaly measured on the surface are exclusively the result of the decay of this combined stretching after the release, with the rounding and volume decrease (C.1, C.5, D.2) [C.2].

Whereas sections C.1 and C.2 defined the initial deformation dimensions, this section computes the transformation of the deformed surface during its mechanical collapse to a perfect spherical shape under a condition of volume decrease (compaction and stiffening of the core) [C.3]. The aim is to determine mathematically which crustal area cells close and contract at the maximum rate, which at the minimum rate, and where the existing craters become crowded [C.3]. The output of the calculation is a measure of the differential density ratio between the poles and the equator, which is robust and independent of the body's overall isotropic contraction rate [C.3].

  • A chronological distinction in the series: the geodynamic model defines three successive deformation stages:
    1. Outward rounding: the initial stage in which the sialic mass detached from the tip of the pear and became an isolated fluid sphere (Paper 3).
    2. The flattening stage: the stage of extreme two-body elongation and flattening near the corotation line.
    3. Inward rounding (the rounding of this paper): the decay of flattening, the collapse of the stretched structure back toward a sphere, which takes place after the release, as the spin of the receding Moon slows [C.3].

The squashed-balloon analogy:

To make the mechanics accessible, imagine a round balloon covered with dots (craters) distributed uniformly per unit area, which is pressed and firmly squashed between two flat palms (the two-body stresses) [B.5, C.3]. Owing to the pressure, its top and bottom become wide, flattened and flat, while the circumferential rim (the equator) is sharply stretched [B.5, C.3].

When the stresses that held the deformation decay (after the release, as the spin slows), the balloon releases its residual elastic energy and springs back toward its spherical shape [C.3]. In this geometric process, the wide, flat surfaces of the ends are rapidly gathered inward and converge into a narrow zone: the dots imprinted on them physically draw closer together at the maximum rate, while the middle rim undergoes the minimum change of area [B.5, C.3].

The geophysical mechanics of fixing the end points at the poles

Why is it precisely the geographic polar regions that function as the main centres of convergence and crowding of the crust [C.3]?

  • Refuting thickness or gravity hypotheses: GRAIL satellite observations rule out the existence of a thickened crust or lateral gravity anomalies in the polar regions relative to the latitude belt in which they lie (B.4) [C.3].
  • The rotation-axis constraint (The Axial Geometric Anchor): the poles are the structural end points through which the body's rotation axis physically passes [C.3]. Since the rotational flattening stresses act completely symmetrically about this axis, all the global meridians were deformed and stretched uniformly, while the two end points on the axis remained static (they have no "outward" momentum component of their own) [C.3].
  • The wheel-spoke mechanism: as the rotational flattening decays, the crustal material that had previously been pushed out returns inward along exactly the same meridians [C.3]. Since all the meridians of a spherical body converge and meet at the poles, these end regions function as a structural hub that gathers into itself the surface of all the meridians [C.3]. This geometric property explains why there are exactly two polar crowding foci in the system, located in exactly opposite positions facing each other [C.3]. The model fixes the ancient rounding poles as the geographic poles observed on the surface today [C.3].

Distribution of the differential tensile stresses over the surface

During the deformation stage, the crust in the polar regions was the flattest, most stretched and most widened in the system [C.3]. By contrast, the Earth's tidal stretching (the Roche effect) stretched the body extremely along the a axis (the radial line), with its near part held at the tip of the pear structure [C.3]. As a result, the surface at both ends of the Earth line (the sub-Earth and anti-Earth points) was compressed and less stretched than any other sector [C.3].

Therefore, as the stresses decayed and the body rounded:

  • Maximum surface contraction: takes place on the polar surface (the return of the maximum rotational stretching), and produces the highest crater-density excess [C.3].
  • Minimum surface contraction: takes place at the ends of the tidal axis (the sub-Earth point), and leaves the crater record in its sparsest state (94 craters per 10⁶ km²) [A.9, C.3].

The geometric balance equation: the combined density factor

The mechanical crowding is not limited to the polar ends alone; it affects a complete global ring standing at an angular distance of 90∘ from the Earth-line axis (the polar-tangential ring passing through both poles and both orbital sides) [C.3]. The reason is that the two ends of the tidal axis, as they collapse inward during rounding, push and send their share of the surface sideways, toward the middle ring [C.3].

The following is a mathematical calibration of the two-directional area-change factors, using the Roche ellipsoid (C.2) as an illustration model [C.2, C.3]:

The sides (leading and trailing)1.38× (tidal contraction)0.83× (polar stretching)1.14×Moderate crowding along the ring [C.3].

  • Decoding the mathematical dynamics: for each small crustal area cell, two perpendicular stress directions along the ground are defined [C.3]. The rounding shortens or lengthens the dimensions of the cell along these two axes, while the total crater count on it remains unchanged [C.3]. Therefore, the final crater density is computed as the product of the inverses of these two area-change factors (ρcombined​=Factor1​×Factor2​) [C.3].
  • System normalisation: the values are expressed relative to the average global change of area [C.3]. A factor ≥1.00 indicates that the area cell closed and contracted in this direction more than the average (the craters drew closer together); a factor <1.00 indicates a contraction below the average (the craters moved relatively apart) [C.3]. As a result, the poles settle at the top of the order (1.21) and the sides after them (1.14) [C.3]. The sub-Earth point widens along both its axes relative to the average, and therefore shows the minimum density value in the system (0.73) [C.3].

The empirical findings are firm: every point located along the polar ring shows a significant density excess compared with the density valley of the sub-Earth point, which contains less than half the number of craters of the poles [C.3]. The internal asymmetry between the trailing and leading sides is explained by the distribution of local ejection vents and the flow of momentum of returned material that lagged behind the rotational velocity and landed behind (A.9) [C.3]. The polar regions are the geometric site where the maximum crowding takes place and where the phenomenon is measured in its most pristine and clean form, and hence the name of the paper's sections [C.3].

C.3 The mathematical calculation of differential surface contraction and the morphometric predictions

This section is the firm analytical core of the paper [C.3]. It translates the geometric shape changes of the body into transformation equations of the surface, and computes precisely the differential crowding ratios between the different crustal regions [C.3]. The calculation is based on a complete physical separation between two independent components of collapse:

1. The change of shape (Anisotropic Deformation): computed under the firm constraint of constant volume toward an equivalent sphere of radius Rs​=(abc)1/3 [C.3].

2. The isotropic change of size (Isotropic Volume Contraction): the Moon underwent a global thermal contraction and release of stretching that reduced its volume by a factor of about 1.5 during rounding [C.3]. Since this shared contraction multiplies and shrinks every area cell on the body by the same constant factor, it cancels out mathematically and does not change any density ratio [B.6, C.3]. Therefore, the crowding measure of the poles versus the equator is entirely immune to the body's overall contraction rate [C.3].

The homogeneous ellipsoidal transformation equation:

The geometric transition is represented as a homogeneous elastic deformation that turns the ellipsoid shape into a sphere, as if the surface were drawn on a uniform rubber sheet [C.3]. Every coordinate along the long, intermediate and short axis is multiplied by the corresponding stretch factors: Rs​/a,Rs​/b, and Rs​/c respectively [C.3]. A small area cell whose outward normal vector (perpendicular to the surface, of unit length) is defined as n^=(nx​,ny​,nz​) changes its area by the combined geometric factor [C.3]:

Area_Factor=J−1=[nx2(Rsa)2+ny2(Rsb)2+nz2(Rsc)2]−1/2\mathbf{\text{Area\_Factor}\mathbf{=J}^{\mathbf{-1}}\mathbf{=}\left[\mathbf{n}_{\mathbf{x}}^{\mathbf{2}}\left(\frac{\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{s}}}{\mathbf{a}}\right)^{\mathbf{2}}\mathbf{+n}_{\mathbf{y}}^{\mathbf{2}}\left(\frac{\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{s}}}{\mathbf{b}}\right)^{\mathbf{2}}\mathbf{+n}_{\mathbf{z}}^{\mathbf{2}}\left(\frac{\mathbf{R}_{\mathbf{s}}}{\mathbf{c}}\right)^{\mathbf{2}}\right]^{\mathbf{-1/2}}}Area_Factor=J−1=[nx2​(aRs​​)2+ny2​(bRs​​)2+nz2​(cRs​​)2]−1/2

Craters imprinted uniformly on the original surface change their densities in inverse proportion to this area factor (J), since the same number of craters compressed into a smaller area cell will show a higher density [C.3].

The meaning of the formula in the space of the crust:

The equation establishes that the surface area of a patch facing along one spatial axis is governed by the product of the stretches of the two axes perpendicular to it [C.3]. Since the product of the three stretches is exactly 1 (volume conservation in the shape stage), the change of area equals exactly the inverse of the stretch along the axis normal to the patch [C.3]:

  • At the polar apex (nz​=1): the factor shrinks to its minimum value, c/Rs​ [C.3]. The surface undergoes the maximum geometric contraction, equally in every tangential direction, and the residual crater density jumps at the maximum rate of Rs​/c [C.3].
  • At the sub-Earth point (nx​=1): the factor takes its maximum value in the system, a/Rs​ [C.3]. The surface undergoes the minimum contraction, and the crater density there is the lowest, standing at Rs​/a [C.3].
  • The radial transition: between the pole and the equator, the contraction factor weakens continuously with distance from the apex of the axis [C.3]. This mechanical property explains geometrically why the density profile of the pristine north pole (A.6) climbs and sharpens inward directly toward the geographic pole point [C.3].

Calibration of the biaxial model (the oblate spheroid)

For a symmetrically flattened body in which the long and intermediate axes are equal (a=4b), the volume-conservation condition dictates Rs3​=a2c [C.3].

  • The polar surface changes by a factor of c/Rs​=(c/a)2/3, representing a uniform biaxial shortening of (c/a)1/3 along every ground direction [C.3].
  • The equatorial surface changes by a factor of a/Rs​=(a/c)1/3, representing an east–west shortening of (c/a)1/3 against a minimal contraction along the north–south axis – this is the area cell that contracts least of all on the body [C.3].

The statistical ratio between these two regions defines the absolute crowding equation of the pole versus the equator, in which the radius of the sphere (Rs​) cancels out completely [C.3]:

ρequatorial​ρpolar​​=Rs​/aRs​/c​=ca​

A firm rule is established: the maximum theoretical crowding at the pole point relative to the equator equals exactly the equatorial/polar axis ratio (a/c) of the original flattened shape [C.3]. A body that was 1.69 times as wide as it was tall at peak deformation will leave the craters imprinted on it at a density exactly 1.69 times higher at the polar apex relative to the equator [C.1, C.3]. However, when the averages over the final empirical caps are computed, the ratio value is smaller, because the contraction decays with angular distance from the pole [C.3].

Calibration of the triaxial model and agreement with the six axes

For a flattened and stretched triaxial body (a:b:c), the same differential equation sets a threefold density order: the density climbs by a factor Rs​/c at the poles, by a factor Rs​/b at the equatorial sides, and by a factor Rs​/a at the base of the Earth line [C.3]. This order (poles → sides → Earth line) reproduces and fully matches the empirical six-axis order measured in section A.9 [C.3].

To test the validity of the model, the original shape of the body is reconstructed from the six-axis data, and this is carried over, unchanged, to predict the clean ratio of the 30∘ caps versus the equatorial belt (∣ϕ∣<15∘) on the pristine crust [A.9, C.3]:
