where the measure f=a−cb−c​ represents the share of the long axis's excess that the intermediate axis also carries (f=0 represents a pure egg, and f=1 represents pure rotational flattening) [C.3]. For each value of f, the axis-ratio value a/c is chosen that yields the exact clean ratio of the 60–100 km class (a value of 1.44, with the sub-Earth point neutralised from the belt on both sides owing to the depletion of the contact disc in A.9.2) [C.3]:

The excess of the value actually measured (f≈0.35−0.60) is direct mechanical proof that the elongation of the tidal axis (the egg part) was physically restrained and curbed relative to the rotational flattening, evidence for the existence of a rigid holding base that restrained the stretching (C.6) [C.3].

The mechanical model of the geometric chronological clock

The mathematical analysis of the transformation sequence is defined as a geometric chronological clock [C.3]. Each geometric stage along the path of inward collapse from peak flattening to a sphere represents a dynamic moment in history, and the residual crowding fixed in the crust depends exclusively on the remaining rounding that took place after the crater formed [C.3]:

Peak flattening (1.8:1.4:1) → predicted 1.49 mid-rounding (1.30) → predicted 1.26 late (1.20) → predicted 1.17

A crater formed at the peak absorbed the full sequence of surface contraction, while a crater formed late received only the closing chord [C.3]. Since ejections of material took place also during the growth, an intermediate shape was crossed twice (on the way up and on the way down); therefore, a large, crowded crater reflects formation near the peak point, and not necessarily earlier in chronological terms [C.3].

The calculation is carried out by direct integration on a 0.05∘ grid of the spatial density-factor function [C.3]:

J(λ,ϕ)=Rs​[cos2λ(a2cos2ϕ​+b2sin2ϕ​)+c2sin2λ​]1/2

where λ,ϕ are the angular coordinates on the surface; the precision achieved between the two analytical calculation methods is 10−7, and the code is fully included in the reproduction package of the system [C.3].

The morphometric determination is firm: the craters themselves kept their original diameter and were carried as rigid elements (tiles) on a solid upper crust; what contracted and closed elastically was the surface and the seam spaces between them (C.7, D.2) [C.3]. The largest craters (100−300 km) show an empirical value of 1.84±0.38, which suggests a shape reading beyond the theoretical peak, but falls within the wide counting error of the sample [C.3].

C.3.1 Mathematical calibration of the volume decrease and the absolute area factors

To complete the development of the mechanism, the mathematical calculation fuses together the two components of the crustal transformation: the geometric change of shape (at constant volume) together with the isotropic change of size (thermal contraction and compaction of the core) [C.3]. In the transition from peak flattening at release (ρ ≈ 1,700 kg/m³) to the compacted sphere after the decay (ρ ≈ 2,600 kg/m³), the global volume of the body falls by a firm factor of 1.53 [C.3.1].

This fall shrinks the equivalent radius of the young Moon by 13% (from 2,180 km at the peak to 1,890 km after compaction), and mathematically reduces the average global surface area by a quarter [C.3.1]. The following are the absolute area-change factors (combining the volume decrease and the rounding together) computed for the centre of the peak-shape family (1.75 : 1.45 : 1) at a density of 1,700 kg/m³ [C.3, C.3.1]:

The surface at the ends of the Earth line (axis a)0.97×Minimum surface contraction in the system [C.3.1].

  • Decoding the mechanical order: Reading the table from top to bottom reproduces precisely the empirical six-axis order: the poles close and contract at the sharpest rate (0.55), the sides after them (0.80), and the ends of the Earth line show the minimum change (0.97) [C.3.1].
  • The motion vectors of the surface: Under this dynamic geometry, the polar regions function as a rigid anchor and hardly move in space (the physical polar radius grows by only about 290 km as a result of the outward rounding, while the body as a whole contracts inward) [C.3.1]. All the other parts of the crust move actively along the body toward them: the areas of the sides retreat inward by about 430 km, and the surface at the ends of the Earth line collapses inward by about 900 km [C.3.1]. This is the squashed-balloon mechanism – the two ends of the axis are fixed, and all the rest of the material of the belly gathers and converges toward them [C.3, C.3.1].

Confirmation of the theoretical peak-density limit

The absolute calculation provides a second physical check for setting the peak-density limit (≈1,700 kg/m3) [C.1, C.3.1]:

  • For all area cells on the body to undergo positive closure and contraction (a factor value <1.00), physics dictates that the density of the body at the peak must be fixed below an upper threshold of about 1,800 kg/m3 (exactly 1,790 kg/m3 for this shape configuration) [C.3.1].
  • Had the body at the peak been denser than this value, the geometric energy would have been too small; in that hypothetical case, the surface at the ends of the Earth line would have been forced to expand and grow (factor ≥1.00) during rounding instead of closing, a finding that contradicts the crater record [C.1, C.3.1].

It is firmly emphasised that the scientific test of the paper does not rest on these absolute factor values, which are sensitive to the theoretical peak density [C.3.1]. The test is based exclusively on the statistical ratio between the last two rows (0.671​=1.49), which is robust and remains completely constant for any value of peak density, because the shared isotropic contraction term cancels out of it completely [C.3.1]. The scientific claim of the study rests on this ratio factor: the poles crowd to the system maximum and the equator to the minimum, without dependence on, or need for, an exact numerical determination of the contraction rate of the equator itself [C.3.1]. (The presence of mechanical strength in the crust would partially restrain the deformation, and yield more moderate contraction factors, a mechanism developed in section E.3) [C.3.1].

The evolution of the Moon's shape in three dynamic stages

Figure 10 brings together the entire geodynamic mechanism in a sequence of three successive stages of development, illustrating how the crater dots, imprinted uniformly on the flattened body, converge and crowd at the two poles as the body tends toward a spherical shape [C.3.1]:

1. Stage 1 ("tip of the pear"): an initial sialic mass consolidates at the tip of the Earth's elongated structure, held at its wide, curved mechanical base (an initial base width of about 6,000 km at an orbital distance of ≈8,991 km) [C.1, C.3.1].

2. Stage 2 ("structural peak flattening"): the mass separates from the pear material and becomes an independent attached body, moving beyond the rigid Roche limit (≈ 13,000 km) toward the corotation line [C.1, C.3.1]. The base narrows to a width of 3,000 km, and the body is stretched extremely between the Earth's gravity inward and the centrifugal force of corotation outward [C.1, C.3.1]. The body takes on a precise triaxial geometry of a : b : c ≈ 1.8 : 1.4 : 1 (computed for the centre of the family 1.75 : 1.45 : 1), reached at the release [C.1, C.3.1]. In this stretched, inflated state, the density of the material stands at about 1,700 kg/m³ and its physical dimensions are set at 5,585 × 4,628 × 3,191 km [C.3.1]. The crater population is deposited over this flattening morphology as it builds up and at its peak, in a uniform distribution per unit area [C.3.1].

3. Stage 3 ("the rounded body after the release"): the Moon is released about 210 km beyond the corotation line at the peak of its flattening, reached at that moment; afterwards its spin slows with recession, the flattening decays, and the body collapses inward with a self-driven decrease in volume to a round, smaller and denser shape [C.1, C.3.1]. The density climbs to 2,600 kg/m³ and the size of the body converges to a spherical diameter of 3,778 km [C.1, C.3.1]. The geometric transition contracts the local area at the poles by a factor of 0.55×, and gives rise to the official bipolar density excess of the 30° caps versus the equatorial belt, fixed at a predicted value of 1.49× [C.3.1].

Summary of the combined mechanism:

It has been shown geodynamically that a flattened body rounding under a condition of ultimate volume decrease closes and reduces its polar surface at the maximum rate, and its equatorial belt at the minimum rate [C.3.1]. Crustal craters imprinted on the crust before the rounding stage end the sequence concentrated and crowded in the polar regions by an exact factor set exclusively by the original geometric shape (excess values of about 1.2 to 1.5 within the counted caps, depending on their time of formation relative to the peak point) [C.3.1]. The six-axis model reproduces and confirms the validity of the empirical phenomenon across all the size classes, without the need for free parameters [C.3.1].

C.4 Gravity as the physical engine, the slope profile, and the energy and pressure balance

This section defines the dynamic engine that drove the rounding process, quantifies the energy output released in the system, and decodes its effects on the interior of the lunar body [C.4]. The mechanism proves that there is no need to assume a new external force: after the release, as the stretching that held the flattening disappears and the rotation of the receding Moon slows, the flattening becomes an excess load, and the Moon's self-gravity field, which strengthens as the volume shrinks and the material is compressed, is what forces the body to round [C.4]. Since the outer shell is rigid, this deformation builds a sharp internal pressure that finds release through the key geological openings already existing in the crust (the maria) [C.4].

1. The two-component decay of the deformation after the release

The original deformation of the body was held by a temporary balance of forces: the stresses of fast synchronous rotation together with the two-body tidal stretching along the Earth line (the Roche effect), while the body was mechanically pressed onto the base of the pear [C.2, C.4]. After the release, the decay of the deformation and the inward collapse proceeded through the separate decay of the two shape components [C.4]:

  • The egg part (the tidal axis a): while attached, this stretching was held by the synchronous spin, the tide and the compressive force against the base of the pear [C.4]. On the corotation line the compression fell to zero and the base let go; after the release the tide weakened rapidly with distance (as the cube of the distance), and the egg part decayed inward [C.1, C.4].
  • The rotational flattening (b/c): this component was undone by the Moon's self-gravity [C.4]. After the release the rotation slowed with recession, lowering the outward centrifugal push, while the density of the material rose from about 1,700 to about 2,600 kg/m³ owing to the combined volume collapse [C.1, C.4]. As a consequence, the measure of the balance of rotation against self-gravity, expressed by the left-hand side of the Maclaurin equation:
πGρΩ2​

fell from 0.28 at the peak, first through the rise in density (to 0.17 at 2,600 kg/m³ at the same spin) and then, much more strongly, through the slowing of the spin (to about 0.02 at 30,000 km) [C.1, C.4]. This parametric fall forced the theoretical equilibrium shape to fall correspondingly from 1.41 toward 1.0 [C.1, C.4]. Gravity is the sole engine of this stage: a slowing rotation can no longer hold a flattened configuration against the internal gravity field of a body that has become dense and pulls more strongly inward [C.1, C.4]. The dynamics are like a figure skater spinning with outstretched arms whose physical weight suddenly increases without her rotation speeding up – she can no longer hold her arms stretched out at the same radius [C.4].

2. The potential slope profile and the crustal flow

On a highly flattened body that has departed from its hydrostatic equilibrium, the effective potential vector changes and reverses its dynamic direction [C.4]. After the release, the structural flattening that the rapid rotation previously held at the low density (1,700) becomes an anomalous excess load that the slowing spin and the enhanced gravity at the high density (2,600) cannot bear [C.4].

As a result, the polar regions become geometrically the absolute minimum points of the effective potential (the floor of a potential valley), while the equatorial belt stands at the top of the order [C.4]. The elastic crustal materials and the whole surface experience a lateral push vector and flow down this energy slope – from the equatorial belt directly inward toward the poles, along all the global meridians [C.4]. The mechanical process works like a bowl of thick honey that has been tilted and returned to the horizontal: the viscous fluid will flow on its own, by its own weight alone, until it reaches a flat surface and a renewed equilibrium, without any need for additional external pressure [C.4].

3. The energy-output equations and the values of thermal compression

The process of rounding and inward collapse releases in the system two independent spatial energy terms, which turn into heat and thermally feed the interior of the body [C.4]:

a. The shape-change term (eccentricity energy):

The inward rounding lowers the global gravitational energy of the body from the deformation level of the ellipsoid to the minimum level of an equivalent sphere of the same volume [C.4]. For a flattened spheroid with eccentricity e (such as an axis ratio a/c=1.69), the gravitational binding energy W (the work required for complete mechanical disassembly of the structure, defined as negative) is computed exactly by [C.4]:

W=−53​Rs​GM2​earcsin(e)​

where M is the mass of the Moon and Rs​ the radius of the equivalent sphere [C.4]. For a perfect sphere, the geometric factor stands at 3/5 (0.60); the flattened shape carries an additional coefficient slightly smaller than 1 that depends exclusively on its eccentricity [C.4]. Since the sphere is the most physically bound shape, the geometric transition releases elastic energy, like a stone lowered into a pit [C.4]. For the system's triaxial peak shape (1.75:1.45:1), the energy difference releases exactly 2×1027 Joule, a value that is 2.1% of the total binding energy of the body (a value of about 3×104 J/kg) [C.4]. This energy, released as internal heat within a viscous core (which behaves mechanically like thick tar), raises the global temperature of the interior by about 30 kelvin [C.4]. This thermal factor supplies energy to keep the interior mobile and viscous, but cannot melt a solid crust [C.4].

b. The volume-decrease term (compression energy):

The second and dominant energy term in the system arises from the radial convergence of the mass [C.4]. The gravitational binding energy of a sphere, −3/5(GM2/R), deepens sharply as the radius of the body (R) decreases [C.4]. As the equivalent radius falls from about 2,180 km to about 1,890 km, the energy released in the system jumps to a value of 1.5×1028 Joule (a value of 2.1×105 J/kg) [C.4].

This compression term is seven times larger than the geometric shape-change term, and it releases a thermal output able to heat the interior of the body by about 200 degrees Celsius on global average (an exact value of 206 kelvin, computed under a fixed heat capacity of 1 kJ/kg⋅K) [C.4]. The energy acts like a cocked spring released from its constraints that returns the stretching work that held it; the work is converted directly into high values of hydrostatic pressure and internal heat, which keep the core in a mobile state and feed the crustal ejection vents (the maria) [C.4].

4. The resistance stresses of the shell and the chronological-clock mechanism of pressure

While the viscous interior of the body tends to round in accordance with the lines of gravity, the solid outer shell (the crust of the young Moon) froze early and has a high rigidity, required to preserve the integrity of the craters imprinted on it (C.7) [C.4].

  • Strain stresses in the crust: forcing a solid shell to change its outer shape from the triaxial peak shape to a spherical structure forces it to undergo strain stresses (relative change of dimension along its length) of between 10% and 20% [C.4].
  • Collapse of mechanical strength: under the elastic rigidity values of a solid rocky crust (tens of GPa), this strain produces an enormous internal stress of between 2 and 12 GPa [C.4]. Since the maximum shear strength of the shell materials is only about 0.1 GPa, the resulting stress is 20 to 120 times higher than the mechanical strength limit of the crust [C.4]. The shell cannot bear this load [C.4].
The decay sequence and the change of pressure in the crustStage A: peak flattening, at the releaseStage B: decay of flatteningStage C: late in the decay

The shell does not need to break or fall apart completely to release these stresses [C.4]. The enormous hydrostatic pressure projected from the interior finds a rapid outlet through the system of conduits and key geological openings already existing and distributed in the crust – the array of mare vents (Paper 5) [C.4]. The mechanism works like a bottle containing a soft filling and a stiff skin pierced at several points: applying hand pressure will eject and spray the interior material out through the holes with high force, which will gradually decay as the pressure relaxes [C.4].

Before the release, the magma and molten rock fed from the pear source were thrown forcefully through the mare vents, performed ballistic flights (Paper 6), and landed back on the solid crust, imprinting the ancient crater population (the returned material) [C.4].

The physical mechanics of the polar-mismatch equation

The dynamic profile of the internal pressure is computed precisely (Figure 12) as a function of the vector of geometric mismatch remaining between the polar surface of the rigid shell and the spherical shape toward which the interior tends:

At the release the craters are already in place — almost all formed before it; during the decay the vents add only small craters, until the maria freeze.   • At peak flattening, at the release (stage A): the mismatch is maximal, and therefore the hydrostatic pressure of the decay reaches its physical peak [C.4]. The craters on the surface are already in place: they formed before the release, the largest of them at peak flattening, when the source pressure that fed the vents was greatest; they now begin the surface-contraction sequence, and those formed at the peak absorb all of it, and therefore today show the maximum density excess at the poles (the geometric chronological clock) [C.4].
  • Through the decay of flattening (stages B and C, after the release): as the body rounds, the mismatch value steadily decreases, and with it the internal pressure profile in the vents falls [C.4]. The ejection through the vents weakens; after the release it produces only small craters, until the maria freeze [C.4].

The chronological clock of the system therefore rests on the stage at which each crater formed, before the release, and not on the pressure of the decay (C.5, D.2) [C.4]. When a perfect spherical shape is reached, the surface becomes a hydrostatic equipotential, the slope vector drops to zero, the structural mismatch disappears entirely and with it the internal pressure in the vents collapses, and the residual crustal flow comes to a complete stop in the system [C.4].

C.5 Stretching in time: the dynamics of loads, the decay of flattening and the timeline of rounding

This section anchors the morphological evolution and the geodynamic forces of sections C.1–C.4 along a firm chronological timeline [C.5]. It defines, at each stage of the attached system and after the release, the strength of the Earth's stretching vectors, the mechanical mechanism that preserved the integrity of the body, and the exact level of triaxial deformation [C.5]. These values determine on which geometric shape each crater was imprinted before the release, and from this is derived mathematically the level of residual polar excess density measured in it today (the geometric chronological clock) [C.5].

1. Dynamics of the tidal-load measure (k) against the stability threshold

The Earth's tidal forces act to stretch the volume of the Moon along the radial axis (axis a), while the Moon's self-gravity field tends to compact the material into a sphere [C.5]. The system stress-balance factor is computed along the sequence using the firm physical measure [C.5]:

k=πGρΩ2​=ρr3ME​​
  • The physical mechanics of the measure: the equation compares the Earth's external tidal pull at a given distance (ME​/r3, represented as the square of the orbital angular velocity Ω2) with the self-gravity field that a uniform body exerts on itself (πGρ) [C.5]. The physical size of the body does not affect the value of the measure – it is set exclusively by the orbital distance (r) and the density of the material (ρ) [C.5]. The tide falls steeply as a function of 1/r3; a moderate recession reduces the load sharply, and the stiffening of the crust (the rise in density ρ) sharpens its decay [C.5].
  • The fluid stability threshold (the Roche limit): a free fluid body (without mechanical strength and detached) can stabilise a closed shape only when the value of the measure firmly satisfies k<0.09 [C.2, C.5]. Inside this Roche limit (k≥0.09), the tidal stresses tear the fluid apart [C.5]. By contrast, a rigid body that elastically resists deformation can hold together much closer to the source: the rigid Roche limit for light material (1,300 kg/m3) is set at a distance of 12,994 km [C.1, C.5].

2. The geophysical mechanics of support by the base and the rigid crust

The numerical analysis reveals a sharp structural anomaly: through all the attached stages, the value of the tidal load (k ranging between 2.01 and 0.26) never reaches the free-fluid stability threshold (0.09) before the moment of release [C.5]. The young Moon moves outward and is released at a distance of about 16,610 km (beyond the equatorial corotation line), deep within the disruptive fluid Roche limit (about 23,200 km at the release density of 1,700 kg/m³, and 20,100 km once compacted to 2,600) [C.2, C.5].

The survival of the structure is explained through a two-stage chain of mechanical support [C.5]:

1. The stage of support by the base of the pear (the flattening stages): the body is not torn or tidally disrupted at the rigid Roche limit (12,994 km), despite an extreme load seven times higher than the tearing threshold, because it sits and is fixed on a wide attachment base 6,000 km wide connected to the parent material [C.5]. The width of the base carries and balances the radial and tidal stress vectors that the self-gravity of the mass cannot bear on its own (Paper 3) [C.5]. As the body moves outward, the base narrows from 6,000 to 3,000 km, and the load decays gradually with arc distance [C.5].

2. The stage of support by the rigid crust (the release and the decay of flattening): on the line the base of the pear narrows and the pressure on it drops to zero, and the body is released still inflated and flattened (about 1,700 kg/m³) [C.5]. From this moment the stiffened outer shell is the sole bearer of the residual stresses and holds the body against tidal disruption, while it recedes, rounds and compacts toward 2,600 kg/m³ [C.2, C.5]. Paper 2 assigns the density of 2,600 to the moment of release; in the present chronology this density is reached after the release, during the decay of flattening [C.5].

3. Chronology of the four moments of geometric transition

The morphological evolution from the tip of the pear to the modern state is governed along four firm dynamic segments [C.5]:

  • Moment A (consolidation at the tip of the pear): light sialic material (1,300 kg/m3) concentrates at the tip of the pear structure, and begins its outward path and the development of initial flattening, while held on the 6,000 km base [C.5].
  • Moment B (structural peak flattening): the mass takes shape as an independent attached body beyond the rigid Roche limit (≈13,000 km) [C.5]. The geometric flattening reaches its extreme peak as the base narrows to 3,000 km near the crossing of the corotation line (a predicted distance of 15,818 km at a period of 5.5 hours) [C.1, C.5]. The Moon is stretched between the two opposing pulls into a triaxial shape of 1.8:1.4:1, in an inflated state with a material density of about 1,700 kg/m3 [C.1, C.5].
  • Moment C (crossing the line and release): the centre of mass crosses the corotation line (the dynamic distance at which the synchronous rotational velocity equals exactly the free orbital velocity) [C.5]. The net compressive force on the base drops to zero, and about 210 km beyond the line the Moon detaches (the lengthening of the spin from 5.5 to 5.77 hours makes the line migrate slightly from 15,818 to 16,399 km) [C.5]. Up to this moment the Moon rotates with the Earth and its flattening grows, reaching its peak at the release; nearly all the craters on it have formed, and none is yet crowded [C.5]. Had the pear not been elongated and carried the mass up to this line, the lunar material would have collapsed back toward the Earth [C.5].
  • Moment D (decay of flattening and freezing): after the release the stretching that held the flattening disappears, and the rotation slows with recession (6.6 hours at 18,000 km, 14 hours at 30,000 km, 40 hours at 60,000 km) [C.5]. The flattening decays with it – the rotational component falls to about 1.04 at 30,000 km and about 1.005 at 60,000 km – the body rounds and compacts toward 2,600 kg/m³, and the polar surface crowds [C.5]. The crowding stops when the interior stiffens and the shape freezes, near 16 Earth radii (Paper 4), leaving today's fossil flattening (f ≈ 0.001) [C.5].

Analysis of the diameter curves and the chronological clock of pressure

Examining the measures derived from the diameter curves (Figure 13) yields the following scientific insights:

The gap between the two curves is the flattening: largest at the peak, reached at the release about 210 km beyond the corotation line (1.8 : 1.4 : 1 at about 1,700 kg/m³; the long diameter is the Earth line, and the middle one, along the orbit, 4,628 km, is not drawn). After the release the gap closes as the flattening decays: through a/c 1.40, 1.30, 1.24 and 1.20, to 1.04 at 30,000 km (a spin of 14 hours) and 1.005 at 60,000 km (40 hours); the shape freezes near 16 Earth radii. The diameters are calculated from the volume of the Moon's mass at the density of each stage and from the shape of the stage (C.1; at the peak 1.75 : 1.45 : 1); both curves fall because the volume decreases — the equivalent diameter falls from about 4,350 km at the peak to 3,778 km after compaction; the ratio between pole and equator, which the paper tests, does not depend on the overall size. 1. Decoding the original gap between the curves: the gap between the red curve (the long equatorial diameter along the a axis) and the blue curve (the short polar diameter along the c axis) represents precisely the value of the geometric flattening [C.5]. This gap reaches its system maximum at peak flattening (5,585 km lengthwise versus 3,191 km across the pole; the intermediate axis b of 4,628 km is not plotted) at the release [C.3.1, C.5]. The curves close after the release, through the decay of flattening: values of 4,871 km versus 3,479 km at the 1.40 stage, converging toward a spherical diameter of 3,778 km once the flattening has decayed [C.5].

2. Combined fall of the baseline (volume collapse): both curves show an overall downward trend along the sequence [C.5]. This trend stems from the fact that the volume of the body shrank drastically and the equivalent radius decreased from about 2,180 km at the stretched, voluminous peak to 1,890 km after compaction [C.1, C.5]. The morphometric ratio between the pole and the equator is robust and unaffected by the overall size of the body [C.5].

3. The epiphany of the crater-size clock: the dynamic arrows linking the empirical diameter groups to the stages of the curve (D.2) represent the law of internal hydrostatic pressure in the vents [C.4, C.5]. The giant craters formed at the most flattened moment, when the pressure in the mare vents was at its extreme peak, and therefore they went through the mechanical maximum of surface contraction during rounding and today record the maximum density excess at the poles [C.4, C.5]. Small craters were imprinted at later stages when the pressure in the vents had already decayed, underwent less residual surface contraction, and therefore show a moderate excess on the surface [C.4, C.5]. The whole array falls precisely within the bounds of the predicted range of the balanced clean count (1.20±0.05) [C.5].

1. The dynamics of differential crowding: why are the large craters the most crowded?

The degree of mechanical crowding of a crater on the crust is not set by its absolute chronological age, but is a geometric record of the body's shape and dynamic flattening at the moment of impact and crater formation [B.7]. The craters kept their original diameter and were carried as intact, rigid elements on the crust; what contracted and closed elastically was the surface and the seam spaces between them (C.7, D.5) [C.3]. The geometric mechanics are defined by the equation of residual rounding [C.3]:

  • Formation at peak flattening: craters that formed when the Moon was at the peak of triaxial deformation (1.8:1.4:1) underwent the full sequence of inward rounding and surface reduction [B.7, C.3]. As a result, they went through the mechanical maximum of surface contraction, and today show a predicted density ratio of about 1.50 in favour of the polar caps.
  • Formation earlier in the build-up of flattening: craters that formed when the Moon was still only slightly flattened (a shape of about 1.20) were stretched apart with the surface as the flattening grew and compressed back in the decay; they keep only the net contraction, and therefore their predicted density ratio drops to about 1.17.
  • Young craters (later impacts from space): craters that formed long after the shape had frozen undergo no surface contraction at all, and therefore their predicted ratio is 1.00 (a completely uniform distribution).

The vent-pressure mechanism and the crater as a clock of shape:

The causal link between crater diameter and its time of formation is governed by the internal pressure profile in the mare vents [C.4]:

1. Peak flattening, before the release: the source pressure that fed the vents was at its maximum, and the returned material was thrown out at maximum force (Paper 6); therefore most of the largest craters in the system formed at this stage [C.4].

2. The build-up of flattening, before the peak: the source pressure grew with the pear, and the later, stronger ejections made larger craters, so the small craters are the earlier ones; each crater kept its own size afterwards (D.5) [C.4].

Material was ejected and landed throughout all the stages of the transition (both on the way up to the peak and on the way down from it), and therefore the enhanced density ratio of the craters records precisely how flattened the body was at the moment of their imprinting [C.3]. Crater size acts as a firm geometric clock of the shape: the larger one formed closer to peak flattening, absorbed more rounding, and ends up more crowded at the poles [C.3, C.4]. This mechanical prediction is confirmed precisely in the clean count (D.2), in which the density ratio climbs from 1.09 in the smallest size class (20–30 km) to 1.53 in the class of giant craters of 60–100 km.

2. The three-stage evolution of the polar regions

The geographic polar regions are older than the formation of the flattening, and their dynamic evolution unfolds through three firm structural stages:

[Stage 1: outward rounding] ──> [Stage 2: the flattening stage] ──> [Stage 3: inward rounding]

(setting of the poles and the rotation axis) (growth of the deformation, creation of the large craters) (surface contraction, crowding of the craters)

  • Stage 1 — outward rounding (fixing the axis): the original sialic mass, which sat on the tip of the Earth's pear, collapsed inward and became an independent fluid sphere (Paper 3 §B.4). At this stage the geographic rotation axis of the body was set; the craters existing on the shell then changed with the surface equally everywhere (without relative deformation), and new craters continued to accumulate [C.3].
  • Stage 2 — the flattening stage (growth of the deformation): as the body moved outward toward the corotation line, the base narrowed from 6,000 to 3,000 km, and the centrifugal and tidal stresses stretched and flattened the structure into an extreme triaxial shape [C.1, C.5]. At this stage the differentiation of material progressed (the ejected material was light and full of water), the pressure profile in the vents soared to its peak, and the largest giant craters were imprinted on the surface in a uniform distribution per unit area [C.4, C.5].
  • Stage 3 — inward rounding (convergence and crowding): after the release, the spin slows and the flattening decays [C.1, C.5]. The surface undergoes a differential collapse: it closes and contracts at the maximum rate at the poles (a factor of 0.55×) and at the minimum rate at the equator (a factor of 0.97×) [C.3.1]. The craters (which kept their original diameter) gather and crowd correspondingly toward the poles, since all the meridians retreat toward the two end points of the rotation axis – the only points that the rotation never moved in space (C.3) [C.3.1].

3. The chronological birth of the month and the orbit of the young Moon

At the moment of release and final mechanical detachment from the Earth, the Moon's spin period and orbital period coincide near a value of slightly more than 5.77 hours:

  • The birth coordinates: the Moon begins the process of separation and rounding on the corotation line [C.5]. On this line, its orbital period and the Earth's spin take exactly the same time – a value of 6.25 hours at an orbital distance of 17,287 km (for the latitudes of 22.5∘) [C.5].
  • The mechanical release: takes place about 210 km beyond the equatorial corotation line (16,400 km), as the Moon is thrown into an independent orbit with a moderate initial eccentricity (ellipticity) of about 0.037 (Paper 4) [C.5].
  • The path of orbital lengthening (Kepler's law): from the moment of detachment onward, the length of the month (the orbital period T) grows and lengthens as a function of the orbital distance (r) according to Kepler's third law alone (T∝r3/2), without the need for further assumptions or free parameters [C.5]:
T=2πG(M⊕​+m)r3​​

The dynamic curve (Figure 14) begins with a completely flat profile (a short month of a few hours near the Earth), and climbs sharply only far out: 14 hours at a distance of 30,000 km → 3.7 days at a distance of 16 Earth radii → until it settles at 27.3 days in its modern state today [C.5]. Once the mechanical release point has been set, the length of the month at every distance follows directly from Newton's law of gravitation [C.5].

Figure 14. Where the month was born: the orbital period of the Moon — the month — against its distance from the Earth, from 5.77 hours at the moment of release (equal to the Earth's day at that time) to 27.3 days today, according to the law 𝜇 = 𝐺(𝑀⊕ +𝑚) ,𝑇 = 2𝜋√𝑟3/𝜇) Kepler, where 𝑟 is the distance between the centres, 𝑀⊕ the mass of the Earth and 𝑚 the mass of the Moon). 4. Chronology of the attached stage, the release and the decay of flattening

The craters were imprinted through the long attached stage, on the body as its flattening built up and at its peak; the crowding of the craters took place after the release, in the decay of flattening, whose rate was set by the slowing of the spin with recession and by the response time of the interior (C.7) [C.5].

The chronological timetable of the model (the 600-million-year window):

The geodynamic model aligns the overall time span of about 600 million years from the start of the bulge to the final release (dated to 3.873 billion years before present, that is about 4.5 billion years before today) [C.5]:

  • Segment A (bulge and pear): about 400 million years for the uplift of the original mass on the pear material of the Earth [C.5].
  • Segment B (dynamic flattening): about 100 million years of extreme triaxial deformation near the corotation line [C.5].
  • Segment C (late build-up of flattening, up to the release): about 100 million years in which the flattening kept growing near the corotation line and reached its peak at the final mechanical detachment [C.5]. Together with the build-up of flattening before it, this is the morphogenetic window in which the craters of the paper were imprinted [C.5].

When was the spherical structure completed?

  • After the release (decay of flattening): the spin slowed with recession and the flattening decayed – about 1.04 at 30,000 km and about 1.005 at 60,000 km; in this decay the craters were crowded at the poles [C.5]. Had the pear structure not lengthened so as to carry the mass beyond the line, the material would have collapsed back to the Earth [C.5].

The Moon detached from the Earth still inflated, at the peak of its flattening, with its outer shell rigid enough to hold it inside the fluid stability limit, and rounded after the release (Paper 2 §B.7 assigns a rigid round body to the moment of release; the present chronology moves the rounding to after it) [C.5].

  • The freezing of the shape: as the interior cooled and stiffened, its response time grew until it could no longer follow the slowing spin, and the shape froze, near 16 Earth radii (Paper 4) [C.5, C.7]. The crater formation of the model had stopped long before this moment; the young craters of D.3, imprinted long after it, carry no polar excess [C.5].

At a distance of about 60,000 km the rotational flattening of a fluid body is only about 1.005, and the Moon was almost a perfect sphere [C.5]. The tiny fossil bulge preserved in it today (f ≈ 0.001, compared with a peak deformation of about 0.44) is the remnant that froze near 16 Earth radii: the extreme flattening held while the Moon was attached decayed after the release, leaving only a small remnant, 400 times smaller than its original state [C.5].

The combined database at the end of Part C

The geodynamic model has completed the construction of the theoretical and mechanistic foundation, and fixes the following core measures [C.5]:

  • kmax​=0.67 — peak mechanical load at the rigid Roche limit (12,994 km), stabilised on the 6,000 km base
  • a:b:c≈1.8:1.4:1 — the geometry of peak flattening on the 3,000 km base, material density 1,700 kg/m³
  • ΔVolume≈1.53 — a global volume collapse that drives the potential slope profile inward toward the poles
  • Trelease ≈ 5.77 hours — the birth of the month, with the flattening at its peak, about 210 km beyond the line

C.6 The wide base: the mechanical support mechanism, the dynamics of accelerations and the point of detachment

This section decodes the mechanical and geodynamic balance of the lunar interior in the attached stage, and explains how the body was protected from tidal tearing [C.6]. As established in section C.5, the external tidal load on the body consistently exceeded the hydrostatic stability limit of a free fluid (k≥0.09) [C.5, C.6]. The following analysis quantifies what carried this energy difference along the separation path, and why the mechanical support lapsed at the moment of release [C.6].

a. The global balance: the structural role of the base width

During the stages of growth and flattening, the young Moon did not act as a free body, but was physically attached and anchored to the parent material [C.6]. This attachment took place on a very wide crustal base, which was physically required to absorb and carry the excess tidal stresses that the self-gravity field of the mass could not balance on its own [C.6].

The mechanics are integrated along the sequence of detachment stages [C.6]:

  • The sector of a body of its own (12,994 km): the moment the mass establishes an independent body configuration at the rigid Roche limit, the load measure climbs to the extreme value of k=0.67 (seven times above the fluid Roche threshold of 0.09) [C.5, C.6]. The body was saved from complete tearing thanks to its anchoring on a rigid base 6,000 km wide [C.6]. The dynamic structure is like a drop of viscous fluid hanging from the tip of a syringe: the drop keeps its morphological integrity under the load of the external gravity field as long as the mechanical opening holds and stabilises it [C.6]. This wide base was required simultaneously both for the balance of radial pressures and resistances of Paper 3, and against the crust-tearing tidal stresses [C.6].
  • The stage of base narrowing and recession: as the mass underwent rotational flattening and was pushed outward on the tip of the pear, the width of the holding base narrowed from 6,000 km to 3,000 km [C.1, C.6]. Despite the structural narrowing, the body remained stable because the tidal factor fell sharply with orbital distance as an extreme ratio of 1/r3 [C.5, C.6].

The moment the centre of mass reaches the corotation line (16,400 km), the base lets go completely [C.6]. The detached body is released about 210 km beyond the line, deep within the fluid limit (about 23,200 km at the release density of 1,700 kg/m³; 20,100 km at 2,600), with the outer shell, stiffened to μ ≥ 10 GPa, carrying the load of the residual stresses alone from then on [C.5, C.6].

b. Dynamic analysis of the profile of accelerations and self-gravity

To decode the physics of the two-body balance in isolation, the static measures can be translated into a system of physical accelerations [C.6]. The equilibrium equation is governed by two opposite vectors that change their values along the timeline [C.6]:

1. The self-gravity vector at the surface (g): undergoes a consistent rise and climb [C.6]. Since the mass of the Moon is constant, the compaction of the core and the decrease in volume (the narrowing of the radius R) bring the surface materials closer to the centre, and sharply increase the inward pull: from 0.87 m/s² in the initial pear stages, to 0.95 m/s² in the middle stages and 1.03 m/s² at the moment of release (about 1,700 kg/m³), up to 1.37 m/s² after compaction to 2,600 (1.62 m/s² modern) [C.6].

2. The tidal acceleration vector across the body (atide​): represents the pure mechanical difference between the Earth's pull on the nearest surface and its pull on the Moon's centre of mass (atide​=r32GME​R​) [C.6]. This value undergoes a sharp fall and decay along the recession path [C.6].

c. The methodological clarification: differences in the definition of the measures

To maintain firm mathematical consistency, the study clarifies the numerical difference between the two tidal measures used in sections C.5 and C.6, and proves that it is a difference of analytical definition and not a physical difference [C.6]:

1. The theoretical load measure (k): defined in section C.5 by k=πρr3ME​​ [C.5, C.6]. The classical fluid Roche threshold, equal firmly to 0.09, is calibrated and formulated relative to this measure [C.5, C.6].

2. The direct ratio of accelerations: defined in the last column of this section as the direct division of the equation of tidal acceleration across the body (r32GME​R​) by the equation of surface self-gravity (34​πGρR) [C.6].

When the mathematical reduction is carried out, the radius of the body (R) cancels out completely, and the equation yields the reduced ratio value [C.6]:

Acceleration_Ratio=32[MEπρr3]=1.5×k\mathbf{\text{Acceleration\_Ratio}\mathbf{=}\frac{\mathbf{3}}{\mathbf{2}}\left[\frac{\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{E}}}{\mathbf{\pi \rho r}^{\mathbf{3}}}\right]\mathbf{=1.5\times k}}Acceleration_Ratio=23​[πρr3ME​​]=1.5×k

A mathematical rule is established: the direct ratio of accelerations is a constant 1.5 times the load measure k of section C.5 [C.6].

This constant dependence dictates that the two systems move in full synchronisation through all the stations of the path [C.6]:

  • A load value of k=0.67 at the rigid Roche limit coincides exactly with an acceleration ratio of 1.0 [C.6].
  • A load value of k=2.01 at the tip of the pear coincides exactly with an acceleration ratio of 3.0 [C.6].
  • A load value of k = 0.26 at the moment of release (density about 1,700 kg/m³) coincides with an acceleration ratio of 0.38 (for a body of 2,600: k = 0.17 and 0.25) [C.6].
  • The theoretical fluid Roche threshold of k=0.09 translates exactly into an acceleration ratio of about 0.135 [C.6].

This consistency (plotted in the graphs of Figures 15 and 16) proves full mathematical closure of the geodynamic system [C.6].

C.6.1 Chronology of the local effective gravity and the dynamic mechanics of detachment

Whereas the first part of section C.6 discussed the global balance of accelerations of the body as a whole, this part breaks down the data to local resolution [C.6]. The effective gravity – the actual force experienced by a free grain lying on the surface (the combination of inward self-gravity, tidal stretching, and outward centrifugal throw) – is not a uniform monolithic value, but varies drastically with the geographic coordinate at which the grain is located [C.6]:

1. In the polar regions (the rotation axis): expressed as g+ω2R (where ω is the angular velocity of rotation and R the radius of the body) [C.6]. Perpendicular to the tidal axis, the tidal forces physically compress and press the body inward, adding positively to the pull of self-gravity [C.6].

2. In the side regions (the axis of orbital motion): equal exactly to the value of pure self-gravity (g), since in this sector the centrifugal component fully offsets and neutralises the tidal factor [C.6].

3. At both ends of the tidal axis (the sub-Earth and anti-Earth points): expressed as g−3ω2R [C.6]. At these coordinates, the external tidal stretching and the centrifugal throw of the rotation act simultaneously and jointly in the direction opposite to the body's self-gravitational pull [C.6].

As the body recedes and compacts the spread narrows further, and in the modern state the gravity field settles at full uniformity of 1.62 m/s² at every point on the surface [C.6].

C.6.2 The mechanics of the collapse of the lower pressure on the corotation line

The dynamic transition from a wide base to complete detachment is governed by the simultaneous intersection of three physical constraints on the corotation line [C.6]:

1. Balance of velocities (inside the line): inside the corotation radius, a body rotating in synchronisation with the Earth moves at a linear velocity lower than that of a free Keplerian orbit [C.6]. As a result, the Earth's gravity pulls the mass inward with a force exceeding the outward centrifugal throw [C.6]. The body is pressed and firmly fixed onto its base, and the base presses back from below (this is the radial balance mechanism of Paper 3) [C.6].

2. The zero point (on the line): at the corotation point, the two force vectors (gravity inward and the throw outward) are exactly equal [C.6]. The vertical compressive force on the base falls mathematically to absolute zero [C.6].

3. The reversed pull vector (beyond the line): on crossing the line and receding beyond it, the velocity of the body is higher than the free orbital velocity, and the compression turns into an active pull directed outward, away from the base [C.6]. The tidal load decays to k=0.17 – a load fully handled by the stiffened shell, while the contact area has narrowed to 3,000 km [C.5, C.6].

Since the base is no longer required to carry a compressive load, the Moon is thrown off and mechanically released about 210 km beyond the line, when about 58% of its mass has already crossed the boundary (Paper 4) [C.6]. With the detachment, the Earth's hydrostatic pressure flow that passed through the pear to the Moon stopped completely, thus closing the chapter of the powerful magmatic ejections [C.6].

The scale for comparing the stresses in the system:

To understand the strength of the geodynamic forces acting in the crust, the data can be set against the mechanical limit values of the body [C.6]:

  • Self-cohesion energy: the self-gravity field binds the two halves of the Moon with a strength of 2.7 GPa over the cross-sectional area of the base [C.6].
  • Strength of the crustal materials: the mechanical strength limit of a solid rocky crust stands at about 0.1 GPa [C.4, C.6].
  • Peak-flattening load: maintaining and sustaining the triaxial peak shape (1.75 : 1.45 : 1) away from a spherical structure requires a shear stress of the order of ρg(a − c), equal to 2.0 GPa at a density of 1,300, and about 2.1 GPa at the release density of about 1,700 (3.7 GPa for a body compacted to 2,600) [C.6].

The geophysical conclusion:

The quantitative cross-check proves that within the bounds of the line, the vertical compression of the Earth produces exactly the order of magnitude of stress required (≈ 3 GPa) to maintain the integrity and deformation of the flattened shape [C.6]. On passing beyond the line, the compression collapses and reverses into an outward pull: the base lets go and the Moon detaches [C.6]. The flattened shape itself does not collapse at this moment: the tidal stretching, which hardly changes along the segment, and the synchronous spin still hold it, and the stiffened shell carries the residual load [C.6]. It decays only after the release, as the Moon recedes, the tide weakens and the spin slows (C.5) [C.6].

Since the compressive load is completely symmetric about the Earth line, it governed the egg part (the tidal axis a) while the body was attached; after the release, the egg part decayed with the weakening tide, and the rotational flattening (the rotation axis b/c) with the slowing spin and the compaction of the core (C.4, C.5) [C.6]. The tidal stretching that remained beyond the line exceeds the fluid stability limit up to a distance of about 23,200 km at the release density (20,100 km at 2,600), and the Moon keeps its integrity thanks to its strong elastic crust until it has receded and compacted [C.2, C.6].

C.6.4 The plug-extraction mechanism and the end of the pear's activity

The geodynamic model establishes a direct causal link between the mechanical detachment of the Moon and the halt in the evolution of the terrestrial pear structure [C.6]:

  • The crustal plug effect: throughout all the attached stages, the mass of the young Moon sat directly on the apex of the tip of the pear and functioned physically as a tight plug hermetically sealing a high-pressure bottle [C.6]. The presence of the plug blocked the main ejection vents of the pear, and forced the internal pressure to feed, stretch and lengthen the pear material further and further outward [C.6].
  • Release of the hydrostatic pressure: at the moment of mechanical detachment and the residual recession of the Moon beyond the line, the plug was pulled out [C.6]. The key openings of the pear were exposed directly to space, and all the enormous internal hydrostatic pressure that had been stored within the pear was released and burst out in a sharp global ejection [C.6].

With the disappearance of the driving internal pressure, the vector that mechanically lengthened the pear structure stopped completely, and this explains geophysically three core puzzles:

  • 1. Why the pear structure retreated and shrank back immediately after detachment, instead of continuing to stretch
  • 2. Why the system was arrested and did not eject or release a second moon or further residual masses into orbit
  • 3. Why the ejecta were thrown and scattered in all directions, imprinting the global crater record

The Earth released its pressure at the moment the plug was extracted, and with that the mechanism was concluded [C.6].

C.7 The mechanical composition of the young Moon's crust: the two-layer model

The geodynamic mechanism detailed in sections C.1–C.6 sets two opposite physical requirements pulling in contrary directions [C.7]:

1. The elastic/flow requirement (the interior): the body of the young Moon had to be soft and viscous enough to round and undo an extreme triaxial deformation of about 1.8 : 1.4 : 1 after the release, as its spin slowed [C.7].

2. The rigid mechanical requirement (the crust): the surface had to be rigid and solid enough to keep the impact craters completely intact – their rims, margins and original diameters – throughout the transformation process [C.7].

The scientific solution to this mechanical paradox is applied through the two-layer model (Two-Layer Rheological Model): dividing the structure of the body into two distinct layers with entirely different viscosity properties, where the geodynamic argument of rounding is exclusively the work of the inner layer [C.7].

The geodynamic relaxation rate and the time window of the decay:

The life cycle of the global attached stage unfolds over a wide time window of about 600 million years (from the start of the bulge about 4.5 billion years ago to the moment of final mechanical release 3.873 billion years ago) [C.5, C.7]. Within this sequence, the build-up of flattening and its peak lasted about 200 million years, and the craters were imprinted during them [C.5, C.7]. The decay of flattening came after the release, and its pace was set by the recession: in a recession calculation with constant tidal friction (an illustrative assumption), the Moon reaches 30,000 km about 300 years after the release, 60,000 km after about 26,000 years, and 16 Earth radii after about 800,000 years [C.5, C.7].

The physical speed at which a planetary body can collapse and adjust its surface morphology is governed by its dynamic viscosity (η), expressed in pascal-seconds (Pa⋅s) [C.7]. The mechanical relaxation time (τrelaxation​) – the time required for a body held by its self-gravity to converge to its new hydrostatic equilibrium shape after a change in stresses – is computed exactly by the limit equation [C.7]:

τrelaxation​≈ρgRη​

For the parameters of the compacted body (density ρ = 2,600 kg/m³, radius R = 1,889 km, surface gravity g = 1.37 m/s²), the following matrix of relaxation times is obtained [C.1, C.7]:

Viscosity of the interior material (η, Pa·s)Estimated mechanical relaxation timeAgainst the decay of flattening (centuries) and the freezing of the shape (~10⁵–10⁶ years)
1019About 47 yearsFollows the decay closely (the decay to 1.04 takes about 300 years) [C.7].
1020About 470 yearsFollows the decay with a lag; the rounding trails the slowing spin [C.7].
1021 (the level of the modern Earth's mantle)About 4,700 yearsCannot follow the fast early decay; follows only its later, slower part [C.7].
1022About 47,000 yearsFollows only the slowest stage, near 60,000 km [C.7].
1023 (the shell measure of Paper 3)About 470,000 yearsThe shape freezes; this is the scale of the freezing near 16 Earth radii (about 800,000 years) [C.5, C.7].
1024–10254.7–47 million yearsFrozen [C.7].

Reading the matrix: every increase of the viscosity by a factor of 10 slows the relaxation by a factor of 10 [C.7]. Since the decay of flattening was fast – most of it within centuries after the release – the interior had to be soft during the decay, with a viscosity of about 1019–1020 Pa·s or less, close to a partially molten state; this agrees with the heating of about 200 kelvin released by the contraction (C.4) [C.7]. As the interior cooled and its viscosity rose toward 1023 Pa·s, its response time reached hundreds of thousands of years and the shape could no longer follow the slowing spin: it froze, near 16 Earth radii, as today's fossil flattening records [C.5, C.7]. This is a requirement of the model: a soft interior during the decay, stiffening afterwards [C.7].

The rheological mechanics of the two layers

The separation of the mechanical properties of the body is defined precisely by the following characteristics [C.7]:

a. The inner layer (the viscous core):

Characterised as a hot, mobile and partly molten zone, with low viscosity values of η≈1021−1022 Pa⋅s [C.7]. This low viscosity responds immediately to the strengthening self-gravity field (C.4), causing the interior to flow and retreat in full accordance toward the shape of a perfect sphere within 1,000 to 10,000 years of any stress fluctuation [C.4, C.7].

b. The outer layer (the rigid shell):

The crust of the young Moon is characterised by an exceptionally high viscosity of η≥1023 Pa⋅s, physically required to preserve the integrity of the craters carved into it (Paper 3) [C.7]. Since the shell is too rigid to flow freely, it cannot follow the collapse of the fluid interior, and is carried passively on top of it [C.7].

As a result, the crust is forced to adjust itself physically to the shrinking and closing surface beneath it, in a way that is not uniform in space [C.7]:

  • In the polar regions: the surface undergoes the maximum contraction (a factor of 0.55×) [C.3.1]. The shell here undergoes sharp shortening: it folds mechanically, is pushed over itself, and thickens [C.7].
  • In the equatorial regions: the surface contraction is minimal (a factor of 0.97×), and therefore the crustal plates and the craters on them undergo almost no relative displacement [C.3.1, C.7].

Preservation of the original crater record

The two-layer model resolves the puzzle of the survival of the crater morphology and explains why the record is readable and normalised today [C.7]:

  • Had the lunar crust been as soft as the core, it would have flowed and continuously lost its shape; a crater undergoing deformation and stretching by a third (≈33%) during local flow would have lost its margins and been erased completely from the record [C.7].
  • Since the shell was considerably more rigid than the interior, the craters were imprinted on and sat upon solid, isolated crustal plates (tiles), and therefore kept their diameter and original rim morphology entirely, without internal deformation [C.3, C.7].
  • The sharp spatial shortening of the polar surface (a reduction of about a third of the area relative to the belt, and almost half of the area of the core itself) was spread over a long time of about 100 million years, and was fully absorbed into the array of joints and elastic seam spaces separating the crustal plates, without damage to the structure of the crater itself [C.3.1, C.7].

Morphological erasure or blurring requires rapid local flow or crustal melting, elements that are not present during the slow rounding sequence [C.7]. The polar craters remained intact and crowded at the same time because the shell was completely rigid while the body beneath it flowed freely [C.7].

Tectonic predictions and the GRAIL crustal-thickness test

The picture of two-layer mechanics sets clear constraints that leave geological signs open to independent empirical testing on the surface [C.7]:

1. The array of tectonic structures: the model predicts the existence of shortening and compression structures (such as thrust ridges and crustal wrinkles) concentrated at high density toward the poles and progressively absent toward the equatorial belt, together with a complete absence of a belt of extensional structures (rifting) in the equatorial regions of the ancient far-side highlands [C.7].

2. Resolving the crustal-thickness constraint (GRAIL): the volume decrease and the undoing of the flattening impose a firm constraint: the global surface area shrank by a quarter, and at the poles a drop of almost half of the original area was recorded [C.3.1, C.7]. Had the shell preserved its volume passively, the compression of the area at the poles would have forced the crustal materials to thicken by about a third overall, producing a polar crust 1.5 times thicker than that of the equatorial belt [C.7].

GRAIL satellite measurements refuted this scenario, and established that the polar crust is not thicker than the latitude belt in which it lies [C.7]. Therefore, the model sets a closed geodynamic requirement: the shell took up and processed the share of the surface that closed at the poles through a combination of mechanical shortening, tectonic thrusting, and residual transport of molten crustal material inward into the soft core beneath it [C.7]. The solution of the quantitative calculation of the compression array and the mass transfer is detailed and fully reconciled in Part E.3 of the paper [C.7].

C.8 External rotational differentiation: the shell beneath the crowded craters

Section C.7 set a closed requirement: the share of the surface that closed at the poles during the rounding did not leave a thick polar crust, as GRAIL shows [C.7]. This section presents the process that meets the requirement, and places it within the single sequence of flattening and rounding that produced the polar crater excess [C.8].

C.8.1 The process

During the attached stage, the young Moon rotated together with the Earth at the rate dictated by the Earth [C.1]. A rotating body has poles from the moment it has a rotation axis, whatever its shape: the centrifugal force is zero on the axis, that is at the poles, and grows gradually to a maximum at the equator. As the pear grew and the material at its tip consolidated into a body, the body flattened [C.1, C.5]. We propose that the flattening was made possible by an exchange at the poles: the light material of the outer shell flowed from the poles to the equator, gradually and in proportion to the strength of the force, so that the equator is the peak, and the heavier material beneath it rose at the poles and made room for the outflow [C.8]. As a result of the stretching, the polar shell remained thin throughout the long build-up of flattening, a window of tens of millions of years, up to the release. During this time material landed on the lunar surface in a uniform distribution [C.4, C.8]. The flattening reached its peak at the moment of release on the corotation line; the decay of flattening and the rounding took place after the release, as its spin slowed with recession [B.7, C.5]. As the flattening decayed, the heavier material that had risen at the poles was the first to sink back inward, to the depths it had come from (C.8.5). As it sank it drew the polar surface toward the pole centres, and the polar shell thickened again, but not to the thickness of the equatorial shell [C.8]. The build-up of flattening and the decay of flattening are thus one process in two stages: the build-up of flattening draws material out of the poles, the decay of flattening returns what was drawn out, and the crater record above responds with a corresponding density. We call the whole process, whose engine is the rotation and which acts on the outer layer, external rotational differentiation. The crater density at the poles is the record it left [C.8].

C.8.2 The rubber sheet

The calculation of C.3 treats the surface as drawn on a uniform rubber sheet [C.3]. External rotational differentiation gives the sheet a varying thickness (Figure 18). In the figure the middle of the sheet is the pole and the ends are the equator. When the sheet is stretched, the middle is thin, and the craters form on it at equal spacing. When the sheet tightens, the thin middle contracts more, and the craters on it are compressed. The same craters, in the same number, occupy a smaller area [C.8].

Figure 18. The rubber-sheet image of external rotational differentiation (C.8.2). The sheet represents the outer shell along one meridian: the middle is the pole and the ends are the equator. (1) Before: a uniform sheet. (2) Peak flattening: the sheet is stretched; the material has flowed from the pole toward the equator, so the middle is thin (about half of the ends), and craters form at equal spacing (red: those that end up in the polar cap). (3) After rounding: the sheet tightens; the thin middle contracts more and the polar craters crowd together; the middle thickens again but remains thinner than the ends. The thicknesses follow measurement and were not fitted: state 3 is today’s measured polar crust (about 38.5 versus 47.6 km at the equator, 81%; GRAIL), and state 2 (about 53%) is back-calculated from two measured values, today’s thickness and the polar crater excess (C.8.4). Thickness exaggerated.

C.8.3 The Moon in three stages

On the Moon the stages of the process follow one another (Figure 19) [C.8]:

1. Onset of flattening: the flattening begins with the peeling of the Moon and grows as the pear grows. The Moon was not a sphere at this stage; the round drawing serves illustration only [C.1, C.8].

2. Peak flattening: the polar shell is thin, and material lands on the surface of the flattened body in a uniform distribution, forming craters at equal spacing [C.4, C.8].

3. Decay of flattening, after the release: the geometry of C.3 carries the surface toward the poles, and the craters crowd there. The shape sets the size of the excess (1.21 computed, 1.20 ± 0.05 measured); the thin shell is where the contraction is concentrated [C.3, D.1, C.8].

(1) Onset of flattening: the flattening began with the peeling of the Moon and the body was not a sphere; it is drawn round for illustration only. (2) Peak flattening (shape exaggerated to 1.7 : 1 for visibility): light material flows gradually from the poles to the equator (blue), the polar shell is thin, and craters are spread at equal spacing along the surface. (3) After the release, the decay of flattening: the surface is compressed toward the pole centres (blue); the red craters, which occupied a long arc at the peak, now occupy a smaller polar cap. The craters were placed by the geometry of C.3 (equal arc length on the flattened body, carried to the sphere), not by hand.

C.8.4 The back-calculation: the shell thickness at peak flattening

Reversing the contraction recovers the thickness of the polar shell before the rounding. The crust thickens as its area contracts, so the thickness ratio at peak flattening equals today's measured ratio divided by the contraction factor read from the crater excess [C.8]:

StageBasisPolar shell thickness relative to the equator
Peak flatteningthe large craters, excess 1.53 [D.2]about 53%
Peak flatteningall craters of 20 km and larger, excess 1.20 [D.1]about 67%
Today, after the roundingGRAIL crustal model [R13]81% (about 38.5 versus 47.6 km)

At peak flattening the polar shell was about half as thick as the equatorial shell. The rounding thickened it again, but not to equality [C.8]. Only a small part of the contraction was taken up by the closing of pore space: the porosity at the poles is lower by 2 to 5 percentage points [D.6]. Most of the contraction went into thickening the shell [C.8].

C.8.5 The body before the flattening and the depth of the exchange

The process does not require a spherical body. Before the flattening, the young Moon was not a ball but a mass organising itself on the tip of the pear, like a deflated football resting on top of a column. Such a body already had poles: it rotated with the Earth about an axis parallel to the Earth's axis, and the poles are the two points where that axis leaves it. The column joined the body on its Earth-facing side, which lies on its equator, so the poles were free [C.1, C.8]. The geometric convergence of C.3, in which all meridians meet at the poles, acts on a geometrically ordered body, after the release [C.3, C.8].

The exchange at the poles involved only the outer layer of the body itself, the inner part of its outer envelope, and not the deep material that flowed through the column. Its depth can be estimated from the numbers of C.8.4. With a uniform initial shell of about 45 km (close to today's equatorial 47.6 km) and constant volume, the polar shell at peak flattening is today's polar thickness divided by the contraction factor [C.8]:

BasisPolar shell at peak flatteningThinning relative to the initial shellDepth from which the material rose
all craters of 20 km and larger, excess 1.20 [D.1]38.5 / 1.20 ≈ 32 kmabout 13 kmabout 32–45 km
the large craters, excess 1.53 [D.2]38.5 / 1.53 ≈ 25 kmabout 20 kmabout 25–45 km

The material that rose at the poles therefore came from about 25 to 45 km below the surface, the base of the shell and the layer just beneath it, and in the contraction it returned to the same depths, a descent of 10 to 20 km. Against a radius of about 1,889 km at release [C.7], this is one to two and a half percent of the radius: a movement of the outer layer only. It agrees with the layered structure of the lunar crust, a light anorthositic upper crust over a denser, more mafic lower crust, so that the material that rose at the poles was heavier than the shell that moved away from them. The estimate rests on two assumptions, a uniform initial shell and constant volume, and gives an order of magnitude, not a measurement [C.8].

PART D

Part D — The four tests and control of the basic assumption

Whereas Part C formulated mathematically and quantitatively the mechanism of rounding and volume decrease of the triaxial body, Part D sets this geodynamic model against the empirical crater record on the surface through a series of firm tests [D].

The testing methodology (the rules behind the equations):

Each test is conducted in steps according to a uniform, restrained academic protocol [D]:

1. Defining the elements of the comparison: identifying the regions compared, with careful confirmation of their full morphological similarity in every factor except the single variable being tested [D].

2. The theoretical prediction and setting of the pass line: defining the predicted value of the model, accompanied by upper and lower threshold lines (Pass/Fail Threshold) set in advance, before running the counts on the catalogue and the age samples (thus completely preventing any artificial fitting of the pass lines to the answers on the surface) [D].

3. The empirical measurement on the surface and the derivation of the result [D].

The "both sides" procedure of the clean count:

The initial run (Part A) processed the whole raw catalogue; once it was revealed that the basalt floors of the maria lower the density in the equatorial belt, all the tests were re-established in the form of the clean count [D]. Under this method, the mare areas and the SPA basin are actively and evenly removed from both sides of the equation simultaneously (the "both sides" rule), ensuring that the two measurement regions (the poles and the equator) differ only in the parameter of geographic latitude, and are normalised on the same type of pristine crust (Highlands) [D].

Mathematical calibration of the uncertainty measures:

Each empirical ratio is reported together with a confidence interval of 95%, except for the clean density ratios (D.1, D.2), written with the notation ±, where the value represents one standard deviation of the count (1σ; the 95% interval is roughly twice as wide) [D]. The 95% interval is defined mathematically so that, were the whole measurement array replicated many times, it would contain the true value in 95 out of 100 runs; therefore, any ratio whose 95% interval does not contain or cross the uniform symmetry value (1.00) is defined as a significant physical difference lying beyond the range of chance [D].

The measurement is carried out using two separate statistical methods:

  • For count ratios (Counts Ratio): the confidence interval is computed from the exact (Clopper–Pearson) range of a binomial distribution without approximations, multiplied by the ratio of the geometric areas of the two regions (an exact translation of coin tosses into density ratios) [D].
  • For median ratios (Medians Ratio): the confidence interval is computed using the Bootstrap method with 20,000 random resamplings with replacement [D]. This technique is immune to prior assumptions about the shape of the size distribution and lets the data dictate independently the degree of scatter of the median from sample to sample [D].

Summary matrix of the five tests of Part D

The following is the quantitative and strict summary of the test results against the theoretical pass lines defined in advance [D]:
