  • Qualitative summary: four of the five tests pass fully and firmly; the data on the young craters (D.3) are morphologically consistent with the model, but their small sample size prevents a significant decision at this stage [D].

D.1 The normalised bipolar density-ratio test

  • The element of comparison: the test computes the number of craters per unit area in the two polar caps (latitude 60∘ and above, defining a cap with an angular radius of 30∘) against the density value of the equatorial belt (∣ϕ∣<15∘) [D.1]. Both regions are counted from the same geometric catalogue, under the same diameter threshold, and with the "both sides" filter of the geological mask applied [D.1]. This is the main basic test, since had the ratio in the clean count dropped to 1.00, the scientific phenomenon would have dissolved [D.1].
  • The theoretical prediction: the model predicting rounding with volume decrease (C.3, C.5) dictates an excess value in the range between 1.20 and 1.50, as a function of the timing of crater formation relative to the point of peak flattening [D.1]. A crater formed at the peak absorbed the full sequence of surface contraction and shows the maximum polar crowding (≈1.50); a crater formed in later stages on a body that had already rounded received only the end of the surface contraction and shows a moderate effect [C.3, D.1]. For the whole combined population of diameter ≥20 km (most of which consists of relatively small craters formed in the later stages), the six-axis equation predicts a stable value around 1.21 [C.3, D.1]. The firm pass line was defined in the safe range between 1.10 and 1.60 [D.1].

The procedure of the cleaning stages of the count:

The following table quantifies the movement of the values as a function of applying the spatial control masks [D.1]:

Cleaning stage of the count applied in the system (craters ≥20 km)Statistical ratio value obtainedThe geodynamic and methodological meaning of the stage
Stage A: the whole raw catalogue (including maria)1.32The young, empty maria concentrated at the equator artificially lower the density of the denominator and inflate the ratio [D.1].
Stage B: removal of the mare polygons only1.11±0.04Cleaning out the residual basalt floors (removing empty area from the equator) lowers the ratio, and reveals the true highland crust [D.1].
Stage C: removal of the maria and the SPA basin system (the clean count)1.20±0.05The clean and final like-for-like comparison; cleaning out the crater-poor floor of the SPA basin in the south raises the numerator and fixes the value of the crustal anomaly [D.1].

The final residual result (1.20±0.05, with a confidence interval of 95% ranging between 1.10 and 1.30) falls precisely at the centre of the predicted theoretical range, and coincides coherently with the 1.21 value of the six-axis model, without the need for free parameters [D.1]. The test passes fully [D.1].

Ruling out the predictions of the external impactor-rain model (Impactor Flux Models)

A classical objection among planetary experts proposes that the density excess at the poles might arise from a probabilistic flux difference, in which the high latitudes received a larger volume of impactors (Bolides) from space [D.1]. The physical and dynamic calculations accepted in the community for the distribution of the flux of external bodies arriving from outside the Earth–Moon system refute this scenario, and yield an entirely opposite mechanical sign [D.1]:

  • Classical dynamic models for determining the global impact flux (such as Le Feuvre & Wieczorek 2008; Gallant et al. 2009) establish that impact fluxes from space are statistically concentrated precisely in the equatorial belt, and yield for the polar regions a depleted value that fixes a ratio of only 0.90 to 0.91 (a built-in deficit of about 10% at the poles) [D.1].
  • A corrected and updated version of the same dynamic models (Le Feuvre & Wieczorek 2011) sharpens the difference, and establishes that the impactor flux leaves the poles at a disadvantage of only 0.80 relative to the equatorial belt, which is rich in head-on impacts [D.1].

The empirical clean count (1.20) stands above these space-flux predictions by a huge margin of 6 to 8 counting standard deviations (6σ−8σ) [D.1]. Since the maximum measurement error is 0.05, a difference of 6σ−8σ entirely rules out the probability of a chance fluctuation or agreement with external space fluxes [D.1]. Within the LEF model, the initial density of impacts was completely homogeneous over the flat morphology of the attached bulge (the ancient poles received a volume of returned material identical to every other sector of the crust), and it is the dynamic collapse of inward rounding that mechanically crowded, contracted and concentrated the record; no external rain of impactors can bring about such a bipolar anomaly [D.1].

The 20 km sector limit (the reason for omitting the small craters):

Below a firm diameter threshold of 20 km, the spatial comparison procedure is stopped completely and not applied [D.1]. The reason is documented in the mechanics of the surface: at these small diameters, the count record is dominated and entirely distorted by three foreign factors – clusters of secondary craters (local debris impacts formed by material thrown out of a large crater), fine spray fields, and a state of crustal saturation (a destructive equilibrium in which every new small crater physically erases an old crater beneath it, and the overall count is arrested and can grow no further) [D.1].

None of these elements (secondaries, spray, saturation) preserves or records the geometric position and state of the surface at the moment of the original planetary impact, and therefore they cannot carry the mechanical signature of the rounding process [D.1]. Comparing secondary spray fields with primary craters fails scientific precision, and was therefore omitted [D.1].

D.2 The diameter-ordering test and the geometric clock

This section puts the crater sizes (diameters) to two firm structural questions [D.2]:

1. The clock test: does the polar density excess rise as a function of crater size and diameter, as dictated by the rounding model in which the largest craters formed near peak flattening [C.4, D.2]?

2. The size-rigidity test: did the craters keep their original diameters while the surface and the seam spaces between them contracted and closed elastically [C.7, D.2]?

a. The density ratio by crater diameter (calibration of the geometric clock):

Within the geodynamic model, the diameter of a crater reflects the stage at which it was imprinted on the crust, and the great majority of them were imprinted before the release [C.4, D.2]. The source pressure that fed the returned material grew with the pear, and the later, stronger ejections made larger craters: the small craters formed early, on a body that was still only slightly flattened, and the giant craters at peak flattening (1.8 : 1.4 : 1) [B.7, C.4]. A crater formed early was first stretched apart with the surface as the flattening built up and then compressed back in the decay; it keeps only the net contraction from its own formation shape to the sphere. The giant craters, formed at the peak, keep the full contraction [C.3, D.2]. Each crater kept its own size throughout; only the spacing between the craters changed (D.5). A small number of small craters may also have formed after the release, from material of the Moon itself or from the Earth [D.2].

To test this prediction, the clean count (removal of the maria and the SPA system from both sides) is divided into isolated diameter classes, and run backward through the ellipsoidal transformation equation (C.3) to reconstruct the axis ratio (a:b:c, with the polar axis c set to 1) and the dynamic stage at which the population was imprinted [C.3, D.2]:

Crater diameter class examinedMeasured clean density ratio (ρpolar​/ρequatorial​)Reconstruction of the original body shape (a:b:c)Estimated geodynamic stage in the sequence (Figure 13)
20 – 30 km1.09±0.071.37:1.03:1.05Onset of flattening, on an almost round body [D.2].
30 – 40 km1.15±0.111.42:1.07:1.11Early build-up of flattening (shape about 1.20) [D.2].
40 – 60 km1.26±0.121.62:1.21:1.34Middle of the build-up of flattening [D.2].
60 – 100 km1.53±0.191.70:1.42:1At structural peak flattening (matching the shape 1.8:1.4:1) [C.3, D.2].
100 – 300 km1.84±0.382.24:1.74:1At the extreme peak deformation, falling within the error intervals [D.2].
  • Decoding the chronological order: reading the matrix from top to bottom reveals a firm correlation: as crater diameter increases, the numerical density excess climbs continuously from 1.09 to 1.53, and the reconstructed shape climbs from an almost spherical body toward the triaxial peak deformation [D.2].
  • Confirmation of the peak shape: the 60–100 km class (the largest craters preserved in a wide and significant sample) reconstructs precisely an axis ratio of 1.70:1.42:1 [D.2]. Its rotational component (b/c=1.42) matches completely the solution of the Maclaurin equation for a rotation period of 5.5 hours at a density of 1,700 kg/m3 (C.1) [C.1, D.2]. By contrast, the small craters reconstruct an almost round shape, indicating that they were imprinted early, before the flattening had built up (C.5) [C.5, D.2].

The overall order and range (between about 1.0 for craters formed on an almost round body and 1.50 for those formed at the peak) are what the model predicts and physically requires, and they are reproduced on the surface in full agreement [D.2]. The 100–300 km class shows values slightly beyond the theoretical peak (1.84), but owing to a small sample (only 46 craters at the poles and 50 at the equator), its statistical uncertainty is wide (1σ = ±0.38) and takes in the peak shape [D.2].

b. Proof of the rigidity of crater size (non-contraction of the diameter):

The model establishes that the craters were carried as intact, rigid elements on a solid upper crust (C.7); they kept their original diameter, and the contraction of the polar Surface area was absorbed and closed within the seam spaces between them [C.7, D.2]. The dynamics are like a crowd standing in a city square whose area is shrinking: the people draw closer and crowd together, but no person becomes shorter or smaller in physical size [D.2].

This geometric prediction is proven by two firm findings [D.2]:

1. Confirmation of the significance of the excess at fixed diameter thresholds (ruling out crater contraction): the cumulative size distribution of lunar craters in the range of 20 to 100 km decays according to a constant power law: N(>D)∝D−b, where the present measurement array gives an exponent of b≈1.8 in the caps and b≈2.0 in the equatorial belt [D.2]. This means that halving the crater diameter multiplies the cumulative population by 4 [D.2]. Had the craters contracted physically together with the surface by a linear factor s, the area cell would have gained a density excess of 1/s2, but at the same time would have suffered a loss of a factor sb≈s2 from the numerator, since craters close to the threshold would have shrunk below it and dropped out of the calculation [D.2]. These two opposite effects would have offset and cancelled each other exactly, and no bipolar density excess would have been measured on the surface [D.2]. The very existence of a significant density excess measured at fixed diameter thresholds is the exclusive mechanical evidence that the craters kept their original diameter and that it was the surface between them that contracted [D.2].

2. The linear median-diameter test: since the large craters are concentrated at the peak and are the most crowded, the polar population must show a structural enrichment in large craters, causing its median diameter to be larger than that of the equatorial belt at the same measurement threshold [D.2].

The following are the empirical values of the median diameters, computed on the clean count by running a Bootstrap matrix of 20,000 resamplings [D.2]:

Firm measurement diameter thresholdThe polar caps: sample (N) and medianThe equatorial belt (∣ϕ∣<15∘): sample and medianMeasured ratio of medians (Medpole​/Medeq​)Normalised confidence interval (95%)
Threshold ≥20 kmN=895, median = 32.5 kmN=1,498, median = 30.5 km1.061.01 – 1.12 (rules out complete equality)
Threshold ≥40 kmN=327, median = 59.2 kmN=470, median = 56.0 km1.060.98 – 1.15

At both separate measurement thresholds, the polar median diameter shows a value significantly higher than the equatorial-belt median (values of 32.5 versus 30.5 at the 20 threshold), as required by the size-clock mechanism [D.2]. At the 20 km threshold, the confidence interval (1.01−1.12) does not contain the symmetry value 1.00, and thus entirely rules out the probability of random equality [D.2]. At the 40 km threshold the ratio value is firmly kept at 1.06, but owing to the threefold reduction of the sample the confidence interval widens and slightly crosses 1 [D.2]. The test passes fully [D.2].

The rise of the excess with crater diameter fits the process of C.8: the large craters formed at peak flattening, when the polar shell was thinnest and the body most flattened, and they are therefore the most crowded [C.8, D.2].

D.3 The test of the young crater population (The Post-Release Control Test)

  • The element of comparison and the definition of "young": young craters are defined in the system as a population of later impacts from space (Copernican, younger than about 1 Gyr), imprinted billions of years after the shape of the Moon had frozen; the crater formation of the model itself – the returned material, and the small craters from the mare vents after the release – had stopped long before the final freezing [D.3]. This population is the main control and calibration group of the entire paper [D.3]. The density excess of section D.1 is not a function of a fixed geographic location that attracts craters today, but evidence of a mechanical transformation that the ground underwent after the formation of the old craters [D.3]. A crater imprinted on a finished perfect sphere was never subject to a condition of crustal surface contraction, and therefore it must physically show a uniform distribution without a polar anomaly [D.3]. Had the young craters shown a density excess at the poles like the old ones, the rounding model would have been refuted, and the anomaly would have been attributed to external space-collection mechanisms [D.3].
  • The theoretical prediction: the young population must be homogeneous and uniform across the latitudes [D.3]. The pass line was set within a narrow range around 1.00, with the lower end adjusted to include the minor polar deficit (0.90−0.91) predicted by models of external impact fluxes from space after detachment [D.1, D.3].

Analysis of the two independent samples:

Dating young craters is complex, and to prevent biases the study combines two separate samples built with entirely different methodologies that check each other [D.3]:

1. Sample A — the Copernican database (LPI): based on the Lunar Impact Crater Database (Losiak et al., 2015) [D.3]. The sample isolates 80 named craters assigned geologically to the Copernican era (the youngest period in the lunar timescale, characterised by bright, sharp ray systems such as the crater Copernicus), of which 65 craters have a diameter of ≥10 km [D.3]. This compiled sample carries a built-in bias toward the near side owing to the nature of historical identification [D.3].

    • The empirical measurement: yields a pole/equator density ratio of 0.92, with a confidence interval of 95% ranging between 0.39 and 2.04 [D.3].

2. Sample B — the thermal boulder sample (Mazrouei et al., 2019): isolates 111 craters of diameter ≥10 km whose physical age is firmly less than a billion years (1 Gyr) [D.3]. The dating is carried out by a physical method free of observational biases: measuring the abundance of exposed blocks and rocks around the rim using the thermal Diviner instrument on board the LRO spacecraft [D.3]. A fresh crater is strewn with rock blocks that emit distinct thermal radiation, which are ground into fine dust over time at a known rate [D.3]. The sample ensures uniform, homogeneous coverage along the whole body in the latitude range between 80∘ S and 80∘ N (the areas of the caps and the belt are cut correspondingly at the 80∘ line to remain compatible with the limits of the instrument) [D.3].

    • The empirical measurement: yields a pole/equator density ratio of 1.12, with a confidence interval of 95% ranging between 0.60 and 2.03 (including or omitting 8 borderline craters aged ≥1 Gyr from the original GitHub file does not change the trend) [D.3].

The result and the statistical decision:

The two independent samples converge coherently around the uniform symmetry value (0.92 versus 1.12), and fit precisely within the predicted pass line [D.3]. The findings confirm the control data: the young crater population does not show the extreme bipolar density excess present in the ancient population [D.3].

However, owing to the small sample sizes (a few tens of craters for the whole globe), the 95% confidence intervals are very wide (0.39−2.04 and 0.60−2.03) and cross the range of random scatter [D.3]. Therefore, the data are fully consistent with the model and confirm its direction, but the existing sample is still too small to give an absolute independent statistical decision, and the study details in section D.3 the exact sample sizes that will be required in future to reach closed significance [D.3].

Rationale for neutralising the mare filter in the young population:

Unlike the ancient population, in which the maria had to be mechanically filtered (because the basalt floors erased the old craters beneath them), the young crater population is counted over the entire global surface without a mare mask [D.3]. For a young crater formed after the basalt froze, the maria are ordinary ground; a Copernican crater will be imprinted on a mare as easily and with the same probability as on the ancient highlands [D.3].

Matrix of confidence intervals and assessment of the probabilities of chance

Since the young samples are very small at global resolution (only 10 and 18 craters within the polar caps), the confidence intervals widen considerably [D.3]. The following table quantifies the 95% intervals together with the statistical probability (P-value) of obtaining the measured result under a hypothetical scenario in which the young population is really crowded like the ancient population [D.3]:

Statistical sample codePole / equator ratio (interval 95%)Probability of obtaining the ratio if the true ratio were 1.20 (clean)Probability of obtaining the ratio if the true ratio were 1.32 (raw)
Copernican LPI (D≥10 km)0.92 (2.04 – 0.39)0.310.22
Mazrouei (all 111 craters)1.12 (2.03 – 0.60)0.470.34

  • Decoding the significance weights: the statistical probability values range widely from 0.22 to 0.52 [D.3]. This means that a sample of this small size could produce such low values from a crowded population with a high frequency of once in every two runs to once in every five runs (a chance distribution) [D.3]. The 95% intervals are wide and contain both the uniformity value (1.00) and the ancient crowding value (1.20) simultaneously [D.3].
  • Defining the required sample constraint (the pass line): both samples stand at or below the level of the ancient population and agree with each other, and cannot rule out or prove significance independently [D.3]. Therefore, the test is formulated as a quantitative constraint for the future: to separate mathematically, at a significance level of two standard deviations (2σ), between a uniform value (1.00) and a crowded value (1.20), physics requires a dated sample several times larger, numbering at least 150 young craters in the caps and 300 in the equatorial belt [D.3]. The project of building this wide database is defined as the second item of the future research tasks (E.3) [D.3].

Proof of longitudinal uniformity and refutation of the static-preservation hypothesis

The data of the Mazrouei thermal boulder sample add a critical geodynamic layer, and prove that the young population is characterised by full uniformity also along the meridians (east versus west) [D.3]:

  • The density of young craters is equal between the two halves of the body, standing at 3.11 on the far side versus 2.84 on the near side per 10⁶ km² [D.3].
  • This trend is reproduced precisely in the 61 fresh rayed craters of Grier et al. (2001) (processed by Tai Udovicic et al. 2021), which show values of 2.01 on the far side versus 1.70 on the near side per 10⁶ km² [D.3]. Rayed craters represent bright post-impact streaks that have not yet faded owing to exposure to the solar wind, and they are the youngest on the body; in the LEF model, these rays are a pristine sub-crustal record that can become fixed only on a crustal floor that has already cooled completely [D.3].

The physical finding is firm: the engine that mechanically crowded the old craters at the poles – and on the trailing face of the maria (A.9) – stopped, froze and ceased to act completely before the young population was imprinted [D.3].

This is the exact confirmation of the frozen-shape prediction, and a complete refutation of the static-preservation hypothesis (B.1) [B.1, D.3]: had the ancient polar density excess been the result of polar environmental conditions that preserve craters or prevent their erosion more effectively than in the equatorial belt, this preservation factor would have had to act simultaneously and also enhance the number of young craters in the same regions [D.3]. The absence of the excess in the young craters proves that this is a transient surface-contraction effect [D.3].

Rejecting classical geological maps (the USGS bias):

The study actively rejects the use of the Copernican crater units of the unified geological map (USGS Unified Geologic Map, Fortezzo et al. 2020; 222 polygons) [D.3]. Processing the data of these polygons shows a sharp artificial anomaly, in which the density on the near side is four times that on the far side (9.2 versus 2.4 per 10⁶ km²), together with an apparent polar deficit of 0.4–0.5 relative to the equator [D.3].

This extreme variance is not a physical property of the Moon, but a serious methodological distortion of historical mapping: the side near the Earth was mapped first, at high resolution and with an extreme level of detail relative to the far side, and therefore the unified map compiled from these sheets takes in an excess of young units in places where the human mappers looked more carefully [D.3]. Therefore, geological maps must not be used as statistical counting arrays, and the uniform geometric catalogue of Robbins (2019) is the exclusive and valid database for the study [A.11, D.3].

D.4 The bipolar symmetry test (north versus south)

  • The element of comparison: the test compares directly the crater-density record of the south pole with that of the north pole, cap by cap, in a series of six concentric spherical caps with angular radii of 10°, 15°, 20°, 30°, 45° and 60° [D.4]. The measurement is carried out on the area remaining after applying the uniform control mask (removal of the 20 Neumann basins and the LROC mare polygons) on both sides [D.4]. The two poles are the cleanest and most balanced reference pair that the surface offers, since they share identical latitudes, an equal distance from the Earth-line axis, identical topographic illumination conditions, and are processed through the same global geometric catalogue [D.4].
  • The theoretical prediction: the inward-rounding mechanism of Part C is governed by the Moon's self-gravity field, and acts completely symmetrically about the body's rotation axis [C.3, C.4, D.4]. Since the rotation axis passes exactly through both geographic poles, every global meridian returns and retreats toward both of them in the same way and at the same geometric rate, and therefore the model predicts full equality and balance in the residual density values [C.3, D.4].

Statistical and morphological analysis of the bipolar convergence

A cross-reading of the residual measures and the density curves yields the following insights:

1. Neutralising the artificial raw asymmetry: in the original raw count (A.6), the two hemispheres gave a misleading appearance of extreme variance: in the inner 15° core the north was considerably denser than the south (300 versus 215), and the northern curve climbed sharply inward while the southern curve remained completely flat [A.6, D.4]. This difference had a clear geological cause: the giant South Pole–Aitken (SPA) basin covers a decisive part of the area of the southern caps, and within the narrow range of 20° from the south polar apex it is the only mask component [A.8.3, D.4]. Once the crater-poor floor of the SPA basin is cleaned out and removed from the denominator, the two residual densities converge to close, tight values, and the ratio between them settles near the uniform symmetry value (1.00) across the whole range between 10° and 60° [D.4].

2. Preservation of the statistical balance in all confidence intervals: in all six nested caps and at both isolated diameter thresholds (≥ 20 km and ≥ 40 km), the 95% confidence intervals contain and anchor the value of complete mechanical equality (1.00) [D.4].

    • The maximum deviation is recorded in the southern 10° core (348 versus 298), but because it is measured deep within the footprint of the basin and rests on a small sample of only 36 craters, its confidence interval widens considerably (0.77-1.74 at the 20 threshold, and 0.62-2.43 at the 40 threshold), which rules out any physical significance for this fluctuation [D.4].
    • As the cap radius widens and the sample takes in a larger number of craters, the uncertainty intervals narrow sharply: in the wide 60° cap, which holds more than 1,000 craters on each side, the ratio value settles tightly at 1.02 and its 95% interval is locked between 0.94 and 1.10 [D.4].

Verdict:

The test passes fully and firmly [D]. The empirical results prove a sharp morphological division of roles: what the two poles share (high density values and a continuous inward radial convergence after filtering) belongs entirely to the geodynamic mechanism of rounding; by contrast, what separated them in the raw state belongs exclusively to the bias of the single SPA basin impact [D.4]. Once the type of crust is normalised and like-for-like on both sides of the comparison, the two poles carry exactly the same factor of mechanical crowding [D.4]. (The distinct internal structure of the crater deficit in the heart of the South Pole–Aitken basin itself is passed on to the focused analysis of Paper 8) [A.10, D.4].

D.5 Control of crater-size preservation in the crust: five firm morphometric tests

  • The element of comparison: the test puts the model's basic analytical assumption – the claim that the craters kept their original diameter and were carried on rigid crustal plates, while the surface and the seam spaces between them shrank elastically (C.7) – to a direct check against the empirical data [D.2, D.5].
  • The theoretical prediction and the rationale: had the craters contracted together with the surface, the inward-rounding process (C.3) would have shrunk them in the same linear proportion [D.5]. The two possibilities are like a crowd standing more densely within a city square whose area has shrunk (the people keep their body dimensions but the gaps close), as against a planetary photograph printed entirely at a smaller scale (both the gaps and the objects shrink simultaneously) [D.5].
    • The original deformation factor: according to the starting flattening model (a/c=1.69), the residual linear factor (the change in length) stands at 0.86 in the polar caps (∣ϕ∣≥60∘), 0.90 in the middle ring (45∘−60∘), and 1.08 in the equatorial belt (∣ϕ∣<15∘) [D.5]. This dictates that had the craters undergone the rheological deformation, a polar crater would have been forced to shrink to a size of only 0.79× compared with its equatorial counterpart, and 0.95× compared with a crater lying just outside the cap [D.5].
    • The shape-family constraint: these factors are normalised and neutralised from the global change of area, and the ratio between them (0.86/1.08) yields the 0.79 value that is the main scale for rejecting the contraction scenario [D.5]. (The values are based on the raw compressed scale and will be updated to the triaxial shape of 1:1.4:1.8 within section E.3) [D.5].

Five size and morphometric tests ask the crater record directly what happened in the crust, using the clean-count data (removal of the maria and the SPA system from both sides simultaneously), to ensure complete isolation of the latitude parameter [D.5]:

Breakdown and analysis of the five size and morphometric tests

(a) The largest craters per equal area (the ranking test):

  • The statistical mechanics: the test compares the median diameter of the largest craters preserved within equal measurement areas in the caps and the belt [D.5]. Since the poles underwent an empirical density excess of 1.20 times (D.1), the cumulative size-distribution law (b≈2) dictates that a denser area will reach a given size rank (such as the 5th, 10th or 20th largest crater) at a diameter larger by a factor of 1.20​≈1.10 [D.2, D.5]. Had the craters contracted together with the area, the crowding effect and the contraction effect would have neutralised each other, and the large craters would have shown identical diameters (a value of 1.00) in both sectors [D.5].
  • The empirical finding: for density samples relative to area of 5, 10, and 20 craters per 10⁶ km², the polar median diameter divided by the equatorial one yields values of 1.02 (0.83−1.28), 1.11 (0.92−1.29), and 1.16 (1.04−1.29) respectively [D.5]. A comparison with the middle ring gives an identical value of 1.16 (0.99−1.30) [D.5]. The median of the widest sample (at the 20 threshold) sets a firm lower end of 1.04, lying significantly above the value of 1.00, and thus statistically rules out the crater-contraction scenario [D.5]. (The means are pulled downward by the presence of residual giant basins in the belt that the mask leaves in place, but the median is immune to this bias) [D.5].

(b) The family-shape test (The R-plot Landmark):

  • The statistical mechanics: a pure power law of the form D−b has no landmarks (Landmarks) and does not change under a change of scale [D.5]. However, the crater distribution in the lunar highlands shows a structural anomaly in the relative plot (R-plot) – it climbs and forms a prominent morphological hump at a defined diameter, drawn as a deviation from a uniform line [D.5]. Had the polar population undergone crustal contraction, the hump would have been forced to migrate to the left toward smaller diameters by a factor of 0.79×; preservation of crater size requires the hump to stay fixed at its original size coordinate [D.5].
  • The empirical finding: in the polar caps the hump stands stable in the range of 80–113 km, in exactly the same size cell where it lies in the equatorial belt (and above the middle ring, which lies at 57–80 km) [D.5]. The polar hump is higher but is not shifted to the left [D.5]. The best-fit scale factor merging the two distributions is set, at a confidence level of 95%, at ≥1.09, a figure confirming that the polar population is morphometrically larger, and ruling out the 0.79 factor of the contraction scenario [D.5].

(c) The old-versus-fresh test (The Degradation Ratio):

  • The statistical mechanics: a change of scale and crustal contraction can affect only ancient craters that existed before the rounding stage; a fresh crater imprinted after rounding never underwent crustal deformation [D.3, D.5]. Therefore, had contraction taken place, the old craters at the poles would have been smaller in size relative to the fresh craters in the same sector, a difference that should not be reflected in the equatorial belt [D.5]. The craters (≥20 km) were ranked by a degradation index and depth/diameter morphology (according to the global digital elevation curve of Wang & Wu 2021), and the most degraded (ancient) third was compared with the freshest (deep and sharp) third [D.5]. The test is formulated as a double ratio (caps divided by belt) that cancels shared age and size biases and isolates exclusively the latitude factor [D.5].
  • The empirical finding: yields a balanced value of 1.02, with a confidence interval of 95% ranging between 0.89 and 1.16 [D.5]. The crater-contraction scenario requires a low value of 0.79, lying far outside the range of statistical scatter [D.5].

(d) The test of ellipticity and tectonic orientation:

  • The statistical mechanics: the laws of geodynamics dictate that the inward-rounding process is isotropic (uniform in every direction) only at the centre of the pole [C.3, D.5]. With distance from the apex of the axis, the inward collapse is not isotropic and shortens the latitude dimension at a rate considerably exceeding the shortening of the longitude dimension, with the peak non-uniform deformation taking place in the equatorial belt (C.3) [C.3, D.5]. Had the craters been elastic and deformed together with the surface, an initial circle would have been squashed into an ellipse, and the craters of the middle latitudes (30∘−55∘) would have shown an ellipticity (ratio of long to short diameter) 1.13–1.40 times higher than their initial state, while at the equator the deformation would have soared to 1.69 times, with all the ellipses oriented coherently along the global meridians [D.5].
  • The empirical finding: the median ellipticity of craters of diameter ≥20 km (from the full global Robbins catalogue) stands uniformly at 1.087 in the caps, 1.100 at middle latitudes (30∘−60∘), and 1.090 in the equatorial belt [D.5]. The excess ellipticity at middle latitudes amounts to only 0.01 (a tenth or less of the predicted deformation potential), and the equatorial belt (the site of the theoretical peak stress) shows no morphological elongation beyond the values of the caps [D.5]. The finding proves that the craters kept their original shape [D.5]. (Further analysis of the remaining orientation in the most elongated craters (e>1.2) along the meridians at middle latitudes, standing at 45%–51% versus 20%–25% along the parallels, is passed on to the focused discussion of section E.2, in which the observation geometry of the catalogue is the main suspect for this bias) [D.5].

(e) The scale within the crater (Simple-to-Complex Transition Benchmark)

  • The element of comparison: the test processes the diameter at which the internal morphological geometry of the craters changes in the polar caps versus the equatorial belt [D.5]. The boundary line at which a lunar crater passes from a simple partial bowl (Simple Crater) to a complex structural form with a central peak and terraced walls (Complex Crater) is set at the moment of impact [D.5]. It is dictated exclusively by the strength of the surface gravity field and the shear strength of the material, and therefore acts as a firm physical scale built into every crater [D.5].
  • The theoretical prediction: a crater that underwent a later geometric contraction keeps its morphological features [D.5]. Therefore, had crustal contraction taken place, the polar regions would show complex craters (with a central peak) deep below the usual transition threshold [D.5]. A crater born just above the transition threshold that developed a central peak, and then contracted together with the surface, would today show a peak at a small diameter at which pristine, fresh craters do not and cannot have a peak [D.5].
    • If size is preserved (the tile model): the transition in the caps must be fixed at a value identical to that of the equatorial belt – about 17 km [D.5].
    • If the craters contracted (s = 0.79): the transition in the caps is forced to migrate to the left and collapse to a dimension of about 13 km [D.5].

The empirical measurement and the methodological constraint:

Fitting the geometric break point in the depth-to-diameter ratio of the freshest population yielded two separate results that depend on the calculation method [D.5]:

  • Method A: yields a value of 16.4 km in the caps (scatter range: 15.8–17.1 km) [D.5].
  • Method B: yields a value of 14.0 km in the caps (scatter range: 13.0–15.2 km) [D.5].
  • The equatorial belt (reference): settles stably at 16.8–16.9 km [D.5].

The two analytical measurement methods do not reach numerical closure with each other within the cap sector, because the craters in these regions are characterised by a general morphological shallowness [D.5]. In addition, a chronological limit was revealed: the most pristine and freshest craters, which set the break point in the system, are for the most part younger than the inward-rounding process [D.5]. Since they were imprinted after the collapse, they were never carried on a contracting surface, and therefore cannot carry the signature of contraction one way or the other [D.3, D.5].

Defining the quantitative constraint for future work:

Owing to these limitations, the specific fifth test is defined as not decisive at the present level of resolution, and is formulated as a dedicated constraint for the next study: a focused count of craters showing a central peak below a diameter of 15 km in the caps versus the equatorial belt (Paper 14, research topics) [D.5]. A significant quantitative excess of peaked craters at these small diameters within the polar caps would be the definitive physical sign of crater contraction [D.5].

Final verdict of the section of empirical tests

The overall morphometric test passes fully and firmly [D].

Four of the five statistical tests of Part D (the ranking test, the hump, the degradation index and the ellipticity) establish unanimously and with wide significance that the crater dimensions were preserved in full, and no test supports the scenario of crater contraction [D.5]. The craters were imprinted on and carried by a solid shell that kept its rigidity, and the inward-rounding process elastically closed only the surface and the seam spaces between them [C.7, D.5].

D.6 The signature test in the shell beneath the poles

If external rotational differentiation (C.8) acted, it left signs in the shell beneath the poles [D.6]. They were tested in rings around both poles, with the maria and the SPA basin removed on both sides of every comparison, as in the clean count [D, D.6]. The crust thickness is taken from the GRAIL-based crustal model [R13]; the porosity from the GRAIL porosity maps [R14]; the grain density from the Lunar Prospector oxide abundances [R15] through the relation of [R16]; and the polar iron from three instruments [R15, R17, R18]. The deep mass test uses the GRAIL gravity field [R19] [D.6].

On the near side the crust is almost uniform (Figure 20). The near side was attached to the Earth, and the centrifugal process acted on it less [D.6]. At the pole itself the two sides are almost equal (38 and 39 km), because there the centrifugal force tends to zero [D.6]. The whole signature lies in the outer layer: beneath the poles there is no deep mass excess in the GRAIL field, and the average atomic mass of the surface does not change with latitude [R15, R19, D.6]. This matches the name of the process: it is external [C.8, D.6].

The combined database and the closing of Part D

With the completion of the five sections, the paper consolidates the following empirical database, which proves the validity of the mechanism [D]:

1. The normalised value of the anomaly: the clean count (removal of the biases of the maria and the SPA basin from both sides simultaneously) fixes an official bipolar density excess of 1.20 ± 0.05, a value falling at the centre of the theoretical range and entirely opposite to the sign produced by models of impact fluxes from space (0.80-0.91) [D.1].

2. Consistency of the geometric clock: the density excess climbs as a direct function of crater size (from 1.09 in the 20–30 km class to 1.53 in the 60–100 km class) [D.2]. The largest well-counted craters reconstruct and project back precisely the dimensions of the triaxial peak-flattening shape (1.8 : 1.4 : 1) [C.3, D.2].

3. Preservation of dimensions in the crust: the polar craters are morphometrically larger (a median diameter of 32.5 km versus 30.5 km in the belt) and not smaller, a figure that rules out a collapse of crater diameter [D.2].

4. Residual bipolar balance: the two hemispheres show similar and fully balanced density values (a tight south/north ratio of 1.02 in the 15° cap), once the floor of the SPA basin is cleaned out of the denominator [A.8.4, D.4].

5. The frozen young control record: the young crater population (Copernican craters and thermal boulders), imprinted after rounding, shows full uniformity without a significant polar excess (0.92 and 1.12), within the error limits of their small samples [D.3].

The pass lines and statistical thresholds were all set blind before the counts were run, and with this the empirical stage of the paper is concluded [D].

PART E

Part E — What remains

This part concludes and summarises the paper [E]. Parts A–D mapped the crater distribution, established the geodynamic mechanism of bipolar rounding with volume decrease, and put it to firm significance tests [E]. The present section brings the findings together in three layers: the physically explained elements (E.1), the preserved anomalies that do not follow from the present model (E.2), and the future work tasks (E.3) [E]. No new measurements are presented in this part; all the numbers and data are taken from the preceding sections [E].

E.1 What is explained: the combined mechanism and the integration of the predictions

A single, exclusive geodynamic process – the flattening of the young Moon while it was attached and rotating with the Earth, and the decay of that flattening after its release, accompanied by volume collapse and compaction of the core – gives a complete, quantitative and systematic answer to six core planetary observations [C.4, E.1]. All the predictions were computed as a blind model before the empirical counts were run [D].

A seventh observation joins the six: a thin, compacted crust beneath the poles that thickens gradually toward the equator. It is the record left in the shell by the same process that crowded the polar craters (C.8, D.6) [E.1].

The sequence of evolution in equations:

The sialic mass consolidated at the tip of the terrestrial pear (ρ≈1,300 kg/m3), and moved outward on a base 6,000 km wide [C.1, C.5, E.1]. As it receded, the base narrowed to 3,000 km and the mass took shape as an independent body stretched extremely between the Earth's gravity inward and the centrifugal force of corotation outward [C.5, E.1]. The peak deformation was reached near the crossing of the corotation line (distance ≈15,818 km), where the body took on a triaxial configuration of 1.8:1.4:1, in an inflated state with a low density of ρ≈1,700 kg/m3 [C.1, C.5, E.1].

The Moon was released about 210 km beyond the corotation line (16,400 km) at the peak of its flattening, reached at that moment, inflated and held by its rigid shell [C.5, C.6, E.1]. After the release, beyond the corotation line, the stretching that had held the flattening – between the Earth's gravity and the point of attachment on the near side, and the centrifugal pull outward – disappeared and the Moon's rotation slowed as it receded; the flattening decayed, the egg part (axis a) and the rotational flattening of the polar axis (c) decayed toward a sphere, and the body rounded with a sharp decrease in volume (a rise in density to 2,600 kg/m³ and beyond, without loss or addition of mass), which reduced the equivalent radius by 13% [C.1, C.3.1, E.1]. The rotational component of the flattening fell to about 1.04 at 30,000 km and about 1.005 at 60,000 km, and the shape froze near 16 Earth radii, leaving today's small fossil flattening [C.5, E.1].

The decay of flattening that crowded the craters took place entirely after the release [E.1]. The dynamic detachment acted like the extraction of a plug: the Moon left the tip of the pear and exposed its openings to space, which caused the collapse of the pressure in the pear and the halt of its elongation, prevented the ejection of a second moon, and scattered ejected material in all directions (C.6) [C.6, E.1]. The flattening itself was held as long as the Moon was attached and rotating with the Earth; the slowing of the spin after release is what undid it, until the shape froze [C.5, E.1].

Breakdown and analysis of the study's basic conclusions

1. The polar-excess anomaly and the variation with crater diameter (a geometric chronological clock):

  • The statistical finding: in the clean count – in which the maria and the SPA basin are removed equally from both sides of the equation ("both sides") to normalise the comparison on a uniform pristine highland crust – the crater density (≥20 km) in the polar caps is 1.20±0.05 times that of the equatorial belt [D.1, E.1]. Divided into isolated size classes, the residual ratio climbs in a consistent order from 1.09 in the 20–30 km class to 1.53 in the class of giant craters of 60–100 km [D.2, E.1].
  • The geodynamic meaning: the inward collapse of the triaxial structure to a spherical shape contracted the local area in the polar regions at the maximum rate (a factor of 0.55×), and thus compressed and concentrated the existing craters closer together [C.3.1, E.1]. The pass line set in advance (1.10−1.60) takes in the finding, together with full coincidence with the 1.21 value of the six-axis model [D.1, E.1]. The climbing trend with diameter is the unequivocal evidence for the existence of a dynamic process along the timeline: the giant craters were imprinted at peak flattening under a maximum pressure profile in the vents, absorbed the full sequence of surface contraction, and therefore today record the maximum density excess [C.4, E.1]. The model of external space impacts is entirely refuted, since it predicts an opposite sign that leaves the poles depleted at 0.80–0.91, a difference standing 6σ−8σ away from the surface data [D.1, E.1].

2. Control of the rigidity of crater dimensions (the tile model):

  • The statistical finding: under the same firm 20 km diameter threshold on both sides, the median diameter of the polar craters is 1.06 times the median of the craters in the equatorial belt (diameters of 32.5 km versus 30.5 km; confidence interval of 95%: 1.01 – 1.12, ruling out equality) [D.2, E.1].
  • The geodynamic meaning: the craters were imprinted on and carried by a solid outer shell that kept its rheological rigidity (η≥1023 Pa⋅s), and they kept their diameter and original rim morphology in full [C.7, E.1]. The surface contraction of rounding was absorbed entirely within the seam spaces between the crustal plates [C.7, E.1]. Had the craters been elastic and contracted together with the surface, the polar median diameter would have been smaller (predicted value 0.79×) owing to craters dropping below the threshold, and the bipolar excess would have been offset and cancelled entirely from the calculation (D.2) [D.2, E.1]. The enrichment in large craters in the polar median is direct confirmation that they kept their size and absorbed the maximum surface contraction during rounding [D.2, E.1].

3. The bipolar axial-symmetry balance:

  • The statistical finding: with the "both sides" geological control mask applied, the remaining density ratio between the southern and northern hemispheres converges exactly to a value of 1.02 in the 15° cap, and the confidence interval contains and balances the equality value (1.00) across the whole family of concentric caps examined (10∘ to 60∘) [D.4, E.1].
  • The geodynamic meaning: the inward-rounding process is governed by self-gravity, and it is completely symmetric about the rotation axis; what the mechanical mechanism brings about at one pole, it reproduces exactly at the opposite pole [D.4, E.1]. The sharp morphological asymmetry observed in the initial raw count (a concentrated north versus a flat south) is not a primary property of the crust, but a transient local distortion arising exclusively from the bias of the mechanical erasure by the South Pole–Aitken basin in the south, which is successfully neutralised [A.8.3, D.4, E.1].

4. The six-axis order and the triaxial geometry:

  • The statistical finding: of the six main axis ends of the body – the sub-Earth point, the anti-Earth point, the two ends of the orbital-motion direction (leading and trailing), and the two poles – the sub-Earth point settles as the sparsest cap on the Moon (148 craters per 10⁶ km² after applying the mask) [A.9]. The poles and sides stand significantly above it in the order [A.9]. Read as an overall geometric shape, the six caps yield an axis ratio of 1.37:1.15:1 for the whole ≥20 km population [A.9, C.3].
  • The geodynamic meaning: the layout of the order proves that the young Moon did not undergo rotational flattening alone; it was extremely stretched along the Earth-line axis (a) between the Earth's gravity inward and the centrifugal pull of corotation outward, while held at the tip of the pear structure [C.5, E.1]. On passing beyond the line and the onset of inward rounding, the two ends of this stretched axis contracted at the minimum rate, while the ring perpendicular to it (passing through both poles and both sides) contracted at the maximum rate [C.3, E.1]. The mechanical contact zone of Paper 3 lies on the near side, around coordinates of 24∘ N,335∘ E, in the space between the sub-Earth point and the north pole [A.9]. The reconstructed 1.37:1.15:1 shape predicts, completely independently and with complete precision, a clean density excess of 1.21 between the caps and the belt, a figure coinciding exactly with the finding measured on the surface (1.19–1.20), without any need to fit free parameters [A.9, C.3].

5. The control record of the young craters:

  • The statistical finding: the two samples of young craters (those imprinted long after the Moon completed its transition to a perfect spherical structure) yield pole/equator ratios of 0.92 and 1.12 [D.3, E.1].
  • The geodynamic meaning: a crustal crater imprinted on the crust after the shape of the body froze and stabilised was never carried on a surface undergoing contraction or compression, and therefore must physically show a uniform distribution without a polar anomaly [D.3, E.1]. The data of the two independent samples agree with this prediction [E.1]. However, owing to their small number (only 10 and 18 craters within the polar caps), the uncertainty intervals are wide and do not allow the 1.20 value of the older population to be ruled out completely [D.3, E.1]. The test is fully consistent with the mechanism, but the definition of a significant and isolated ordering is passed on to the determination of the enlarged sample detailed in section D.3 [D.3, E.1].

6. Reconstruction of the peak-point geometry from the giant craters:

  • The statistical finding: the class of the largest craters, 60–100 km in diameter, carries a density excess that projects back and fixes an original shape of 1.70:1.42:1 [D.2, E.1].
  • The geodynamic meaning: the empirical data confirm the physical prediction and place the moment of maximum deformation at the stage when the body converged onto the 3,000 km base near the corotation line, a shape it reached at the release, before the decay of flattening and the rounding [C.1, C.5, E.1]. The theoretical peak dimensions were set at about 1.8:1.4:1 [C.1, E.1]. The isolated rotational component of the reconstructed shape (b/c=1.42) is exactly the hydrostatic equilibrium shape that a fast spin of 5.5 hours raises on a fluid body with a low density of 1,600–1,750 kg/m3 (highlighted in C.1) [C.1, D.2]. This is exactly the stretched, inflated structure that the equation of volume decrease and surface closure requires geometrically [C.1, C.3]. The giant craters reconstruct this early moment within the bounds of their error intervals [E.1].

Summary of the methodology and the rheological closure

The integration of the parts of the paper is based on firm physical laws and on coherent closure between the parts of the scientific series [E.1]:

1. Analysis of the global shape: the shape of the whole combined population is derived directly from the six-axis data, and predicts the clean-count ratio without any tuning or artificial fitting [C.3, E.1]. The original peak shape is isolated from the giant craters, and its mechanical rotational part is confirmed directly against the Maclaurin relation (Maclaurin Spheroid) under the rotation rate of Paper 2 and the density bounds dictated by the volume decrease (C.1) [C.1, E.1]. The Maclaurin equation is a classical physical law that defines the axis ratio of a uniform rotating fluid body without free parameters; the rotation rates and densities were taken consistently from the earlier papers, and the translation of the geometric dimensions into area-crowding factors is pure mathematics [C.1, E.1].

2. The empirically learned element (the size clock): the only variable learned directly from the data on the surface and not set as a prediction in advance is the specific assignment of each crater-diameter group to its dynamic stage (D.2) [D.2, E.1]. The mechanism physically requires that larger craters form closer to the peak point and absorb the maximum surface contraction, but the determination of the exact numerical ordering (which diameter reflects which moment) is learned from the empirical counts on the surface [D.2, E.1].

3. Unifying the crustal constraints (the C.7 shell): the mechanical crust found in section C.7 to be essential for preserving the crater dimensions is exactly the same crust defined in Paper 3 from an entirely different rationale [C.7, E.1]. In Paper 3 a crust with a high viscosity of η≥1023 Pa⋅s was required to ensure the morphological survival of the craters imprinted while the body was near the Earth; in the present paper, the same rigid shell functions as a mechanical tile that prevents the collapse of crater diameter, and forces the surface contraction to be absorbed in the seam spaces between them [C.7, E.1]. A single structural requirement serves and unites two independent papers in the series [E.1].

Final scientific conclusion:

We now have a unified geodynamic process, governed and fixed by numerical values taken from the earlier papers and by the shape that the craters themselves record around the six axes [E.1]. This process gives a full quantitative answer and explains precisely the density excess, the size ordering (the clock), the axial-symmetry balance, and the spatial axis order of the ancient craters, while remaining fully consistent with the control record of the uniform young craters [E.1].

E.2 Anomalies and findings not explained by the present model

In the course of developing the scientific argument and processing the empirical data, five main observations were recorded that do not follow from, and are not explained by, the rounding mechanism in its present form [E.2]. These findings are isolated and detailed below together with the tools that will decide them in future, in order to block methodological bias and to prevent them from being mistakenly presented as part of the paper's core results [E.2].

1. The anomaly of the biaxial excess of the trailing face

  • The empirical finding on the surface: the crust in the sector of the trailing face (around the coordinates of 90∘ E) is characterised by a sharp density excess compared with the leading face (around 90∘ W) [A.9, E.2]. The numerical difference shows an excess of 1.96 times in the full raw catalogue, and keeps a significance of 1.45 times after applying the filtering mask (A.9) [A.9, E.2].
  • The mechanistic failure and the proposed explanation: the phenomenon reverses the physical expectation of the "space meteorology" model (frontal collection of impactors on a windscreen), since the front of the orbital flight (the leading face) is the sparsest and emptiest in the system [A.9.1, E.2]. The model proposes two alternative geophysical causes [A.9.4, E.2]:
    1. The correlation with local vents: there is a direct link (a ratio of 1.96) between the crater excess and the excess of units and areas of independent maria on the same flank, which function in the model as ejection vents that threw out ballistic returned material that landed in their surroundings [A.9.2, A.9.3].
    2. The dynamic rotational-lag effect (Lag Effect): material ejected forcefully from vents located in other regions of the body experienced a physical lag relative to the fast synchronous rotation rate of the system, and landed behind on the orbital rear (the trailing side) [A.9.4, E.2].
  • The analytical rule: until the full quantitative calculation of the history of ejections, flights and crater yield is completed in section E.3 (item 8) and in Part K of Paper 6, the longitudinal correlation remains a firm requirement of the model, and not an explained result derived from it [E.2].

2. The density anomaly of the far-side crown (the anti-Earth point)

  • The empirical finding on the surface: the crust around the coordinates of the anti-Earth point (the centre of the far side, 0∘,180∘) carries an exceptionally high density of 221 craters per 10⁶ km² after applying the mask [A.9, E.2].
  • The mechanistic failure and the open question: according to the geometric equations of surface contraction (C.3), the two ends of the Earth–Moon axis are the least stretched surfaces of any sector of the tidal ellipsoid, and therefore they must undergo the minimum surface contraction (minimal relaxation) during rounding [C.3, E.2]. The prediction dictates that these two axis ends will be sparse density valleys in the system [E.2]. The sub-Earth point (the near side) matches this physical constraint precisely (148), but the anti-Earth point (the far side) bypasses it entirely and merges with the density level of the poles [A.9, E.2].
  • The analytical rule: the study formulates this finding as an open structural requirement – the crown of the dome of Paper 3 did not undergo contraction or relaxation as an ordinary free end, and the present model does not derive this [E.2]. Decoding the mechanics of the crown is passed on to the investigation of the geometric dynamics of a body fixed at its mechanical base (E.3, item 5) [E.2].

3. The anomaly of the morphological shallowness of the polar craters

  • The empirical finding on the surface: initial geometric measurements of the surface reveal that the craters located in the polar regions in the size classes of 20–100 km are significantly shallower morphologically than corresponding equatorial craters [E.2]. For the 20–30 km group, the depth-to-diameter ratio (d/D) stands at about 0.062 at the poles versus about 0.074 in the equatorial belt [E.2]. The anomaly decays and disappears in the giant craters of 100–300 km [E.2].
  • The mechanistic failure and the open question: the depth-to-diameter ratio is a scale for determining the degree of degradation, with a pristine crater being deep and sharp, and its floor gradually filling with material over time [D.5, E.2]. The present study cannot separate and decode two opposite mechanisms [E.2]:
    1. The mechanical-shortening mechanism (C.7): the result of shortening stresses and compression of the crustal plates around the crater margins during the slow rounding [C.7, E.2].
    2. A late chronological degradation mechanism: an ordinary degradation process of the crust unrelated to rounding [E.2].
  • The analytical rule: these two interpretations must leave distinct geological signatures on the surface (focused tectonic shortening structures around the rims, versus ordinary thermal/isostatic softening with age) [E.2]. Since the morphometric measurement that distinguishes between the two has not yet been carried out, the finding remains outside the scope of the mechanism's solution [E.2].

4. The anomaly of meridional orientation at middle latitudes

  • The empirical finding on the surface: the craters characterised by sharp ellipticity (e>1.2, where e is the ratio of the long axis of the rim to the short axis) at middle latitudes (30∘−60∘) show a tendency to align along the geographic meridian (north to south) with a high frequency of 45%–51%, compared with a frequency of only 20%–25% along the parallel (east to west) [D.5, E.2]. In the equatorial belt the trend reverses [E.2].
  • The mechanistic failure and the open question: the quantitative amplitude of the effect is minimal, amounting to a tenth or less of the geometric deformation that an elastic collapse of the surface would have imposed on the craters (section D.5-d found that the median ellipticity at these latitudes is higher by only about 0.01, compared with a sharp predicted deformation of 0.13–0.40) [D.5, E.2]. Therefore, the first methodological suspect for this anomaly is an optical illumination bias (Sun-Angle Bias) in the catalogue [E.2]. In images taken at a low sun angle (characteristic of high latitudes), a rim facing directly toward the light source and a rim lying in shadow are drawn and measured differently by the mappers, producing a distortion that makes the crater look elongated and stretched in a fixed direction [E.2].
  • The analytical rule: determining the physical meaning depends on a future test: if the meridional orientation survives and persists also under analysis of images illuminated from opposite sun angles and directions, it will be defined as a real crustal property requiring a geodynamic explanation; at present it is outside the model [E.2].

5. The internal crater structure of the South Pole–Aitken basin

  • The empirical finding on the surface: within the SPA basin system, the geographic central core zone holds a clearly low crater density, amounting to only 0.59 (a deficit of about 41%) relative to the control ground located in the ring outside its rim (A.10) [A.10.2, E.2].
  • The analytical rule: the phenomenon is isolated, quantified and empirically confirmed within this paper (A.10), but the physical mechanism, the detailed ellipticity, and the geodynamic dynamics of the basin's formation lie entirely outside the present Part C, and are passed on in full as the exclusive core of the study of Paper 8 (the SPA basin) [A.10.5, E.2].

E.3 Further work and future research tasks

This section brings together the series of steps, analytical treatments and statistical extensions that will turn the remaining components of the LEF model from firm geodynamic requirements into precise and closed physical calculations [E.3]. Each item is defined strictly and ends by stating the exact scientific goal it is expected to prove [E.3]:

1. The model of mechanical shaping with strength (The Rigid Shell Shaping Effect):

  • The substance of the study: the solutions of sections C.1–C.2 assume a purely hydrostatic collapse of a homogeneous fluid [C.1, C.2]; the presence of a stiff crustal shell restrains the two-body deformation and reduces the amplitude of the stretching [E.3]. Applying mechanical strength functions along the rounding sequence will narrow the intervals of the theoretical predictions from below [E.3].
  • What it will show: it will quantify precisely what share of the fluid rotational flattening survived and was actually imprinted on a crust with elastic rigidity, and will derive the minimum bipolar density-excess value that the mechanism can produce – a tight, focused prediction to compare with the measured 1.20 value [E.3].

2. Extended verification of the list of young craters:

  • The substance of the study: replacing the raw input file of section D.3 with the official, verified Table S1 of Mazrouei et al. (2019), together with processing the spatial coordinates of the 1,615 rayed craters of Werner & Medvedev (2010) [D.3, E.3]. Bright ray systems are a pristine sub-crustal record reflecting the youngest impacts on the body [D.3].
  • What it will show: it will establish at a firm level of significance whether the young population is completely uniform across the latitudes within a verified, wide sample, and will bring the control test of D.3 to statistical dimensions that can give an absolute independent decision [D.3, E.3].

3. Solving the two-layer rheological relaxation equation:

  • The substance of the study: developing a dynamic mathematical solution to the two-layer flow problem over the time window of the attached stage (∼108 years), under the parameters of section C.7 – a hot core with a viscosity of η≈1021−1022 Pa⋅s carried beneath a rigid crust with a viscosity of η≥1023 Pa⋅s [C.7, E.3]. The calculation will derive precisely the remaining contraction that was completed and the stress profile fixed in the shell [E.3].
  • What it will show: it will map precisely how much of the share of surface contraction was completed by the core, and exactly how the stiff shell took up and processed the remaining load – the rate of mechanical shortening focused at the poles versus the minimal change in the equatorial belt – in place of the static order-of-magnitude estimates of section C.7 [C.7, E.3].

4. Isolation and processing of the two crustal background topics:

  • The substance of the study: an independent analysis, separated from this model, of two anomalies that were examined and set aside: measuring the rim-elongation measures of elliptical craters at the poles or toward them, and calibrating the bipolar density excess against the marginal belt of Paper 13 instead of the equatorial belt (the marginal belt, without the polar components, hosts a density of 149 craters per 10⁶ km², versus 219 in the caps) [A.11, E.3].
  • What it will show: under dedicated spatial definitions, the first study will determine whether a real residual ellipticity is preserved in the craters beyond the meridional orientation bias of E.2; the second study will derive the pure crowding factor relative to the marginal regions of the near side [E.2, E.3].

5. Deriving the contribution of the tidal stresses (the egg part) from the force vectors:

  • The substance of the study: developing a mechanical solution that decomposes the dimensions of the reconstructed triaxial shape (1.37:1.15:1) and derives the egg part (the stretching along axis a) directly from the two-body force equations, instead of reading it empirically from the six axes [A.9, C.3, E.3]. The calculation will measure the tidal ellipsoid of a body fixed at its mechanical base and its rate of relaxation during recession, together with an examination of its agreement with the ratio of the giant craters (1.84±0.38 in section D.2) [D.2, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will set the dimensions of the tidal axis in a computed, theoretical way for comparison with the order of A.9; it will establish whether the giant craters that exceed the peak shape owe their statistical excess to the early tidal stresses; and it will decode the mechanics of the preservation of the far-side crown (E.2) [E.2, E.3].

6. The absolute tangential crater-spacing test (Nearest-Neighbor Distance):

  • The substance of the study: direct measurement and mapping of the distances to the nearest neighbour (Nearest-Neighbor Distance) as a function of crater diameter, with a continuous statistical comparison between the polar-cap regions and the equatorial belt in the clean count [D.2, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will provide a direct and isolated geometric measure of the closing of the physical spaces between the craters in the crust, constituting definitive proof of surface contraction independent of, and not mathematically derived from, the spatial density measures [E.3].

7. Mapping the tectonic structures and geological imprints in the shell:

  • The substance of the study: mapping and analysing the global latitude distribution of tectonic shortening and compression structures (such as wrinkle ridges and thrust faults) located outside the young mare surfaces, which are the tectonic records that the stiff shell was obliged to leave (C.7) [C.7, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will confirm empirically whether the crust underwent maximum mechanical shortening toward the poles and minimum toward the equator, while confirming the absence of a belt of extensional structures at the equator – a direct geological test of the two-layer model, robust and independent of the crater record [C.7, E.3].

8. Developing the balance equation of the ejection vents and the returned material:

  • The substance of the study: developing the combined quantitative and dynamic calculation for the mare systems at 90° east and 90° west [A.9, E.3]. The analysis will merge the ejection history of each vent, the ballistic flight equations of Paper 6, and the crater-imprinting yield of the returned material (≥20 km) in the landing regions, as a function of radial distance from the centre of the source vent [A.9.4, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will prove mathematically whether the volume of returned material from the vents of the trailing flank (90° E), combined with the momentum trap of the material that lagged behind the rotation and landed behind, provides the energy required to produce the density excess preserved on the trailing side (E.2) – an analytical reversal that will turn the longitudinal correlation from an observational correlation into a result explained by the model [E.2, E.3].

9. The extreme-resolution test of the innermost caps:

  • The substance of the study: enlarging the counting samples within the narrow ∣θ∣≤10∘ cores (currently limited to 86 craters in the north and 36 in the south) by incorporating the next generation of digital topographic catalogues, which allow intact primary craters to be identified and counted below the 20 km diameter threshold [D.4, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will decode the variation of the density-curve profile in the last degrees around the end points of the poles, the sector in which physics predicts the peak of surface contraction and in which the present sample is too small to decide significantly [E.3].

10. A dynamic solution for the compressive stresses on the base and the egg part:

  • The substance of the study: developing an elasto-plastic model that computes how a vertical compressive load of about 3 GPa (prevailing inside the corotation line about 1,000 km before the point) stabilises, restrains and governs a body stretched along the tidal axis, and how the collapse of the residual pressure to 0  GPa on the corotation line affects the release of the egg part (C.6) [C.6, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will define mechanically how a holding base 3,000 km wide preserves the radial stretching deformation against the gravitational forces, and how fast the relaxation of the surface of axis a takes place at the moment the compressive component disappears [C.6, E.3].

11. Computing the stresses in the shell beyond the corotation line:

  • The substance of the study: a quantitative calculation of the profile of tangential stresses generated within the crust along the segment between the corotation line and a distance of 20,100 km, the sector in which the tidal stretching exceeds the fluid stability limit and the rigid shell is forced to absorb the load and stabilise an axis ratio of at most 1.04 [C.1, C.6, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will define the stress curve in the shell along this critical segment, and set it directly against the maximum shear-strength limits of the crustal materials [E.3].

12. Solving the mass balance of the vanishing crust (GRAIL Coherence):

  • The substance of the study: developing a mechanical transport and displacement model that resolves the constraint of area decrease (a global drop of a quarter of the area, and almost half of the polar areas at the peak) against the uniform crustal-thickness data of the GRAIL satellites [C.3.1, C.7, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will establish the physical path by which the crust took up the excess areas that closed at the poles (mechanical thickening, tectonic thrusting, or transfer and transport of molten crustal material into the interior of the soft core) while preserving a uniform thickness profile, without departing from the actual measurements [C.7, E.3].

13. Refining the dimensions of the peak shape using an extended crater catalogue:

  • The substance of the study: enlarging the sample of giant craters of 60–100 km (currently limited to 13 to 68 craters per cap and scattering the peak shape) by using adapted geometric cap sections or incorporating complementary data, to calibrate tightly the parameters a/c and f of the peak shape (C.3) [C.3, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will set the geometry of the triaxial peak shape within a narrow, isolated confidence interval, and set it directly against the solution of the rotational-shape equation of the Maclaurin relation (C.1) [C.1, E.3].

14. Reproducing the five size tests on the triaxial morphology:

  • The substance of the study: recomputing and recalibrating the combined linear factors of section D.5 (the values 0.86, 0.90, 1.08 and the contraction factor of 0.79) together with the ellipticity profile of test D.5-d, using the configuration of the true triaxial peak shape (1.8:1.4:1), instead of the biaxial oblate spheroid of 1.69 [D.5, E.3].
  • What it will show: it will put the five crustal morphometric tests under the exact scale of the triaxial shape, and set their final agreement percentages [E.3].

A shell of varying thickness:

  • The substance of the research: the area calculation of C.3 treats the surface as a uniform sheet [C.3]; external rotational differentiation gives the shell a thickness that varies from the poles to the equator [C.8]. A quantitative model of a shell of varying thickness will follow the contraction of the rounding stage through such a shell [E.3].
  • What it will show: how much of the polar crater excess follows from the change of shape and how much from the contraction concentrated in the thin polar shell, and the thickness profile of the shell at each stage [E.3].

Availability of the digital code and the database of the study

All the calculations, the processing of the counts, the computation of cap and belt areas, the solutions of the equilibrium equations of the Maclaurin spheroid and the Roche ellipsoid, the matrices of relaxation factors, the triaxial fitting functions for the six main caps, the volume-decrease data and the net-pull graphs of section C.6 are reproduced in full, in a closed and clean form, by the scripts of the official reproduction package of the model [E.3]. The package is developed in Python 3, using the numpy and scipy libraries, and is deposited in full alongside the scientific series (a dedicated Zenodo record identifier will be assigned and published later) [E.3].
